title: Forcing a Letter Suppresses Refusal: Mechanistic Evidence from WMDP
comment: Accepted to BlackboxNLP 2026 (EMNLP 2026 workshop). 17 pages, 15 figures
summary: Safety benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) commonly use multiple-choice question (MCQ) format. However, prior studies documented that MCQ format reduces refusal rates, which may significantly affect the safety behavior of the model. We provide a first mechanistic explanation of this effect on the Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy (WMDP) dataset across two models - Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B. First, we use the tuned lens technique to show that when processing MCQ the model commits to an answer-letter token very quickly, which is in contrast to the gradual refusal build-up in open-ended formats. Additionally, we observe that activations on the MCQ format lie roughly 3x further from the refusal direction, compared with their open-ended counterparts. Moreover, ablating the attention heads that carry the MCQ format answer increases the refusal, which is a direct evidence that the MCQ answer-selection competes with refusal. These findings indicate that MCQ safety scores primarily measure knowledge capabilities and do not assess the safety-mechanisms.

AI.tldr: Forcing a multiple-choice answer letter suppresses refusal in LLMs; a mechanistic analysis on WMDP with Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B shows that MCQ safety scores mainly measure knowledge capability rather than safety mechanisms.
AI.motivation: MCQ is a common format for safety benchmarks, but prior studies found it reduces refusal rates, so MCQ safety scores may not reflect safety behaviour, and no mechanistic explanation of this effect existed.
AI.method: Tuned lens analysis of how the model commits to an answer-letter token during MCQ processing, comparison of activations with the refusal direction against open-ended counterparts, and ablation of the attention heads that carry the MCQ answer, on WMDP across two models.
AI.result: In MCQ the model commits to an answer-letter token very quickly, unlike the gradual refusal build-up in open-ended formats; MCQ activations lie roughly 3x further from the refusal direction; ablating the answer-carrying attention heads increases refusal.
AI.conclusion: MCQ answer selection competes with refusal, so MCQ safety scores primarily measure knowledge and do not assess safety mechanisms.

title: FinEvolveKG: Controlled and Attributable Prompt Evolution for Financial Knowledge Graph Construction
comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables
summary: Financial institutions construct knowledge graphs (KGs) from shared SEC 10-Ks to serve risk analysis, portfolio management, and investment research, whose analytical needs differ. Extraction must adapt without fragmenting shared grounding, typing, and temporal rules. Hand-authored persona prompts and fine-tuning add cost. Weight-free prompt optimization offers an alternative, but unconstrained evolution of a monolithic prompt can rewrite shared rules alongside persona guidance, obscuring changes and complicating review. We introduce FinEvolveKG, a KG-construction harness separating reusable general and persona-policy blocks and mechanically confining GEPA, a reflective prompt optimizer, to the designated block. During persona adaptation, the approved general block remains byte-stable and every optimizer edit is localized to a separately versioned persona policy. A dual objective balances generic temporal-KG quality with persona-relevant facts, motifs, and multi-hop connectivity. We evaluate five mutation scopes on ticker-disjoint 10-K splits, with three seeds for the persona-conditioned arms (v3-v5) across three personas. On the three-seed mean, the complete two-stage block-constrained workflow (v4) improves over the frozen prompt baseline (v1) by 19.4-30.9% and over the tested unconstrained full-prompt workflow (v5) by 2.2-6.4%, leading v5 on both objective components and winning all nine paired-seed comparisons with the lowest seed variance in every persona. Without further optimization, v4 also exceeds v5 across all evaluated out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts. An SME audit supports using the generated triplets as ground truth; a blinded two-SME audit favors v4 over v5 in 70.1% of contrast-enriched judgments. These results show that mechanically attributable evolution can coexist with strong empirical performance, without attributing the gains causally to the boundary.

AI.tldr: FinEvolveKG confines GEPA prompt optimization to a persona-specific block of a knowledge-graph construction prompt, keeping the shared general block byte-stable; the two-stage block-constrained workflow (v4) beats the frozen baseline by 19.4-30.9% and the unconstrained full-prompt workflow (v5) by 2.2-6.4%.
AI.motivation: Financial institutions need persona-specific knowledge graphs built from shared SEC 10-Ks, but unconstrained prompt evolution rewrites shared extraction rules together with persona guidance, obscuring changes and complicating review; hand-written persona prompts and fine-tuning add cost.
AI.method: A harness that separates reusable general and persona-policy prompt blocks and mechanically restricts the reflective optimizer GEPA to the persona block, with a dual objective balancing generic temporal-KG quality against persona-relevant facts, motifs and multi-hop connectivity, evaluated on ticker-disjoint 10-K splits across five mutation scopes.
AI.result: On the three-seed mean, v4 improves over the frozen prompt v1 by 19.4-30.9% and over v5 by 2.2-6.4%, leads v5 on both objective components, wins all nine paired-seed comparisons with the lowest seed variance in every persona, and exceeds v5 on all out-of-distribution shifts without further optimization; in a blinded two-SME audit, v4 is preferred over v5 in 70.1% of contrast-enriched judgments.
AI.conclusion: Mechanically attributable prompt evolution can coexist with strong empirical performance, although the gains are not attributed causally to the block boundary.

title: Compression of Emotion in Language Model Representations
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have been evaluated on their ability to identify emotions expressed in text and produce fluent emotional language. However, output predictions alone do not reveal how fine-grained emotion distinctions are organized internally. We study seven LLMs on GoEmotions, an English Reddit dataset annotated with 27 fine-grained emotion categories plus neutral. We compare model predictions and emotion-prompted final-token representations with the 28 GoEmotions categories and with coarser emotion-family and sentiment groupings. We find a consistent pattern of $\textit{overcompression}$ relative to the fine-grained GoEmotions taxonomy. Under the tested KMeans protocol, when we cluster their hidden representations without using emotion labels, the clearest split is into two groups that largely separate positive from negative emotion. Coarser emotion groupings are also recovered with fewer clusters than the full 28-category taxonomy. Yet linear probes retain substantial fine-grained predictive information. These results suggest that fine-grained emotion information remains accessible even though broader affective structure more strongly organizes the unsupervised geometry.

AI.tldr: Probing seven LLMs on GoEmotions shows that their hidden representations overcompress fine-grained emotion categories: unsupervised clustering mainly separates positive from negative emotion, yet linear probes still retain substantial fine-grained information.
AI.motivation: Evaluations of LLM emotion recognition rely on output predictions, which do not reveal how fine-grained emotion distinctions are organized inside the model.
AI.method: Model predictions and emotion-prompted final-token representations of seven LLMs on GoEmotions (27 emotion categories plus neutral) are compared with the 28-category taxonomy and with coarser emotion-family and sentiment groupings, using KMeans clustering without emotion labels and linear probes.
AI.result: A consistent overcompression relative to the fine-grained taxonomy; the clearest unsupervised split separates positive from negative emotion; coarser groupings are recovered with fewer clusters than the 28 categories; linear probes retain substantial fine-grained predictive information.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained emotion information remains accessible, but broader affective structure more strongly organizes the unsupervised geometry of LLM representations.

title: Contextuality and Contradictions: Exploring Real-World Identifications of AI-Generated Writing
summary: As AI-generated content spreads into nearly every domain of human interaction, practices and discourses of AI detection, both formal and informal, have become an everyday part of how people interact with text and with each other. In this paper, we explore the real-world practices and discourses of AI identification that have emerged in response to a shifting discursive landscape where the human provenance of a text can no longer be taken for granted. We pair qualitative coding with computational analysis of lexical change, grounded in linguistic anthropological perspectives on language and communication, to investigate AI identifications among English Wikipedia editors and students. We find that these identifications draw on a diversity of evidentiary types, from discrete textual features and judgments about content to circular sense-making claims and presumptions about the author's moral character, and that they are contradictory, dynamic, and contextually dependent. In practice, what often motivates an AI identification is not the presence of any specific textual element, but pragmatic infelicity: a perceived mismatch between the elements present and those deemed appropriate within the text's particular context. Consequently, real-world identifications of AI-generated writing do not merely neutrally point out the perceived presence of "AI-like" features, but can be leveraged as a discursive resource to maintain and define sociolinguistic norms: what can be said in a given context, what is appropriate, and, ultimately, what is human. Further, the design and implementation of systems and tools that treat AI-likeness as a context-free property of text may therefore inherit, and enforce at scale, the norms of whichever contexts they were trained on.

AI.tldr: A qualitative coding study paired with computational lexical-change analysis finds that AI-writing identifications by English Wikipedia editors and students are contradictory, dynamic and context-dependent, and are often driven by pragmatic infelicity rather than specific textual features.
AI.motivation: As AI-generated content spreads, the human provenance of text can no longer be assumed, and informal and formal AI detection practices have become routine, yet their evidence and discourse are poorly understood.
AI.method: Qualitative coding combined with computational analysis of lexical change, grounded in linguistic anthropological perspectives, applied to AI identifications among English Wikipedia editors and students.
AI.result: Identifications draw on diverse evidence, from discrete textual features and judgments about content to circular sense-making claims and presumptions about the author's moral character; they are contradictory, dynamic and contextually dependent; what usually motivates them is pragmatic infelicity, a perceived mismatch with what is appropriate in the context.
AI.conclusion: AI identifications act as a discursive resource that defines sociolinguistic norms and what counts as human, so tools that treat AI-likeness as a context-free property of text may enforce the norms of their training contexts at scale.

title: RL-ATTACK: A Generalized Black-Box Adversarial Attack on Language Models via Reinforcement Learning
comment: Accepted as a regular paper at IEEE EdgeCom 2026
summary: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit vulnerabilities to adversarial perturbations that can induce unintended responses. These vulnerabilities can be identified via intentional attacks and subsequently used to improve model safety. In black-box settings where gradients are inaccessible, existing methods tend to guess adversarial transformations using external knowledge, ignoring the information provided by the target model. To mitigate this, we propose a trainable black-box framework based on reinforcement learning, which learns from the target model to generate tailored adversarial transformations. We demonstrate that our approach achieves lower post-attack accuracy, greater query efficiency and better semantic preservation on both natural language inference and generative Q&A tasks. On natural language inference, it drives post-attack accuracy to 2% within 20 queries. Against generative language models, our trained attacker consistently achieves lower post-attack accuracy than the untrained attacker and wins in 4 out of 6 settings when compared to a strong optimization-based baseline. We further experiment with multiple reward designs and training settings, and we find that no design or setting is consistently dominant. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: RL-Attack is a trainable black-box adversarial attack that uses reinforcement learning on the target model's responses to generate tailored adversarial transformations, reducing post-attack accuracy on natural language inference to 2% within 20 queries.
AI.motivation: Black-box attacks on language models usually guess transformations from external knowledge and ignore the information the target model provides, which limits their effectiveness and query efficiency.
AI.method: A trainable black-box attacker, trained with reinforcement learning on the target model, that generates tailored adversarial transformations; multiple reward designs and training settings are explored.
AI.result: Lower post-attack accuracy, greater query efficiency and better semantic preservation on natural language inference and generative Q&A; on NLI, post-attack accuracy reaches 2% within 20 queries; against generative models the trained attacker beats the untrained attacker and wins in 4 of 6 settings against a strong optimization-based baseline; no reward design or setting is consistently dominant.
AI.conclusion: Learning from the target model is an effective, query-efficient route to black-box attacks that can be used to find vulnerabilities and improve safety, though no single reward design is consistently best.

title: Structuring Survey Histories for LLM Digital Twins: A Controlled Study of Background, Decision Procedure, and Evaluation Profiles
comment: 10 pages. Camera-ready version for SocialAgent: Second Workshop on Large Language Models for Social Reasoning and Simulation, NeurIPS 2026
summary: LLM-based digital twins aim to predict how individuals would respond in new settings from representations of their prior responses. Existing evidence that compression of survey histories need not reduce predictive accuracy suggests that representation structure, rather than information volume alone, may be an important design choice. We study BDE, a fixed representation that organizes each respondent's survey history into Background, Decision procedure, and Evaluation. We evaluate it on Twin-2K-500 (Toubia et al., 2025) by predicting each respondent's held-out answers on 17 tasks. In a paired evaluation with 100 respondents, a fully inferred BDE profile improves overall accuracy over the raw survey transcript by 1.27 percentage points (pp) on gpt-5.4-nano (p < 0.01) and 1.19 pp on gpt-5.4-mini (p < 0.001). Three analyses then examine the schema, extraction depth, and component composition. Against a length-matched free-form profile written from the same transcript by the same extractor, BDE improves pricing accuracy on both simulators (2.15 pp on nano, p < 0.01; 1.38 pp on mini, p < 0.05), while its overall advantage is significant only on nano (1.05 pp, p < 0.05). Allowing deeper inference during extraction yields no statistically significant gain on either simulator. By contrast, adding Evaluation to a Background--Decision procedure profile improves overall accuracy by 1.44 pp on nano (p < 0.001) and 1.22 pp on mini (p < 0.001). These results indicate that the advantage over raw transcripts is not explained by compression or length alone, and attribute it primarily to profile composition rather than deeper extraction.

AI.tldr: BDE organizes each respondent's survey history into Background, Decision procedure and Evaluation; on Twin-2K-500 this profile improves held-out prediction accuracy over raw transcripts by about 1.2-1.3 percentage points on gpt-5.4-nano and gpt-5.4-mini.
AI.motivation: LLM digital twins predict individual responses from prior responses, and compressed survey histories can retain predictive accuracy, which suggests representation structure may matter more than information volume.
AI.method: A fixed three-part representation (BDE) of survey histories, evaluated on Twin-2K-500 by predicting held-out answers on 17 tasks for 100 respondents, with comparisons against a length-matched free-form profile, variants of extraction depth and analyses of component composition.
AI.result: A fully inferred BDE profile improves overall accuracy over raw transcripts by 1.27 pp on gpt-5.4-nano (p<0.01) and 1.19 pp on gpt-5.4-mini (p<0.001); against the length-matched free-form profile it improves pricing accuracy on both simulators, but its overall advantage is significant only on nano (1.05 pp, p<0.05); deeper extraction gives no significant gain; adding Evaluation to Background-Decision procedure improves overall accuracy by 1.44 pp on nano and 1.22 pp on mini.
AI.conclusion: The advantage over raw transcripts is not explained by compression or length alone; it comes mainly from profile composition, especially the Evaluation component, rather than from deeper extraction.

title: Semantic Conditional Similarity (SCS): A Formal Mathematical Framework
comment: 34 pages, 6 figures, 8 tables, to be submitted for publication
summary: Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) operates on document pairs, returning a single scalar per comparison. In a multi-document setting where several sources may have contributed to one or more targets, pairwise STS cannot disentangle each source's marginal semantic contribution from their shared vocabulary. In this paper, Semantic Conditional Similarity (SCS) is introduced as a conditional form of STS that computes similarity between two documents after eliminating semantic elements shared with a third via set-theoretic operations. SCS makes four contributions: 1) it introduces directionality, partitioning pairwise relations into lateral (inter-source) and vertical (source-to-target) classes; 2) conditioning induces role-dependent asymmetry by extending the comparison domain from unordered pairs to ordered, conditioned triples of a target, a reference, and a conditioning document; 3) SCS introduces inter-document conditioning by subtracting shared content from a third document, complementing the intra-document conditioning in recent C-STS work; and 4) the set-theoretic decomposition achieves threshold-free partitioning of shared and residual content, requiring no arbitrary similarity cutoff. Although developed for the $n \to 1$ configuration, the framework extends to $1 \to n$ via vertical role reversal and to $m \to n$ via independent composition of source- and target-side conditioning. With the established $1 \to 1$ case, these span the full spectrum of document cardinality. SCS scores should be interpreted ordinally, as rankings of marginal contributions rather than absolute measurements. The broader implication is that metric space axioms commonly assumed in similarity formalizations constrain expressiveness in role-differentiated multi-document settings, and that extending the domain to conditioned triples can recover information that pairwise-symmetric comparisons suppress.

AI.tldr: Semantic Conditional Similarity (SCS) is a formal framework that computes the similarity of two documents after removing content shared with a third document, giving directional, threshold-free comparisons for multi-document settings.
AI.motivation: Pairwise semantic textual similarity returns one scalar per pair and cannot separate each source's marginal contribution from vocabulary shared with other documents when several sources contribute to one or more targets.
AI.method: Set-theoretic conditioning that subtracts elements shared with a third document, yielding lateral (inter-source) and vertical (source-to-target) relation classes, ordered conditioned triples of target, reference and conditioning document, and extensions to 1-to-n and m-to-n configurations.
AI.result: The abstract reports no experiments; it states four contributions: directionality, role-dependent asymmetry from conditioned triples, inter-document conditioning that complements intra-document conditioning in C-STS work, and threshold-free partitioning of shared and residual content; the framework is said to span the full range of document cardinalities together with the 1-to-1 case.
AI.conclusion: SCS scores should be read ordinally as rankings of marginal contributions, and metric space axioms constrain expressiveness in role-differentiated multi-document settings, which conditioned triples can recover.

title: Guardrail Erosion in Domain Fine-Tuned Large Language Models: A Paired Audit of Knowledge-Centric Abstention in Biomedical LLMs
comment: To be published in the Proceedings of the 6th Machine Learning for Health Symposium (ML4H 2026), PMLR volume 346
summary: The number of domain fine-tuned models, particularly in the biomedical domain, is rapidly expanding. Fine-tuning promises high-performing models at a fraction of the cost of training a base model, but it can also produce unintended behavioral changes. Multiple studies have shown that safety guardrails can erode with fine-tuning, yet large-scale studies across model architectures, data mixtures, and fine-tuning methodologies remain limited. Where prior work in this space has studied value-centric refusal, this work focuses on knowledge-centric abstention. We audit 25 biomedical domain fine-tuned large language models against 11 paired base checkpoints on MedAbstain and ClinDet-Bench to evaluate the impact of fine-tuning on knowledge-centric abstention. We find that defined appropriate abstention measured by these benchmarks, already low in base models (median 8.3% on MedAbstain), falls further after fine-tuning (median 4.2%, decreasing in 21 of 25 pairs on MedAbstain), and that the magnitude and direction of change are heterogeneous across pairs. These results motivate fine-tuning methods that improve domain-specific capability while preserving appropriate caution.

AI.tldr: An audit of 25 biomedical domain fine-tuned LLMs against 11 paired base checkpoints finds that knowledge-centric abstention, already low in base models, falls further after fine-tuning, with the median dropping from 8.3% to 4.2% on MedAbstain.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning can cause unintended behavioural changes and erode safety guardrails, but large-scale studies of knowledge-centric abstention across architectures, data mixtures and fine-tuning methods are limited, since prior work focused on value-centric refusal.
AI.method: A paired audit comparing 25 biomedical fine-tuned models with 11 base checkpoints on MedAbstain and ClinDet-Bench, measuring defined appropriate abstention.
AI.result: Median appropriate abstention on MedAbstain is 8.3% for base models and 4.2% after fine-tuning, decreasing in 21 of 25 pairs; the magnitude and direction of change are heterogeneous across pairs.
AI.conclusion: Fine-tuning can erode appropriate abstention, which motivates fine-tuning methods that improve domain-specific capability while preserving appropriate caution.

title: Richness Is Not Evenness: Ordered Renyi Crossings under Self-Training
summary: Recursive self-training of language models, a setting studied in model collapse, can reduce vocabulary while making frequent words, mostly function words, less dominant. We fine-tune English GPT-2 on its own output for nine generations, vary the training-data sampling temperature, and measure every model with one fixed sampler. As training temperature rises, Renyi entropy changes turn from loss to gain at distinct temperatures: min-entropy first, then collision entropy, Shannon entropy and observed richness. Between the outer crossings, word types fall while the most-common word becomes less dominant. Untruncated training at T = 1 lies in this interval: at 13,000 words, generation 9 has 24% fewer types than generation 0 yet collision entropy is 0.91 bits higher. The ordering persists with a finer grid, different measurement samplers, a fixed word budget and five fresh training seeds. Min-entropy again crosses before richness in four further settings (in Hindi only at interpolated roots) and in 12 of 13 distinct measurements under eight text representations. Next-token identities and a categorical simulation isolate decoding and sampling effects; the crossing order remains empirical. Fine-tuning on human text can produce the same split while likelihood improves, and no single order's sign reliably identifies worse likelihood across the tested settings. We recommend reporting entropy profiles at stated budgets with an independent quality measure.

AI.tldr: Recursive self-training of GPT-2 on its own output, with varied training sampling temperature, produces Renyi entropy crossings in a fixed order (min-entropy first, then collision entropy, Shannon entropy and observed richness), so word types can fall while the most common word becomes less dominant.
AI.motivation: Model-collapse studies show that recursive self-training can reduce vocabulary while making frequent words less dominant, and entropy and richness measures can move in different directions, so their joint behaviour needs examination.
AI.method: English GPT-2 fine-tuned on its own output for nine generations at varied training temperatures, with every model measured by one fixed sampler; checks include a finer temperature grid, different measurement samplers, fixed word budgets, five fresh seeds, further languages and text representations, and next-token and categorical simulations.
AI.result: Between the outer crossings word types fall while the most common word becomes less dominant; at T=1 and 13,000 words, generation 9 has 24% fewer types than generation 0 yet collision entropy is 0.91 bits higher; min-entropy crosses before richness in four further settings and in 12 of 13 distinct measurements under eight text representations.
AI.conclusion: Entropy profiles can split in ways that do not indicate quality, and no single order's sign reliably identifies worse likelihood, so the authors recommend reporting entropy profiles at stated budgets together with an independent quality measure.

title: From Procedures to Permissions: Learning Precise Subagent Authorization from Agent Skills
summary: As language agents tackle increasingly complex tasks, they increasingly rely on multiple agents to coordinate specialized work, requiring decisions not only about what each subagent should do but also which tools and workspace resources it should access. Existing agent systems provide mechanisms for controlling tools and execution environments, but do not directly specify the resources required by each delegated subtask. Moreover, task outcomes and execution trajectories alone provide limited supervision for determining whether a subagent has received appropriate permissions. We observe that Agent Skills encode procedural knowledge describing the operations, tools, and files required at each step, providing a natural source of supervision for authorization. Building on this observation, we synthesize tasks and step-by-step procedures from Skills, execute them through subagent delegation in interactive environments, and use verified trajectories to construct training data for task execution and authorization. On ClawArena-Team, our method improves tool permission precision by 13.4 percentage points and workspace permission precision by 24.1 percentage points, while increasing overall task success by 11.6 percentage points for Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. On Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SkillsBench, our method remains competitive with existing agent data synthesis approaches. These results show that the procedural knowledge embedded in Agent Skills provides a source of supervision for precise subagent orchestration that task outcomes alone cannot provide.

AI.tldr: The paper synthesizes tasks and step-by-step procedures from Agent Skills, runs them through subagent delegation and trains on verified trajectories to learn subagent tool and workspace permissions, raising Qwen3.5-35B-A3B's tool permission precision by 13.4 points and workspace permission precision by 24.1 points.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent systems must decide which tools and workspace resources each delegated subagent may access, but existing mechanisms do not specify the resources each subtask requires, and task outcomes or trajectories give limited supervision for permissions.
AI.method: Procedural knowledge in Agent Skills, which describes the operations, tools and files needed at each step, is used as supervision: tasks and procedures are synthesized from Skills, executed via subagent delegation in interactive environments, and verified trajectories build training data for task execution and authorization.
AI.result: On ClawArena-Team, tool permission precision rises by 13.4 points, workspace permission precision by 24.1 points and overall task success by 11.6 points for Qwen3.5-35B-A3B; on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SkillsBench the method remains competitive with existing agent data synthesis approaches.
AI.conclusion: Procedural knowledge embedded in Agent Skills is a source of supervision for precise subagent orchestration that task outcomes alone cannot provide.

title: On the Incompleteness of do-calculus for Universal Identifiability
summary: We study the problem of causal effect identification from an arbitrary set of observational and/or interventional distributions, which we call Universal Identifiability (uID). The uID problem generalizes existing classical identifiability (ID) and general identifiability (gID) problems, which considered the identification problem from either mere observational distributions or a specific type of interventional distributions. Prior research has established graphical criteria to determine when a causal effect is identifiable in ID and gID problems. Moreover, algorithms that leverage do-calculus and basic probability manipulations have been proposed to compute these effects. Consequently, it has been shown that do-calculus is both sound and complete in these problems. Despite these well-established results, a formal definition of what it means for the do-calculus to be complete does not exist. We propose a rigorous formalization for the completeness of the do-calculus and show that the completeness results in previous work remain valid. However, for more general problems, such as uID, the rules of do-calculus are no longer complete. This is perhaps the reason why the uID problem has remained open thus far.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes what completeness of do-calculus means and shows that for Universal Identifiability (uID), which combines observational and interventional distributions, the rules of do-calculus are no longer complete.
AI.motivation: Do-calculus is known to be sound and complete for classical identifiability (ID) and general identifiability (gID), but no formal definition of its completeness existed, and the more general uID problem has remained open.
AI.method: A rigorous formalization of completeness for do-calculus, checked against the completeness results of prior ID and gID work, and an analysis of the broader uID problem.
AI.result: The completeness results of previous work remain valid under the formalization; for uID the rules of do-calculus are not complete.
AI.conclusion: The incompleteness for uID may be the reason this problem has remained open, so do-calculus alone is not sufficient for universal identifiability.

title: Using an LLM to Tackle Difficult Cases in NER for Nepali Tweets
summary: Named entity recognition (NER) is challenging for social media data in a low-resource language. LLMs often lag behind pretrained language models (PLMs) in NER performance, but they show promise in handling cases that PLMs struggle with. Using a dataset of Nepali tweets, we split the test set into "easy" and "hard" cases using token probabilities from a fine-tuned pretrained language model (PLM). We then evaluate an LLM on the hard test cases using 16 different prompt configurations. We find that selecting examples based on semantic similarity and increasing the number of examples improves F1 score by almost 10 points from the baseline configuration. Although the LLM underperforms the PLM on the full and easy test sets, it surpasses the PLM on the hard test set, resulting in an improved score when the two models are combined.

AI.tldr: Using token probabilities from a fine-tuned PLM to split Nepali tweet NER test cases into easy and hard sets, the paper finds that an LLM with 16 prompt configurations underperforms overall but surpasses the PLM on the hard set, so combining the two models improves the score.
AI.motivation: LLMs usually lag behind pretrained language models (PLMs) on NER, but may handle the cases PLMs struggle with, which matters for NER on social media text in a low-resource language.
AI.method: A Nepali tweet NER test set is split into easy and hard cases by token probabilities from a fine-tuned PLM; an LLM is then evaluated on the hard cases under 16 prompt configurations that vary example selection and the number of examples.
AI.result: Selecting examples by semantic similarity and increasing their number improves F1 by almost 10 points over the baseline configuration; the LLM underperforms the PLM on the full and easy test sets but surpasses it on the hard set, and combining the two models yields an improved score.
AI.conclusion: An LLM can complement a PLM on hard NER cases in a low-resource language, and the combined system scores better than the PLM alone on this dataset.

title: Beyond Truncation? Entailment-Licensed Elision and the Limits of Semantic Preservation in LLM Decoding
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables
summary: Instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs) answer at greater length than a request needs. We ask whether a training-free controller inside the decoding loop can remove that surplus while preserving content, judged against the simplest possible baseline: truncating the model's own answer to the same length. An entropy-gated logits processor removes 25.5-34.9% of tokens on MT-Bench development questions and 19.9-34.2% on a sealed test split within pre-registered BERTScore non-inferiority margins, yet we prove and confirm by audit that its output is always a prefix of the unmodified answer: the saving is truncation. A survey of 23 training-free mechanism families finds none that selects content better than truncation without oracle labels. We therefore introduce Entailment-Licensed In-Decoding Elision (ELIDE), which, at each sentence boundary, withholds a span from the reader only when a natural-language inference model judges it entailed by the text already shown, while leaving the model's generation unchanged. ELIDE beats matched-length truncation on three model families, but reading 936 of its elisions on 670 public prompts shows that 59% harm the answer, a failure that no automatic measure detects. Scoping the licence to its discourse unit reduces the harmful share to about one elision in ten on two fresh tests.

AI.tldr: An entropy-gated decoding controller that trims LLM answers turns out to output only prefixes, which is equivalent to truncation; the paper introduces ELIDE, which withholds sentence spans entailed by already-shown text, beating matched-length truncation while 59% of its elisions harm the answer, a share reduced to about one in ten by scoping the licence to discourse units.
AI.motivation: Instruction-tuned LLMs answer at greater length than requests need; a training-free decoding controller could remove the surplus while preserving content, but the simplest baseline is truncation, and no training-free mechanism selects content better than truncation without oracle labels.
AI.method: An entropy-gated logits processor, audited to be prefix-only; a survey of 23 training-free mechanism families; and ELIDE, which at each sentence boundary withholds a span from the reader only when a natural-language inference model judges it entailed by the text already shown, leaving generation unchanged, with the licence scoped to the discourse unit.
AI.result: The entropy-gated controller removes 25.5-34.9% of tokens on MT-Bench development questions and 19.9-34.2% on a sealed test split within pre-registered BERTScore margins, but its output is always a prefix of the unmodified answer; no surveyed family selects content better than truncation without oracle labels; ELIDE beats matched-length truncation on three model families, yet reading 936 of its elisions on 670 public prompts shows 59% harm the answer, a failure no automatic measure detects; scoping the licence to its discourse unit reduces the harmful share to about one in ten on two fresh tests.
AI.conclusion: Automatic measures do not detect harmful elisions, so token savings alone do not show that content is preserved; scoping the entailment licence to discourse units substantially reduces harm.

title: Language, Not Code Abstraction: Natural-language Training Shapes Brain-aligned Geometry
comment: Accepted for the Neureps Workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Code-trained language models produce positive brain scores, which raises the question of whether abstract structure learned from programming languages can substitute for natural-language training. We trained 25 GPT-2-small models on TinyStories, Python, C functions, x86-64 assembly, and the corresponding machine code, and scored them using a shared tokenizer and encoding procedure against matched random-weight models. On Pereira-243 and Tuckute2024, TinyStories exceeds the mean of the four code models by $\Delta r = 0.053$ and $0.059$ (Holm-corrected $p<0.001$), while code training leaves alignment near the random-weight level. The language advantage is benchmark-specific: Blank2014 shows no corrected language-code difference, and Fedorenko2016 shows no language benefit. Geometry tracks the encoding result on Pereira-243: TinyStories seeds converge on the most similar representations, and its fit-free correspondence with neural dissimilarity peaks at $\rho = 0.14$, twice the code and random-weight levels. Binary-trained models have about three effective dimensions, so seed agreement alone does not imply neural correspondence. Updating only the embedding matrix on English improves mean-over-depth alignment for every code model more than an equal update on its own corpus. Within this architecture and training setup, natural-language training produces a distinct representational geometry with closer neural correspondence on Pereira-243

AI.tldr: GPT-2-small models trained on TinyStories align better with brain responses on Pereira-243 and Tuckute2024 than models trained on Python, C, x86-64 assembly or machine code, which stay near random-weight level.

title: Failure Profiling and Reachable Trajectory Selection for Reasoning Distillation
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. The source code and trained weights are available at \url{this https URL}
summary: Training smaller language models on reasoning solutions generated by a larger teacher model is the prevailing approach for transferring mathematical reasoning capabilities. However, the student tends to overfit the output distribution of the teacher and generalizes poorly when its own behavior at inference time deviates from the training data. Recent methods attempt to bridge this gap by incorporating error data, yet the corrective trajectories still reflect the reasoning patterns of the teacher, which the student cannot reliably reproduce, leaving the distribution mismatch largely unresolved. We propose a method, Failure Profiling and Reachable Trajectory Selection (FPRT), built on the insight that effective training data should be jointly determined by what the student fails on and what it can realistically learn. Our method first profiles the failure behavior of the student on each problem through repeated sampling, characterizing it in terms of error rate and error consistency to reveal qualitatively distinct failure modes. Each mode demands a fundamentally different training signal. The diagnosed mode then guides candidate generation from the teacher via distinct prompting strategies tailored to each failure type. Among the correct candidates, our method selects the one whose initial reasoning steps after the point of divergence are most reproducible by the student. These first corrective steps constitute the primary bottleneck, while the remaining steps follow an already corrected context and can therefore be continued more readily. This contrasts with standard reranking approaches, which score the trajectory as a whole and thereby dilute the signal at the critical reasoning transition. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves the SOTA performance across the five benchmarks on both student backbones.

AI.tldr: FPRT profiles a student model's failures on each problem through repeated sampling, asks the teacher for corrective candidates tailored to the failure mode, and selects the candidate whose first post-divergence steps the student can most reproduce, reaching state-of-the-art performance on five benchmarks with two student backbones.
AI.motivation: Students distilled from a teacher's reasoning overfit the teacher's output distribution and generalize poorly, and error-corrective trajectories still reflect teacher patterns the student cannot reliably reproduce, so the distribution mismatch remains unresolved.
AI.method: Repeated sampling characterizes each problem's failure by error rate and error consistency to reveal distinct failure modes; each mode guides teacher candidate generation through a tailored prompting strategy; among correct candidates, selection favours the one whose initial corrective steps after the divergence point are most reproducible by the student, rather than reranking whole trajectories.
AI.result: The method achieves state-of-the-art performance across five benchmarks on both student backbones.
AI.conclusion: Effective training data should be determined jointly by what the student fails on and what it can realistically learn, and focusing on the first corrective steps targets the critical reasoning transition.

title: Does Reasoning Improve Psychological Depth in Large Language Models?
summary: Benchmark gains from reasoning-enhanced large language models encourage the assumption that these models should broadly perform better on complex generative tasks, but this remains underexplored in open-ended, creative domains shaped by nuances of reader experience. We tested this assumption through the lens of psychological depth in short stories. We compared DeepSeek-R1 vs. DeepSeek-V3, our closest available contrast for reasoning-oriented post-training, and GPT-5 vs. GPT-4o, through 60 blinded pairwise evaluations in which seven human annotators and an ensemble LLM-as-a-Judge rated prompt-matched story outputs. Human evaluations showed no universal reasoning advantage: GPT-5 was slightly preferred over GPT-4o (60.0-62.9% across two reasoning-effort settings), whereas DeepSeek-R1 fell behind DeepSeek-V3 (42.9%). Although this pattern was marked by low inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's $\alpha = 0.070$), our annotation-quality checks suggested genuine evaluative subjectivity, plausibly reflecting distinct annotator decision schemes rather than annotation failure. In contrast, the LLM-as-a-Judge showed a strong pro-reasoning bias (98.3% of pairs vs. 55.2% of human votes), consistent across its five configurations and partly tracking sentence length. These findings suggest that, at the frontier, reasoning-related quality differences are small enough to be dominated by reader subjectivity, and that LLM-as-a-Judge evaluators can obscure this subjectivity in nuanced creative-generation tasks.

AI.tldr: In 60 blinded pairwise comparisons of short stories, humans show no universal reasoning advantage: GPT-5 is slightly preferred over GPT-4o, while DeepSeek-R1 falls behind DeepSeek-V3; an LLM-as-a-Judge instead strongly favours the reasoning-oriented side.
AI.motivation: Benchmark gains from reasoning-enhanced LLMs encourage the assumption that they should also do better on open-ended creative tasks, which is underexplored for psychological depth in short stories.
AI.method: 60 blinded pairwise evaluations of prompt-matched story outputs by seven human annotators and an ensemble LLM-as-a-Judge in five configurations, comparing DeepSeek-R1 with DeepSeek-V3 and GPT-5 with GPT-4o under two reasoning-effort settings.
AI.result: GPT-5 was preferred over GPT-4o in 60.0-62.9% of human judgments across the two reasoning-effort settings, while DeepSeek-R1 won only 42.9% against DeepSeek-V3; inter-annotator agreement was low (Krippendorff's alpha = 0.070); the LLM judge preferred the reasoning side in 98.3% of pairs versus 55.2% of human votes, consistently across its five configurations and partly tracking sentence length.
AI.conclusion: At the frontier, reasoning-related quality differences are small enough to be dominated by reader subjectivity, and LLM-as-a-Judge evaluators can obscure this subjectivity in nuanced creative-generation tasks.

title: The Invisible Gap: Romanized Indic Generation Fails Where Automatic Metrics Succeed
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. All authors contributed equally
summary: Hundreds of millions of Indians communicate with digital systems in romanized Latin characters -- typing "aap kaise hain" rather than native script -- yet romanized Indic generation is absent from NLP benchmarks and evaluation frameworks. We demonstrate that automatic metrics (BGE-M3, BERTScore) systematically misrepresent the quality of romanized Hindi, Telugu, and Kannada generation. We evaluate four LLMs (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 2.5-flash, Qwen3.5-35B) on 142 OpenAssistant query-response pairs. On a 72-response diagnostic subset, native speakers rate GPT-5.5 1.43 points higher than Claude Opus 4.8 on a 12-point rubric, whereas their full-dataset BGE-M3 means differ by only 0.004. Two distinct model-specific failure modes emerge: Gemini produces script spillage (16.9% of Telugu responses leak native script), while Qwen collapses to English-only output (16.2% of Kannada responses). We introduce a failure-aware evaluation policy that assigns zero to empty outputs, script-corrupted responses, and instruction collapses -- revealing failures metrics alone cannot detect. Our results show that evaluating romanized Indic generation requires a coordinated bundle: semantic similarity, script compliance, failure coverage, and native-speaker acceptability.

AI.tldr: Automatic metrics such as BGE-M3 and BERTScore misrepresent the quality of romanized Hindi, Telugu and Kannada generation: native speakers rate GPT-5.5 well above Claude Opus 4.8 while the full-dataset BGE-M3 means differ by only 0.004, so the paper proposes a failure-aware evaluation policy.
AI.motivation: Hundreds of millions of Indians use romanized Latin script with digital systems, yet romanized Indic generation is absent from NLP benchmarks and evaluation frameworks.
AI.method: Four LLMs (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 2.5-flash, Qwen3.5-35B) are evaluated on 142 OpenAssistant query-response pairs; native speakers rate a 72-response diagnostic subset on a 12-point rubric; a failure-aware policy assigns zero to empty outputs, script-corrupted responses and instruction collapses.
AI.result: Native speakers rate GPT-5.5 1.43 points higher than Claude Opus 4.8 on the diagnostic subset, while their full-dataset BGE-M3 means differ by 0.004; Gemini leaks native script in 16.9% of Telugu responses and Qwen collapses to English-only output in 16.2% of Kannada responses; the failure-aware policy reveals failures that metrics alone cannot detect.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating romanized Indic generation requires a coordinated bundle of semantic similarity, script compliance, failure coverage and native-speaker acceptability.

title: MARS: Training Multilingual Search Agents for Retriever-Free Evidence Acquisition
summary: Existing multilingual retrieval-augmented generation relies heavily on learned retrievers and similarity-based ranking from multilingual collections, which are vulnerable to cross-lingual retrieval errors and indexing overhead. In this paper, we explore retriever-free multilingual search, where the model directly interacts with raw corpora through executable shell commands. This paradigm shifts the bottleneck to multilingual search action generation, where exact search is sensitive to entity surface forms and outcome-only supervision provides limited guidance for multi-turn search. To address these challenges, we propose MARS, a multilingual search agent in direct corpus interaction (DCI) with reinforcement learning (RL). MARS introduces corpus-native entity grounding to recover reliable lexical anchors from corpus evidence, mitigating failure to retrieve evidence. Meanwhile, we present a redundancy-aware search reward to encourage concise and effective search trajectories, addressing training collapse in RL of multilingual scenarios. Experiments show that \ours~consistently outperforms strong retrieval-based and DCI baselines, while demonstrating robust cross-lingual generalization and substantially reducing redundant corpus interactions.

AI.tldr: MARS is a multilingual search agent that interacts directly with raw corpora through executable shell commands, trained with reinforcement learning; it outperforms retrieval-based and direct corpus interaction baselines and substantially reduces redundant corpus interactions, without a learned retriever.
AI.motivation: Existing multilingual RAG depends on learned retrievers and similarity-based ranking, which suffer cross-lingual retrieval errors and indexing overhead, while exact search is sensitive to entity surface forms and outcome-only supervision gives limited guidance for multi-turn search.
AI.method: Retriever-free multilingual search in direct corpus interaction (DCI) through shell commands, trained with RL; corpus-native entity grounding recovers reliable lexical anchors from corpus evidence, and a redundancy-aware search reward encourages concise and effective trajectories.
AI.result: MARS consistently outperforms strong retrieval-based and DCI baselines, generalizes robustly across languages, and substantially reduces redundant corpus interactions.
AI.conclusion: Direct corpus interaction with grounded entities and a redundancy-aware reward is a viable retriever-free alternative for multilingual evidence acquisition, and the reward addresses training collapse in multilingual RL.

title: AlienBench: A Benchmark of Structural Novelty in Language Model Outputs
comment: 21 pages, 2 figures, 13 tables
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for creative tasks such as writing, design, and idea generation. For these uses, it matters whether a model's ideas depart from familiar examples or stay close to them. Novelty is one standard measure of creativity, and current creativity evaluations ask human experts or LLM judges to rate how novel an output is. However, these ratings have no fixed reference for what counts as novel (or, in other terms, departure from the familiar). Measuring this departure requires a task with known familiar defaults. The structured imagination task from cognitive psychology is such a task. In this creativity test, people imagine a creature from another planet. The departure from features of Earth animals, such as bilateral symmetry and legs as mode of locomotion, is used as measure of creativity. We introduce AlienBench, a benchmark that adapts the structured imagination task to language models. Models describe alien creatures, and a panel of three LLM judges extracts ten biological features from the description and labels them as either Earth-typical or a departure. The sum of feature departures is the score of a description, from 0 to 10. Each model describes alien creatures under six prompt conditions that vary the framing of the task and the planetary environment. Each model generates 30 descriptions per condition (180 in total), and its overall score is the mean across these descriptions. We evaluate 10 language models, from frontier to open-weight models. Overall scores range from 3.28 (GPT-6 Luna) to 6.55 (Ministral 3 14B). Interestingly, open-weight models score higher than proprietary models in this task (5.40 vs. 4.58). Under the baseline prompt, the models depart from Earth defaults more often on average than 100 human participants on every feature. We release all prompts, generations, judge outputs, and scores.

AI.tldr: AlienBench adapts the structured imagination task to LLMs, scoring how far alien creature descriptions depart from Earth-typical biology on ten features; overall scores across 10 models range from 3.28 (GPT-6 Luna) to 6.55 (Ministral 3 14B), and open-weight models score higher on average than proprietary ones.
AI.motivation: Novelty ratings in creativity evaluations have no fixed reference for what counts as novel, so a task with known familiar defaults is needed to measure departure from the familiar.
AI.method: Models describe alien creatures under six prompt conditions that vary the framing and planetary environment, 30 descriptions per condition; three LLM judges extract ten biological features from each description and label each as Earth-typical or a departure, and the summed departures give a 0-10 score.
AI.result: Overall scores range from 3.28 (GPT-6 Luna) to 6.55 (Ministral 3 14B); open-weight models average 5.40 versus 4.58 for proprietary models; under the baseline prompt, models depart from Earth defaults more often on average than 100 human participants on every feature.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark gives a fixed reference for measuring structural novelty in model outputs, and the authors release all prompts, generations, judge outputs and scores.

title: PhoPunct: A Large-Scale Benchmark of Transformer Architectures for Vietnamese Punctuation Restoration
comment: Accepted at PACLIC 40 (2026)
summary: Vietnamese punctuation restoration is often evaluated on relatively small benchmarks, limiting conclusions about how architectural choices scale with data volume. We present a controlled benchmark on News and Novels corpora containing 22.1 million labeled tokens (19.9M News and 2.2M Novels). We evaluate 17 architectures formed from four pretrained Transformer backbones and optional bidirectional long short-term memory (Bi-LSTM) and conditional random field (CRF) layers, together with a PhoBERT-large-Bi-LSTM-CRF model, PhoPunct. Every model is trained for eight epochs with the same learning rate and without architecture-specific tuning. Under this fixed budget, adding Bi-LSTM and CRF layers does not reliably improve macro F1: in seven of eight matched domain-backbone comparisons, a plain Transformer classifier matches or outperforms its Bi-LSTM-CRF counterpart. PhoPunct obtains the best News result (61.35), whereas XLM-R with a CRF obtains the best Novels result (50.18), exceeding PhoPunct (48.97). These results show that the value of recurrent and structured-prediction heads depends on their optimization regime and motivate explicit separation between architectural improvements and improvements due to architecture-specific tuning. Our source code is available at: this https URL

AI.tldr: Across a 22.1-million-token Vietnamese News and Novels benchmark, 17 Transformer architectures are compared under a fixed training budget, and adding Bi-LSTM and CRF layers does not reliably improve macro F1 over a plain Transformer classifier.
AI.motivation: Vietnamese punctuation restoration is usually evaluated on small benchmarks, which limits conclusions about how architectural choices scale with data volume.
AI.method: A controlled benchmark of 17 architectures built from four pretrained Transformer backbones with optional Bi-LSTM and CRF layers, plus PhoPunct (PhoBERT-large-Bi-LSTM-CRF), each trained for eight epochs with the same learning rate and no architecture-specific tuning.
AI.result: In seven of eight matched domain-backbone comparisons, a plain Transformer matches or outperforms its Bi-LSTM-CRF counterpart; PhoPunct gets the best News score of 61.35, while XLM-R with a CRF gets the best Novels score of 50.18, above PhoPunct's 48.97.
AI.conclusion: The value of recurrent and structured-prediction heads depends on the optimization regime, which motivates separating architectural improvements from improvements due to architecture-specific tuning.

title: Calibrated concept profiles: making the reading of a model's neurons a measurement
comment: 25 pages, 5 figures, 11 tables. Dataset: AtlasOpenCoder, tag v1, doi:https://doi.org/10.57967/hf/11472. Code: this https URL
summary: Interpretability has largely moved from reading a model's neurons directly to reading a second model trained on the first: a probe, a sparse autoencoder, a crosscoder. The move answered real faults -- mixed meanings, thresholds without a unit, readings that did not transfer from one study to the next -- but gave up what a direct reading alone provides: nothing trained in between, the neurons themselves named, and a reading that can be repeated and compared. Here the direct reading is made a measurement. A neuron's activation varies with the prompt, so its reading is a distribution over a population of stimuli. We declare that population: every factor around a target construct is drawn at its rate in a reference corpus and logged. From the declared distribution we generate a battery of prompts, and draw it twice. From the battery we compute the calibrated concept profile, one number per neuron, stated in units of the neuron's own spread on ordinary input; the two draws give every number a noise unit. Before the profile is read, a fixed set of checks licenses the battery on the model, and the smallest change the profile can resolve across training checkpoints is measured. Realised for Python on OpenCoder-1.5B and followed across checkpoints spanning two trillion training tokens, the profile gives what the alternatives do not report: a unit on every number, a chance level for every comparison, and which neurons carry a construct at every checkpoint. The battery, the code and the data behind every result are released.

AI.tldr: Proposes calibrated concept profiles, which turn reading a model's neurons directly into a repeatable measurement by declaring a stimulus population and scoring each neuron in units of its own spread on ordinary input. Applied to OpenCoder-1.5B across checkpoints spanning two trillion training tokens, it gives every number a unit and a chance level.
AI.motivation: Interpretability has moved from reading neurons directly to training probes, sparse autoencoders and crosscoders, which fix mixed meanings and unitless thresholds but lose the direct reading, the named neurons and repeatable comparison.
AI.method: The stimulus population is declared by drawing every factor around a target construct at its rate in a reference corpus and logging it; a prompt battery is generated from it and drawn twice to give a noise unit; one calibrated concept profile number per neuron is computed; fixed checks license the battery on the model and the smallest resolvable change across checkpoints is measured.
AI.result: Realised for Python on OpenCoder-1.5B across checkpoints spanning two trillion training tokens, the profile reports a unit on every number, a chance level for every comparison, and which neurons carry a construct at every checkpoint.
AI.conclusion: A direct neuron reading can be made a measurement with units, chance levels and repeatability; the battery, code and data behind the results are released.

title: Representational drift in a code model: behaviour settles, which neurons carry it does not
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Dataset: AtlasOpenCoder, tag v1, doi:https://doi.org/10.57967/hf/11472. Code: this https URL
summary: In neuroscience, representational drift is a change in which neurons carry a representation while behaviour stays the same; we measure its analogue in OpenCoder-1.5B during pretraining, for 169 Python constructs over two trillion tokens at a constant learning rate, with a noise unit on every change, at checkpoints as close as 1,000 training steps. For 16 of the 169, those whose grammar fixes a next token, the loss at those positions reaches its floor within the first 4% of training, while the model's reliance on the neurons carrying them grows to the end: removing them costs 0.06, 0.25 and 0.40 nats more than removing a random set, at 4 billion, 84 billion and 2 trillion tokens. Which neurons carry a construct never settles: for all 169 the carrier set is still changing at the last checkpoint, and an abrupt settling at any date from 84 billion to 1.5 trillion tokens, or a gradual one before 500 billion, would have been detected in 99% of injected cases. The set measured at 84 billion tokens, removed at the end, cannot be separated from a random set, so the function is carried by whichever neurons are current. Up close the change is a persisting pool and a changing sample: a neuron that leaves a construct's set returns at three times the rate of a matched neuron, and no set reassembles. The hypothesis we fixed in advance, that the carriers settle, is refuted; we discuss candidate causes and name the experiment that would separate them.

AI.tldr: Measures representational drift in OpenCoder-1.5B during pretraining for 169 Python constructs and finds that behaviour settles early while the neurons carrying each construct never settle. The hypothesis fixed in advance, that the carriers settle, is refuted.
AI.motivation: In neuroscience, representational drift is a change in which neurons carry a representation while behaviour stays the same; the authors ask whether an analogue exists in a code model during pretraining.
AI.method: Checkpoints as close as 1,000 training steps over two trillion tokens at a constant learning rate, with a noise unit on every change; loss at grammar-fixed positions and ablation of carrier neurons compared against random sets; injected-change tests of how reliably a settling would be detected; tracking of which neurons belong to each construct's set.
AI.result: For 16 of the 169 constructs, those whose grammar fixes a next token, loss reaches its floor within the first 4% of training while reliance on their carriers grows; removing them costs 0.06, 0.25 and 0.40 nats more than removing a random set, at 4 billion, 84 billion and 2 trillion tokens. For all 169 the carrier set is still changing at the last checkpoint, and an abrupt or gradual settling would have been detected in 99% of injected cases. The set measured at 84 billion tokens, removed at the end, cannot be separated from a random set. A neuron that leaves a construct's set returns at three times the rate of a matched neuron.
AI.conclusion: The function is carried by whichever neurons are current, so the change is a persisting pool with a changing sample rather than settled carriers; the authors discuss candidate causes and name an experiment that would separate them.

title: Khmer PFGen-Bench: Building a Judge-Free Benchmark for Open-Ended Generation in a Low-Resource Language
summary: Benchmarks for open-ended generation often rely on large language model (LLM) judges, whose reliability in low-resource languages is uncertain. We introduce Khmer PFGen-Bench, to our knowledge the first judge-free benchmark for multi-sentence answers to questions composed directly in Khmer, a low-resource language. Khmer PFGen-Bench adapts the scorer of PFGen-Bench, a benchmark for Japanese that scores responses with keyword rules and n-gram statistics from LLM-generated references. This scoring requires references that are both valid and varied, which LLMs may not produce in Khmer, so we examine how to build such references. We find that post-trained models can give more valid but less varied references than their base variants, and that mixing model families increases variety for the same number of references. Using references from post-trained models in nine families, the benchmark yields model rankings that are stable across reference sets and consistent with a native speaker's ratings. These findings offer guidance for building judge-free benchmarks in other low-resource languages.

AI.tldr: Introduces Khmer PFGen-Bench, a judge-free benchmark for multi-sentence answers to questions written in Khmer, which scores responses with keyword rules and n-gram statistics against LLM-generated references. Model rankings are stable across reference sets and consistent with a native speaker's ratings.
AI.motivation: Open-ended generation benchmarks often rely on LLM judges whose reliability in low-resource languages is uncertain, and the keyword and n-gram scorer needs references that are both valid and varied, which LLMs may not produce in Khmer.
AI.method: Adapts the scorer of PFGen-Bench, a Japanese benchmark, to Khmer; compares references from post-trained models with those from their base variants; tests whether mixing model families increases the variety of references for a fixed number.
AI.result: Post-trained models give more valid but less varied references than their base variants, and mixing model families increases variety for the same number of references. Using references from post-trained models in nine families, the benchmark yields model rankings that are stable across reference sets and consistent with a native speaker's ratings.
AI.conclusion: The findings offer guidance for building judge-free benchmarks in other low-resource languages.

title: KLEAR: Knowledge-Matched LLM Evaluation in Korean across Application Requirements via Controlled Benchmark Transformation
comment: 34 pages, under review
summary: Existing Korean benchmarks for Large Language Models (LLMs) evaluate performance across diverse knowledge domains, but their accuracy scores cannot distinguish whether incorrect responses arise from a lack of required knowledge or a failure to apply that knowledge correctly. Our analysis of existing Korean benchmarks reveals that most questions can be answered through factual recall alone, while those demanding greater application also differ in required knowledge, making it difficult to isolate application ability. To address this, we introduce KLEAR, a framework that constructs knowledge-matched contrasts by varying application demand while preserving the required knowledge. During construction, KLEAR identifies the knowledge underlying each source question as an explicit anchor bundle to guide generation of questions requiring more complex application. Generated candidates then undergo automated and human validation, with iterative revision based on evaluation feedback. Experiments demonstrate that the resulting knowledge-matched sets largely satisfy the intended constraints, enabling controlled evaluation across diverse LLMs. These evaluations reveal that increasing application demand exposes failures that persist even when the required knowledge is provided.

AI.tldr: Presents KLEAR, a framework that builds Korean question sets in which application demand varies while the required knowledge is held fixed, so that application ability can be separated from factual recall. The knowledge-matched sets largely meet their constraints and expose application failures that persist even when the required knowledge is provided.
AI.motivation: Korean LLM benchmarks mix knowledge and application: most questions can be answered by factual recall alone, so accuracy cannot tell a lack of required knowledge from a failure to apply it.
AI.method: Identifies the knowledge underlying each source question as an explicit anchor bundle and uses it to guide generation of questions demanding more complex application; generated candidates undergo automated and human validation, with iterative revision based on evaluation feedback.
AI.result: The resulting knowledge-matched sets largely satisfy the intended constraints and enable controlled evaluation across diverse LLMs. Increasing application demand exposes failures that persist even when the required knowledge is provided.
AI.conclusion: Application failures are not explained by missing knowledge alone, so knowledge-matched contrasts allow evaluation to separate the two causes.

title: DUET: Dual-Sparse Inference for Block Diffusion Language Models
summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) enable parallel token generation through iterative denoising, yet their inference remains costly due to repeated attention over a growing historical prefix and repeated processing of the entire current generation block. Historical attention becomes increasingly expensive as generation progresses, while all current-block positions are propagated through the Transformer at every denoising step even though only a small fraction are typically resolved at that step. In this paper, we introduce Duet, a training-free dual-sparse inference framework that addresses these challenges through prefix Key-Value (KV) sparsity and early query sparsity, respectively. Specifically, Duet exploits the concentration and cross-step stability of historical attention within each generation block to construct a compact historical KV subset that is reused across denoising steps. For query sparsity, Duet predicts update positions from shallow representations and propagates only the corresponding queries through the suffix Transformer layers, avoiding deep computation at positions unlikely to be updated in the current step. Experiments show that Duet maintains competitive accuracy while achieving 1.34$\times$/2.83$\times$ end-to-end/per-step speedups on LLaDA2.1-mini and 2.41$\times$/4.72$\times$ on SDAR-8B-Chat-b32 at a 32K context length.

AI.tldr: Proposes DUET, a training-free dual-sparse inference framework for block diffusion language models that sparsifies prefix attention and propagates only a few queries through the suffix layers. It reaches 1.34x end-to-end and 2.83x per-step speedups on LLaDA2.1-mini and 2.41x and 4.72x on SDAR-8B-Chat-b32 at a 32K context length, with competitive accuracy.
AI.motivation: Diffusion language model inference is costly because attention repeatedly covers a growing historical prefix and all current-block positions pass through the whole Transformer at every denoising step, although only a small fraction are resolved at each step.
AI.method: Prefix KV sparsity builds a compact historical KV subset within each generation block, using the concentration and cross-step stability of historical attention, and reuses it across denoising steps. Early query sparsity predicts update positions from shallow representations and propagates only their queries through the suffix Transformer layers.
AI.result: Competitive accuracy with speedups of 1.34x end-to-end and 2.83x per-step on LLaDA2.1-mini, and 2.41x end-to-end and 4.72x per-step on SDAR-8B-Chat-b32, both at a 32K context length.
AI.conclusion: Removing redundant prefix attention and deep computation at positions unlikely to be updated makes block diffusion decoding substantially faster without any training.

title: Multilingual Artificial Datasets for AI-Driven Cardiology: the CliTe and ParaCliTe corpora
summary: Background and Aims. Comparable, multilingual, validated cardiology corpora are critical to advance trustworthy natural language processing (NLP) models for cardiology but such resources are scarce due to privacy concerns. This study aimed to cover this gap by presenting suitable artificial corpus creation guidelines and by releasing 3 multilanguage corpora. Methods. Following purpose-specific publicly-available corpus construction guidelines, cardiologists from 7 European hospitals generated artificial clinical records in Czech, Dutch, English, Italian, Romanian, Spanish and Swedish, ensuring clinical diversity and sex balance, resulting in the CliTe corpus. A CliTe subset underwent a multi-stage manual translation into the other 6 languages, resulting in the parallel ParaCliTe corpus, while the remaining reports were automatically translated, constituting ParaCliTe Silver. Results. CliTe is a collection of 699 artificial cardiology reports, mostly outpatient notes (340 documents), discharge reports (263), and inpatient notes (89), describing fictional patients with ischaemic heart disease (199 patients), heart failure (188), and valvular disease (79), among others. ParaCliTe contains reports from 94 fictitious patients, each available in seven languages with sentence-level alignment, resulting in 658 documents. The corpus mainly comprises discharge reports (322 documents), and outpatient (196) and inpatient (140) notes, describing patients with heart failure (399 documents), ischaemic heart disease (287), and valvular disease (238). Empirical results illustrate the utility of ParaCliTe and highlight the limitations of state-of-the-art NLP models adapted to the cardiology domain. Conclusions. The creation of multilingual, equitable and realistic corpora of artificial patients capable of strengthening NLP performance for cardiology is feasible when supported by detailed guidelines.

AI.tldr: Releases CliTe, 699 artificial cardiology reports written by cardiologists from seven European hospitals, and ParaCliTe, a parallel corpus of 94 fictitious patients in seven languages with a silver automatically translated extension, together with guidelines for building such corpora.
AI.motivation: Comparable, validated, multilingual cardiology corpora are needed to build trustworthy NLP models, but real clinical records are scarce because of privacy concerns.
AI.method: Following public corpus construction guidelines, cardiologists from seven European hospitals generated artificial clinical records in Czech, Dutch, English, Italian, Romanian, Spanish and Swedish, with clinical diversity and sex balance. A CliTe subset was manually translated in several stages into the other six languages to form ParaCliTe; the remaining reports were automatically translated to form ParaCliTe Silver.
AI.result: CliTe contains 699 reports, mostly outpatient notes (340), discharge reports (263) and inpatient notes (89), describing fictional patients with ischaemic heart disease, heart failure and valvular disease among others. ParaCliTe contains 658 documents from 94 fictitious patients, each available in seven languages with sentence-level alignment. Empirical results illustrate the utility of ParaCliTe and the limitations of state-of-the-art NLP models adapted to cardiology.
AI.conclusion: Creating multilingual, equitable and realistic corpora of artificial patients is feasible for cardiology NLP when supported by detailed guidelines.

title: Asymmetric Correspondence Learning for Lexical and Style Embeddings: Interpreting Latent Space via Acoustic Features
comment: Accepted to Spoken Language Technology 2026. 6 pages
summary: Self-supervised speech embeddings jointly encode lexical, speaker, and prosodic information, complicating feature isolation. We introduce Asymmetric Correspondence Learning (ACL), distilling HuBERT features into separate Acoustic Word Embeddings (AWEs) and Acoustic Style Embeddings (ASEs) via a split-latent correspondence bottleneck. Through probing and clustering evaluations on single-word utterances, we demonstrate that substantial variance from extrinsic sources remains encoded within each latent space, despite linear probing indicating the information has been stripped. Whilst the AWE space exhibits cohesive lexical clustering (AP$\approx$0.90, Fisher$\approx$6.28), linear probing on the ASE space achieves 97.9\% speaker accuracy across a diffuse topology (Fisher$\approx$1.01), yet preserves substantial lexical variance (Fisher$\approx$0.86) that remains linearly unrecoverable (0.17\%). To explain these findings, we apply group-level permutation feature importance over eGeMAPS acoustic features, finding that AWEs partition by vocal tract filters and ASEs by $F_0$ dynamics. These findings suggest that standard diagnostic benchmarks may be insufficient for verifying feature isolation, as substantial speech structure can be retained even when it remains entirely hidden from probes.

AI.tldr: Introduces Asymmetric Correspondence Learning, which distils HuBERT features into separate acoustic word embeddings and acoustic style embeddings through a split-latent bottleneck. Substantial extrinsic variance remains in each space, and permutation importance attributes the word space to vocal tract filters and the style space to F0 dynamics.
AI.motivation: Self-supervised speech embeddings jointly encode lexical, speaker and prosodic information, which complicates isolating each kind of feature.
AI.method: A split-latent correspondence bottleneck distils HuBERT features into acoustic word embeddings (AWEs) and acoustic style embeddings (ASEs); probing and clustering are evaluated on single-word utterances; group-level permutation feature importance over eGeMAPS acoustic features is used to explain the findings.
AI.result: The AWE space shows cohesive lexical clustering (AP about 0.90, Fisher about 6.28). Linear probing on the ASE space reaches 97.9% speaker accuracy over a diffuse topology (Fisher about 1.01) yet preserves substantial lexical variance (Fisher about 0.86) that is linearly unrecoverable (0.17%). AWEs partition by vocal tract filters and ASEs by F0 dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Standard diagnostic benchmarks may be insufficient for verifying feature isolation, since substantial speech structure can remain even when it is hidden from probes.

title: Syn2DRE: Synergistic Dual Teacher-Student Framework for Document-level Relation Extraction
summary: Document-level Relation Extraction (DocRE) aims to identify relations between entities across a document but typically relies on costly large-scale annotations. While pseudo-labelling enables the use of low-quality data, existing methods often suffer from inefficiency and confirmation bias. To address these challenges, we propose Syn2DRE, a semi-supervised framework that combines self-supervised learning with cross-supervision in a lightweight teacher-student architecture to produce more reliable pseudo-labels. Additionally, we introduce a unified end-to-end training strategy to further improve efficiency of the framework. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that Syn2DRE consistently outperforms prior state-of-the-art semi-supervised DocRE methods.

AI.tldr: Proposes Syn2DRE, a semi-supervised framework for document-level relation extraction that combines self-supervised learning with cross-supervision in a lightweight teacher-student architecture to produce more reliable pseudo-labels. It consistently outperforms prior state-of-the-art semi-supervised DocRE methods on multiple benchmarks.
