AI.motivation: Document-level relation extraction relies on costly large-scale annotation; pseudo-labelling can use low-quality data, but existing methods suffer from inefficiency and confirmation bias.
AI.method: A teacher-student architecture combining self-supervised learning with cross-supervision to generate more reliable pseudo-labels, plus a unified end-to-end training strategy to improve efficiency.
AI.result: Syn2DRE consistently outperforms prior state-of-the-art semi-supervised DocRE methods on multiple benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Cross-supervised pseudo-labelling in a lightweight teacher-student design, trained end to end, offers a more efficient and reliable route to semi-supervised DocRE.

title: A Spiking Neural Model of the Mental Lexicon: Representations, Similarity Structure, and Associative Retrieval in Perception and Production
comment: 28 pages, 3 figures; code, lexical data and recorded simulations available on GitHub; ancillary figure-generation scripts and provenance documentation
summary: A neural account of lexical access requires an explicit distinction between the structure of lexical representations, the associations linking representational levels, and the activity generated during retrieval. This paper specifies a spiking neural implementation of the mental lexicon within the Neural Engineering Framework and Semantic Pointer Architecture. Conceptual and phonological form representations are constructed recursively from relational graphs, whereas lemma representations provide independent lexical identities. The implementation contains 613 lexical entries and supports two directed processing pathways: perception maps a phonological form to its associated concept via a lemma, whereas production maps a concept to its associated phonological form via a lemma. Each pathway combines two associative-memory variants, winner-take-all (WTA) selection (competition) and thresholded transfer, and uses 199,400 leaky integrate-and-fire neurons. We formalize within-level similarity, cross-level associative retrieval, and the interpretation of decoded activity. Simulations show successful retrieval of eight selected words from the lexicon in both processing directions, with retrieval evaluated against all 613 lexical entries. These simulations use complete phonological forms as input for perception and complete concepts as input for production, illustrating lexical retrieval through the corresponding processing pathways. This paper provides a transparent description of lexical representations and neural retrieval mechanisms, supported by accessible code, lexical data, and online simulation documentation.

AI.tldr: Specifies a spiking neural implementation of the mental lexicon within the Neural Engineering Framework and Semantic Pointer Architecture, supporting perception from phonological form to concept and production from concept to phonological form via lemmas. Simulations retrieve eight selected words in both directions against a 613-entry lexicon.
AI.motivation: A neural account of lexical access needs an explicit distinction between the structure of lexical representations, the associations linking representational levels, and the activity generated during retrieval.
AI.method: Conceptual and phonological form representations are built recursively from relational graphs, with lemmas providing independent lexical identities. Each of two directed pathways combines winner-take-all selection and thresholded transfer, implemented with 199,400 leaky integrate-and-fire neurons; within-level similarity, cross-level associative retrieval and the interpretation of decoded activity are formalised.
AI.result: Simulations successfully retrieve eight selected words in both processing directions, with retrieval evaluated against all 613 lexical entries, using complete phonological forms as input for perception and complete concepts as input for production.
AI.conclusion: The paper gives a transparent description of lexical representations and neural retrieval mechanisms, with code, lexical data and online simulation documentation released.

title: An Effective Spoken Language Understanding Approach Leveraging Query-Adaptive Intent Detection
comment: Accepted for oral presentation at TAAI 2026. 6 pages
summary: Large language models enable fine-tuning-free spoken language understanding (SLU) through in-context learning, but direct query-based retrieval may select semantically similar yet intent irrelevant demonstrations. This paper presents Query-Adaptive Intent Detection via Prototype Extraction (APEX), a two-stage retrieval framework that first selects candidate intents using intent-level prototypes and then retrieves contextual exemplars within the selected intent space. Experiments on the SLURP dataset evaluate joint SLU performance using Exact Match Accuracy (EMA) under full-transcript and perplexity-stratified conditions, with additional retrieval analysis on ASR-generated transcripts. Compared with query-based retrieval, APEX improves EMA by 4.34 and 3.97 percentage points with Qwen3 4B and Gemma-3-4B, respectively, on full transcripts. Under high-perplexity inputs, APEX also yields EMA gains of 7.66 and 2.13 percentage points. Retrieval analysis further indicates that prototype-guided candidate selection achieves higher ground truth intent coverage across multiple input conditions.

AI.tldr: Proposes APEX, a two-stage retrieval framework for in-context spoken language understanding that first selects candidate intents using intent-level prototypes and then retrieves exemplars within the selected intents. On SLURP it improves exact match accuracy over query-based retrieval by 4.34 and 3.97 points with Qwen3 4B and Gemma-3-4B on full transcripts.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning-free SLU with LLMs through in-context learning depends on demonstrations, but direct query-based retrieval may select semantically similar demonstrations whose intents are irrelevant to the query.
AI.method: Two-stage retrieval: candidate intents are chosen with intent-level prototypes, then contextual exemplars are retrieved within the selected intent space. Evaluation uses exact match accuracy (EMA) under full-transcript and perplexity-stratified conditions, plus retrieval analysis on ASR-generated transcripts.
AI.result: Compared with query-based retrieval, APEX improves EMA by 4.34 and 3.97 points with Qwen3 4B and Gemma-3-4B on full transcripts. Under high-perplexity inputs it yields gains of 7.66 and 2.13 points. Prototype-guided candidate selection achieves higher ground-truth intent coverage across multiple input conditions.
AI.conclusion: Restricting exemplar retrieval to prototype-selected intents improves in-context SLU accuracy, including on high-perplexity inputs, without fine-tuning.

title: On the Effectiveness and Limitations of Open-Weight LLMs for Low-Resource Offensive Language Detection in Danish
comment: Accepted to the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Big Data (BigData 2026)
summary: We study the effectiveness and robustness of open-weight large language models (LLMs) for Danish offensive language detection, an underexplored low-resource task. We evaluate four model families (Llama, Mistral, Gemma, and Qwen) across eleven prompting strategies spanning five design categories, cross-prompt generalization, Danish orthographic variation, and robustness under balanced and naturally imbalanced class distributions. We compare against three BERT-family baselines with distinct pre-training strategies, evaluated via both masked language model prompting and supervised fine-tuning. Even without task-specific fine-tuning, LLMs can surpass all three fine-tuned BERT baselines, and lightweight finetuning yields substantial further gains. No single model or prompt category dominates, underscoring that prompt design interacts with model pre-training in ways that cannot be predicted a priori. Semantically grounded prompts transfer more robustly, while format-constrained patterns consistently fail to generalize. ASCII transliteration of Danish-specific characters (æ, ø, å) generally degrades performance, indicating these characters encode meaningful signal. At the same time, the gap between a balanced test set (best F1 of 0.84) and the corpus's natural class skew (0.62 trained on skewed data, 0.70 trained on balanced data) -- relative drops of 26.2\% and 16.7\% -- shows that class imbalance remains a critical open challenge. Our code and configurations are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Evaluates open-weight LLMs (Llama, Mistral, Gemma, Qwen) for Danish offensive language detection across eleven prompting strategies and against three BERT-family baselines. LLMs surpass all three fine-tuned baselines even without task-specific fine-tuning, and class imbalance remains a critical open challenge.
AI.motivation: Danish offensive language detection is an underexplored low-resource task, and the effectiveness and robustness of open-weight LLMs on it were not known.
AI.method: Four model families across eleven prompting strategies in five design categories, tested for cross-prompt generalisation, Danish orthographic variation, and robustness under balanced and naturally imbalanced class distributions; the BERT-family baselines are evaluated by masked language model prompting and by supervised fine-tuning.
AI.result: Even without task-specific fine-tuning, LLMs surpass all three fine-tuned BERT baselines, and lightweight fine-tuning yields substantial further gains. No single model or prompt category dominates. Semantically grounded prompts transfer more robustly, format-constrained patterns consistently fail to generalise, and ASCII transliteration of the Danish characters æ, ø and å generally degrades performance. The best F1 is 0.84 on the balanced test set, against 0.62 when trained on skewed data and 0.70 when trained on balanced data on the natural class skew, relative drops of 26.2% and 16.7%.
AI.conclusion: Prompt design interacts with pre-training in ways that cannot be predicted a priori, and class imbalance remains a critical open challenge for this task.

title: Benchmarking Speaker Embedders in the Sub-Second Regime for Real-Time Voice AI Agents
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables. Accepted at AIST 2026
summary: Real-time Voice AI agents must separate the active user from intelligible background speech that survives conventional noise suppression. Background sources include television audio, family members, and colleagues. Production denoisers remove non-stationary environmental noise effectively. Background speech shares the spectral characteristics of the target and passes through, causing false acceptances in downstream speaker verification (SV) and automatic speech recognition (ASR). We benchmark open-source speaker embedders TitaNet-Large, TitaNet-Small, ECAPA-TDNN, CAM++, and SpeakerNet under a strict sub-second latency budget. Evaluation combines a controlled benchmark with a weighted human-annotated production set. Our controlled benchmark is built from real calls in which a second real speaker is injected into silence intervals at modulated amplitude. We report three findings. First, denoising before embedding is generally harmful and raises equal error rate (EER) across architectures. Second, truncating audio below the full voice-activity segment degrades every model. Third, roughly half of the TitaNet embedding is redundant for this task. Trailing dimensions encode population attributes such as language and gender. Such attributes carry little discriminative value in a demographically homogeneous user base. We distill these results into deployment guidance. Verification should run on raw audio with full voice-activity chunks. Thresholds should favor precision over F1. Truncated embeddings reduce the cost of similarity search.

AI.tldr: Benchmarks five open-source speaker embedders (TitaNet-Large, TitaNet-Small, ECAPA-TDNN, CAM++ and SpeakerNet) under a sub-second latency budget for separating the active user from background speech in real-time voice AI agents. Denoising before embedding is generally harmful, and verification should run on raw audio with full voice-activity chunks.
AI.motivation: Voice AI agents must separate the active user from intelligible background speech that survives conventional noise suppression, because such speech passes the denoiser and causes false acceptances in speaker verification and ASR.
AI.method: A controlled benchmark built from real calls in which a second real speaker is injected into silence intervals at modulated amplitude, combined with a weighted human-annotated production set; the models are compared under a strict sub-second latency budget.
AI.result: Denoising before embedding generally raises the equal error rate across architectures; truncating audio below the full voice-activity segment degrades every model; roughly half of the TitaNet embedding is redundant for this task, with trailing dimensions encoding language and gender.
AI.conclusion: Deployment guidance: verify on raw audio with full voice-activity chunks, set thresholds to favour precision over F1, and use truncated embeddings to reduce the cost of similarity search.

title: Query-Guided RoPE Modulation for Lost-in-the-Middle Mitigation in Long-Context LLMs
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Long-context language models often neglect information in the middle of the input, a phenomenon known as "lost-in-the-middle". Part of this gap may stem from the long-range decay of rotary position embedding (RoPE), which weakens the positional signal between distant tokens. Existing input compression deletes low-importance tokens, and attention reweighting acts only after RoPE has weakened this signal. RoPE-level methods modify positions directly but apply the same remapping to every query. To address these limitations, we propose QGPM (Query-Guided Positional Modulation), a training-free method that reshapes RoPE positions using query relevance from the model's own attention heads. QGPM builds a broad relevance map for lower layers and a sharp one for upper layers. Low-relevance tokens advance by less than one position on fast-rotating planes, pulling relevant evidence toward the query. Slow-rotating planes keep the original layout, with every token in place. Experiments on NoLiMa and RULER with multiple context lengths show that QGPM improves over base models and strong baselines, with the largest gains on retrieval tasks, and generalizes across multiple backbones. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes QGPM, a training-free method that reshapes RoPE positions using query relevance from the model's own attention heads, pulling relevant evidence in the middle of long inputs toward the query. It improves over base models and strong baselines on NoLiMa and RULER, with the largest gains on retrieval tasks.
AI.motivation: Long-context LLMs neglect information in the middle of the input, possibly because of the long-range decay of RoPE; input compression deletes tokens, attention reweighting acts after RoPE has already weakened the signal, and RoPE-level methods apply the same remapping to every query.
AI.method: Query-guided positional modulation builds a broad relevance map for lower layers and a sharp one for upper layers; low-relevance tokens advance by less than one position on fast-rotating RoPE planes, while slow-rotating planes keep the original layout.
AI.result: Experiments on NoLiMa and RULER across multiple context lengths show gains over base models and strong baselines, largest on retrieval tasks, and generalisation across multiple backbones.
AI.conclusion: Query-dependent reshaping of RoPE positions is an effective training-free way to reduce the lost-in-the-middle effect, with retrieval tasks benefiting most.

title: RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers
comment: 22 pages, 10 figures, 10 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) extends RL with verifiable rewards to open-ended tasks by scoring each response against query-specific rubrics. Under group-relative optimization, however, a rubric that every sampled response fails (unreachable) or passes (saturated) gives all responses the same outcome and no learning signal; in Qwen3-4B medical training, 60.88% of query-rubric observations are inactive. We find that the two states lack different supervision: stating an unreachable rubric in the prompt raises its satisfaction from 1.13% to 91.25%, whereas responses that all pass a saturated rubric still differ in quality. We therefore propose RuACT (Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers), which assigns each inactive rubric the role that supplies what it lacks. Rubric as Teacher uses unreachable rubrics as privileged information for reward-gated on-policy self-distillation, and Rubric as Critic decomposes saturated rubrics into child rubrics that separate current responses while sharing the parent's weight. RuACT outperforms GRPO, rubric reweighting, and rubric-guided exploration on all four medical and scientific benchmarks with Qwen3-4B and achieves the best average with Qwen3-1.7B. On initially unreachable rubrics, unguided recovery rises from 35.02% to 42.86%, while child refinement improves reward-quality alignment on independent rollouts from 57.74% to 60.77%. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes RuACT, which recovers inactive rubrics in rubric-based RL by giving unreachable rubrics a teacher role (reward-gated on-policy self-distillation using them as privileged information) and saturated rubrics a critic role (decomposition into child rubrics). It outperforms GRPO and two other rubric methods on four medical and scientific benchmarks with Qwen3-4B.
AI.motivation: Under group-relative optimisation, a rubric that every response fails or passes gives all responses the same outcome and no learning signal; in Qwen3-4B medical training 60.88% of query-rubric observations are inactive, and the two states lack different kinds of supervision.
AI.method: Rubric as Teacher uses unreachable rubrics as privileged information for reward-gated on-policy self-distillation; Rubric as Critic decomposes saturated rubrics into child rubrics that separate current responses while sharing the parent's weight.
AI.result: RuACT outperforms GRPO, rubric reweighting and rubric-guided exploration on all four medical and scientific benchmarks with Qwen3-4B, and achieves the best average with Qwen3-1.7B. Unguided recovery on initially unreachable rubrics rises from 35.02% to 42.86%, and child refinement raises reward-quality alignment on independent rollouts from 57.74% to 60.77%. Stating an unreachable rubric in the prompt raises its satisfaction from 1.13% to 91.25%.
AI.conclusion: Inactive rubrics carry usable supervision when they are assigned the role that supplies what they lack, turning otherwise wasted rollouts into learning signal.

title: Steerable Multi-Objective Group-Relative Preference Optimization with Jointly Trained Low-Rank Adapters
comment: Preprint. Under review
summary: Language model deployment often requires different trade-offs between competing objectives as user preferences change, yet standard post-training methods typically produce a single policy for a fixed objective weighting. We introduce LambdaMix, a new parameter efficient method for learning a preference conditioned family of policies with group-relative online reinforcement learning. LambdaMix jointly trains one low-rank adapter per objective over a frozen base model. One preference vector selects the adapter mixture that generates responses and weights the separately normalized rewards used to update the adapters. A single training run supports changing preferences at inference without further optimization. We experiment with four models on helpfulness and harmlessness and on solving math problems while following instructions. We also evaluate the two largest models on rewriting comments to preserve wording while reducing clues about personal attributes. On the first two tasks, LambdaMix achieves higher hypervolume than all evaluated conditioned and policy merging baselines across all four models. LambdaMix uses fewer training completions and stores fewer adapter parameters than a set of GRPO specialist policies. With architecture and initialization fixed, varying adapter mixtures and objective weights together gives wider score ranges and higher coverage than varying either alone.

AI.tldr: Introduces LambdaMix, which jointly trains one low-rank adapter per objective over a frozen base model, so that a preference vector selects an adapter mixture and weights the rewards, allowing trade-offs to change at inference after a single training run. It achieves higher hypervolume than conditioned and policy-merging baselines on helpfulness-harmlessness and instruction-following math tasks across four models.
AI.motivation: Deployments need different trade-offs between competing objectives as user preferences change, but standard post-training produces a single policy for a fixed objective weighting.
AI.method: A preference-conditioned family of policies trained with group-relative online reinforcement learning; one low-rank adapter per objective over a frozen base model; the preference vector sets the adapter mixture that generates responses and weights the separately normalised rewards that update the adapters.
AI.result: On helpfulness-harmlessness and math-while-following-instructions, LambdaMix achieves higher hypervolume than all conditioned and policy-merging baselines across all four models, with fewer training completions and fewer adapter parameters than a set of GRPO specialist policies. Varying adapter mixtures and objective weights together gives wider score ranges and higher coverage than varying either alone. On comment rewriting, which preserves wording while reducing clues about personal attributes, the two largest models were also evaluated.
AI.conclusion: A single training run yields a steerable policy family that trades off objectives at inference without further optimisation, at lower training and storage cost than GRPO specialists.

title: How Much Conversation History Does an AI Agent Need?
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures
summary: How does using less conversational history change reader-token use and benchmark scores? We examine this question on 1,100 BEAM questions. We held the retrieval ranking and reader constant across five fixed passage budgets, and mean assigned scores rose as the passage budget grew. The score gain per additional token became smaller at the upper tested budgets. Answerable questions generally received higher scores with more context. Pooled abstention scores sometimes rose as the passage budget shrank. We also tested message retention in a controlled task with explicit conversational-state targets and compared retained user messages with token-matched recency. Qwen matched the full state more often for direct requirements when user messages were retained. Its full-state matching declined when answers depended on references to earlier offers. Mistral produced near-floor results across the retention conditions. A scoring audit leaves the correctness of BEAM answers unresolved. These experiments characterize the token and score consequences of the tested memory budgets. Reliable budget selection depends on retaining the evidence each question requires and validating the measure used to assess answer quality.

AI.tldr: Examines how the passage budget for retrieved conversation history affects reader-token use and benchmark scores on 1,100 BEAM questions; mean scores rise with budget, with smaller gains per additional token at the upper budgets. Message retention experiments show that retaining user messages helps Qwen on direct requirements, while Mistral stays near floor.
AI.motivation: Agents must decide how much conversational history to give a reader, and the token and score consequences of tested memory budgets were not characterised.
AI.method: Retrieval ranking and reader held constant across five fixed passage budgets on 1,100 BEAM questions; a controlled task with explicit conversational-state targets compares retained user messages with token-matched recency; a scoring audit checks BEAM answer correctness.
AI.result: Mean assigned scores rise with the passage budget, with diminishing gains per token at the upper budgets; answerable questions generally score higher with more context, while pooled abstention scores sometimes rise as the budget shrinks. Retaining user messages let Qwen match the full state more often for direct requirements, but its full-state matching declined when answers depended on references to earlier offers. Mistral gave near-floor results across retention conditions. The scoring audit leaves BEAM answer correctness unresolved.
AI.conclusion: Reliable budget selection depends on retaining the evidence each question requires and on validating the measure used to assess answer quality, which the audit shows is not yet settled.

title: Language as Trait, Politeness as Strategy: Controlled Tests of Linguistic Effects in LLM Social-Deduction Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents coordinate through conversation, and the same message can be phrased in simpler or more complex language, bluntly or politely. We test whether such differences change how other agents judge and act, using the LURK Werewolf framework, which separates each utterance's speech-act predicate from its natural-language realization. We rewrite only the realization, check that the game content is preserved, and replay each game day from saved checkpoints against a re-sampled control. We vary linguistic range consistently across a speaker's messages and politeness strategy per utterance. Across 30 games and 4,335 replays, neither manipulation changes the trust other agents place in the speaker, and no effect on votes or night actions survives correction for multiple comparisons; the largest uncorrected effect is that shifting range away from a neutral paraphrase changes about 4 percentage points more of the other players' votes. In natural play, 88% of face-threatening speech is bald on-record regardless of role.

AI.tldr: Tests whether linguistic range and politeness strategy in LLM Werewolf agents change how other agents trust, vote or act, by rewriting only the realisation of utterances and replaying saved game days against re-sampled controls. Across 30 games and 4,335 replays neither manipulation changes trust, and no vote or night-action effect survives correction for multiple comparisons.
AI.motivation: LLM agents coordinate through conversation, and the same message can be phrased in simpler or more complex language and bluntly or politely; whether such differences change other agents' judgement and action was not known.
AI.method: Within the LURK Werewolf framework, which separates each utterance's speech-act predicate from its natural-language realisation, only the realisation is rewritten, with game content checked for preservation; linguistic range is varied consistently across a speaker's messages and politeness strategy per utterance; each game day is replayed from saved checkpoints against a re-sampled control.
AI.result: Across 30 games and 4,335 replays, neither manipulation changes the trust other agents place in the speaker, and no effect on votes or night actions survives correction for multiple comparisons. The largest uncorrected effect is that shifting range away from a neutral paraphrase changes about 4 percentage points more of the other players' votes. In natural play, 88% of face-threatening speech is bald on-record regardless of role.
AI.conclusion: Under these controls, linguistic range and politeness strategy show no effect on trust, votes or night actions that survives multiple-comparison correction.

title: ROSE: Risk-Aware Orthogonal Subspace Navigation for Lifelong Knowledge Editing in Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) require continuous factual updates to stay current, yet lifelong knowledge editing remains a daunting challenge. The primary obstacle is the severe Locality Erosion and Catastrophic Forgetting, where sequential edits inevitably interfere with pre-trained capabilities and prior updates. In this paper, we propose \textbf{ROSE}, a \textbf{R}isk-aware \textbf{O}rthogonal \textbf{S}ubspace navigation framework for lifelong knowledge \textbf{E}diting. ROSE addresses forgetting by aiming to restrict parameter updates to the orthogonal complement of previously edited subspaces. Crucially, it introduces a risk-guided mechanism that utilizes a dynamically computed risk mask to safeguard specific factual parameter subspaces essential for model stability. During inference, ROSE employs a multi-granularity knowledge integration strategy, featuring prototype-anchored semantic gating and perturbation-driven subspace fusion to precisely activate edited knowledge for relevant queries while limiting interference on unrelated inputs. Comprehensive experiments on two prominent multimodal benchmarks show that ROSE is competitive with state-of-the-art approaches across five key metrics, while maintaining outstanding stability over $1,000$ sequential updates. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes ROSE, a lifelong knowledge editing framework for multimodal LLMs that restricts parameter updates to the orthogonal complement of earlier edited subspaces, with risk-guided protection of factual subspaces and multi-granularity knowledge integration at inference. It is competitive with state-of-the-art approaches on five key metrics across two multimodal benchmarks and remains stable over 1,000 sequential updates.
AI.motivation: Multimodal LLMs need continual factual updates, but sequential edits cause Locality Erosion and Catastrophic Forgetting, interfering with pre-trained capabilities and with prior updates.
AI.method: Parameter updates are restricted to the orthogonal complement of previously edited subspaces; a dynamically computed risk mask safeguards factual parameter subspaces essential for model stability; at inference, prototype-anchored semantic gating and perturbation-driven subspace fusion activate edited knowledge for relevant queries.
AI.result: Competitive with state-of-the-art approaches across five key metrics on two multimodal benchmarks, while staying stable over 1,000 sequential updates.
AI.conclusion: Orthogonal subspace updates with risk-aware protection and gated inference offer a way to sustain lifelong editing of multimodal LLMs with limited interference on unrelated inputs.

title: Are These Programmers Ripe Enough to Eat? Evaluating How LLMs Handle Lexical Knowledge Conflicts in Translation
summary: External lexical resources can help large language models (LLMs) translate texts in low-resource languages and specialized domains, but these resources may conflict with models' prior lexical knowledge. To isolate this conflict, we construct a controlled Mandarin-to-English translation task in which familiar source words are assigned new meanings within and across semantic categories. We treat these prompt-supplied meanings as contextual knowledge (CK) and systematically evaluate the effects of word frequency, sentence context, and prompt framing on the translated outputs. Across nine models, CK reliance is greater for less frequent source words and in sentence contexts that support the supplied meanings. Prompt framing can reduce CK reliance, but seven of nine models favor CK even when explicitly instructed to ignore the supplied meanings. Within model families, larger models are more likely than smaller models to utilize CK in their outputs. Three follow-up experiments further show that modal weakening lowers CK reliance, the effect of repetition depends on prompt layout, and the effect of reasoning varies across models. Overall, our controlled study reveals how CK reliance varies across conditions and models, motivating new methods to detect and evaluate lexical conflicts and guide models' lexical choices in LLM-based translation.

AI.tldr: Builds a controlled Mandarin-to-English translation task in which familiar source words are given new meanings, and finds across nine models that LLMs rely more on prompt-supplied contextual knowledge for less frequent words and supportive sentence contexts, with seven of nine favouring it even when told to ignore it.
AI.motivation: External lexical resources can help LLMs translate low-resource languages and specialised domains, but they may conflict with models' prior lexical knowledge, and the conflict needs isolating to be studied.
AI.method: A controlled Mandarin-to-English task in which familiar source words are assigned new meanings within and across semantic categories, treated as contextual knowledge (CK); effects of word frequency, sentence context and prompt framing are evaluated across nine models; three follow-up experiments test modal weakening, repetition and reasoning.
AI.result: CK reliance is greater for less frequent source words and in sentence contexts that support the supplied meanings. Prompt framing can reduce CK reliance, but seven of nine models favour CK even when explicitly instructed to ignore the supplied meanings. Within model families, larger models are more likely to use CK. Modal weakening lowers CK reliance, the effect of repetition depends on prompt layout, and the effect of reasoning varies across models.
AI.conclusion: CK reliance varies with condition and model, motivating new methods to detect and evaluate lexical conflicts and to guide models' lexical choices in LLM-based translation.

title: Compaction, decay and reinforcement in a two-tier conversational memory: a paired evaluation against retrieval-augmented generation
comment: 7 figures. Data and code: this https URL
summary: A conversational agent that remembers has to decide what to keep. Retrieval-augmented generation keeps the transcript and searches it; the alternative is to compact each turn into atomic facts and search those. We compare the two on LoCoMo, with both arms answering all 1,985 questions in one window, against the same stores, with the same generator and judge, and both predictions on one row, which licenses McNemar's exact test on the 512 questions where they disagree. On the four categories comparable work reports, compaction scores 71.4 per cent against 64.6, a lead of 6.8 points (p = 5.5e-08) at 34 per cent fewer prompt tokens. On all five, including the adversarial set comparable work drops, the lead falls to 2.0 and stops being significant, because the baseline leads adversarial by 14.6. That loss has a structure. Our lead falls as the reference answer demands more source wording, 9.6 points ahead at one or two reference words and 3.1 behind past eight, with token overlap moving the same way, so the judge is not the cause. Compaction keeps what a fact asserts and discards how it was said, so it wins where the answer is a value and loses where it is a phrasing. We also report four negative results with their power calculations.

AI.tldr: Compares compaction, which turns each conversational turn into atomic facts for search, with retrieval-augmented generation over the raw transcript on LoCoMo. Compaction leads by 6.8 points on the four comparable categories with 34% fewer prompt tokens, but the lead falls to 2.0 and is not significant once the adversarial category is included.
AI.motivation: A conversational agent with memory must decide what to keep: retain the transcript and search it, or compact each turn into atomic facts and search those.
AI.method: Paired evaluation on LoCoMo in which both arms answer all 1,985 questions in one window against the same stores, generator and judge; McNemar's exact test is applied to the 512 questions where the two predictions disagree.
AI.result: On the four categories comparable work reports, compaction scores 71.4% against 64.6% for retrieval-augmented generation, a lead of 6.8 points (p = 5.5e-08) at 34% fewer prompt tokens. On all five categories, including adversarial, the lead falls to 2.0 and is not significant, because the baseline leads on adversarial questions by 14.6 points. The lead falls as the reference answer demands more source wording: 9.6 points ahead at one or two reference words and 3.1 points behind past eight. Four negative results are reported with power calculations.
AI.conclusion: Compaction keeps what a fact asserts and discards how it was said, so it wins where the answer is a value and loses where the answer is a phrasing.

title: CodeQuant2: Enhanced Outlier Mitigation and Adaptive Clustering for Low-Precision LRMs
summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) improve task performance by generating longer intermediate reasoning traces, but this substantially increases inference costs and makes low-precision quantization increasingly important. However, aggressively quantized models often perform poorly on reasoning tasks. We observe larger activation fluctuations during the first decoding steps of reasoning. Calibration that omits these early states may miss their activation fluctuations. To address these reasoning-specific quantization challenges, we propose \textbf{CodeQuant2}, a clustering-based LUT quantization framework for low-precision large reasoning models. CodeQuant2 mitigates activation outliers with rotation and scaling, uses clustering to represent non-uniform weight distributions, and adapts codebook sizes to the quantization difficulty of each layer. Guided by our observation of reasoning-time activation behavior, CodeQuant2 further improves calibration sample selection to better match actual decoding statistics. Combined with our customized LUT CUDA kernel, CodeQuant2 delivers substantial accuracy improvements on reasoning benchmarks while achieving up to $2.85\times$ speedup over BF16.

AI.tldr: CodeQuant2 is a clustering-based lookup-table quantization framework for low-precision large reasoning models that targets the larger activation fluctuations seen in the first decoding steps of reasoning. It reports substantial accuracy gains on reasoning benchmarks and up to 2.85x speedup over BF16 with a customized LUT CUDA kernel.
AI.motivation: Large reasoning models generate long traces that raise inference cost, making low-precision quantization important, but aggressively quantized models often perform poorly on reasoning tasks, and calibration that omits the early decoding states may miss their activation fluctuations.
AI.method: CodeQuant2 mitigates activation outliers with rotation and scaling, uses clustering to represent non-uniform weight distributions, adapts codebook sizes to the quantization difficulty of each layer, and selects calibration samples to better match actual reasoning-time decoding statistics, with a customized LUT CUDA kernel.
AI.result: Substantial accuracy improvements on reasoning benchmarks, with up to 2.85x speedup over BF16. The abstract does not name the specific benchmarks or baselines.
AI.conclusion: Calibration and quantization for reasoning models should account for reasoning-time activation behavior, since calibration that ignores the early decoding states can miss fluctuations that affect accuracy.

title: Rethinking Data Selection as Distribution Matching on Semantic Manifolds
summary: Instruction tuning of large language models and large vision language models relies on massive training data, which incurs substantial computational and storage costs. Meanwhile, training data often contains redundancy, noise, and low quality samples. Existing data selection methods mostly rely on diversity, importance, or a combination of both, without explicitly constraining the distributional consistency between the selected subset and the full data in the embedding space. We propose QMAC, a quality aware multiband characteristic function matching method that formulates data selection as a joint optimization problem of distribution matching and quality filtering. QMAC matches the empirical characteristic functions of the selected subset and the full data across multiple frequency scales, capturing both global semantic coverage and local perturbations, while using task related quality scores to filter noisy and low quality samples. We systematically evaluate QMAC on 4 data types, 8 target models, and 44 benchmarks. Experimental results show that QMAC outperforms existing data selection baselines on standard image-text instruction data, substantially surpasses random selection on standard text instruction, image-text reasoning, and text reasoning data, and exceeds full data training in multiple model and budget combinations. The code will be made publicly available upon acceptance of the paper.

AI.tldr: QMAC selects training data by matching the characteristic functions of the selected subset and the full data across multiple frequency scales, combined with task-related quality scores that filter noisy and low-quality samples. It outperforms existing selection baselines and random selection, and in some model and budget combinations exceeds full-data training.
AI.motivation: Existing data selection methods rely on diversity, importance, or both, without explicitly constraining the distributional consistency between the selected subset and the full data in embedding space, while training data often contains redundancy, noise and low-quality samples.
AI.method: Data selection is formulated as a joint optimization of distribution matching and quality filtering. QMAC matches the empirical characteristic functions of the subset and the full data across multiple frequency scales, capturing both global semantic coverage and local perturbations, while task-related quality scores filter noisy samples.
AI.result: Evaluated on 4 data types, 8 target models and 44 benchmarks. QMAC outperforms existing selection baselines on standard image-text instruction data, substantially surpasses random selection on text instruction, image-text reasoning and text reasoning data, and exceeds full-data training in multiple model and budget combinations.
AI.conclusion: Distribution matching combined with quality filtering can produce data subsets that match or exceed full-data training at a reduced training cost. The code will be released upon acceptance.

title: Improving Contextual Retrieval for Long Documents using Semantic Chunking and Hybrid Retrieval Strategies
summary: The vast amount of information available in lengthy, distributed documents makes finding relevant answers difficult, especially when the answer requires connecting evidence from multiple sources. Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems often struggle with this type of "multi-hop" reasoning and frequently face issues with context fragmentation. In this paper, we propose a hybrid RAG framework that integrates the structured reasoning of knowledge graphs with the broad semantic coverage of dense vector retrieval. Our approach employs a multi-stage pipeline using transformer-based summarization and semantic chunking to improve context retention. We construct a dynamic knowledge graph to capture explicit relationships between entities while simultaneously maintaining a dense vector index. During inference, the system uses a hierarchical mechanism that prioritizes graph traversal for precision and falls back to vector retrieval when necessary. We evaluated our framework on the MultiHop-RAG dataset. The results show that this hybrid approach outperforms standalone vector and graph-based baselines, achieving higher Exact Match scores and improved retrieval accuracy for complex queries. This confirms that merging structured reasoning with standard vector retrieval creates a more robust system for handling complex knowledge-intensive questions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hybrid RAG framework that combines knowledge-graph traversal with dense vector retrieval, using semantic chunking and transformer-based summarization. On the MultiHop-RAG dataset it reports higher Exact Match scores and better retrieval accuracy than standalone vector and graph-based baselines.
AI.motivation: Standard RAG systems struggle with multi-hop reasoning that connects evidence across lengthy, distributed documents and suffer from context fragmentation.
AI.method: A multi-stage pipeline with transformer-based summarization and semantic chunking builds a dynamic knowledge graph of explicit entity relationships alongside a dense vector index. At inference, a hierarchical mechanism prioritizes graph traversal for precision and falls back to vector retrieval when necessary.
AI.result: On the MultiHop-RAG dataset, the hybrid approach outperforms standalone vector and graph-based baselines, with higher Exact Match scores and improved retrieval accuracy for complex queries. The abstract gives no numerical values.
AI.conclusion: Merging structured reasoning over knowledge graphs with standard vector retrieval yields a more robust system for complex, knowledge-intensive questions.

title: Structure is in the zoom: probing neural symmetry through dimensionality scaling
comment: 63 pages, 20 figures. Code, data and the rung tool: this https URL
summary: How much of a neural population's measured dimensionality is the code, and how much is the act of measuring it? The slope of the participation ratio against subsample size is reported for cortical populations and for the layers of language models as a number that belongs to the system. It does not. One patch of eleven thousand mouse V1 neurons returns three slopes, 0.25 along random stimulus subsets, 0.31 along drift direction, 0.35 along neuron count, and only the middle one carries structure; the other two are the sampling floor. We split every exponent into that floor and a shift earned along a declared axis, and read the shift against two nulls: permuting the labels, and permuting them only among samples that share a nuisance. On V1 the direction-aligned shift clears the label null in eight of eight grating recordings, is positive in 32 of 32 animals in a second laboratory, and reads both sectors of the code's O(2) symmetry. The even sector sets how the ladder starts: it decides which order of adding classes climbs faster, predicts the opposite order in an equivariant network, and flows under coarse-graining by a closed-form factor that says what orientation columns do to mesoscale signals. The odd sector, carried by the direction-selective neurons, keeps the ladder climbing past half the classes. On language models the same split separates content inherited from the tokens from construction built with depth, on five architectures, and the second null shows that a grammaticality signal of twenty standard deviations is entirely carrier composition. With a floor and a declared axis, dimensionality scaling is an axis-resolved measurement, and where the axis follows a known symmetry it resolves the sector content of the code. The instrument, rung, trains no probe and reads any array or any Hugging Face model layer by layer (this https URL).

AI.tldr: The paper argues that the participation-ratio dimensionality slope against subsample size mixes a sampling floor with genuine structure, and it splits each exponent into that floor plus a shift along a declared axis, tested against two nulls. On mouse V1 and on language models the direction-aligned shift carries structure, and on V1 it resolves sectors of the code's O(2) symmetry.
AI.motivation: Dimensionality scaling slopes are reported for cortical populations and for language model layers as if they were properties of the system, but the abstract argues that the slope is not intrinsic, since a sampling floor contributes to it.
AI.method: Each slope is split into a sampling floor and a shift earned along a declared axis, and the shift is read against two nulls: permuting the labels, and permuting them only among samples that share a nuisance factor. The even and odd sectors of the O(2) symmetry are read from the shift. The instrument, called rung, trains no probe and reads any array or Hugging Face model layer by layer.
AI.result: On a patch of 11,000 mouse V1 neurons, three slopes were obtained (0.25 for random stimulus subsets, 0.31 for drift direction, 0.35 for neuron count), and only the drift-direction slope carries structure. The direction-aligned shift clears the label null in 8 of 8 grating recordings and is positive in 32 of 32 animals in a second laboratory. On five language model architectures the split separates content inherited from tokens from construction built with depth, and a grammaticality signal of 20 standard deviations is entirely carrier composition under the second null.
AI.conclusion: With a sampling floor and a declared axis, dimensionality scaling becomes an axis-resolved measurement, and where the axis follows a known symmetry it can resolve the sector content of the code.

title: Subliminal Learning in Vision-Language Models
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027
summary: Subliminal learning is a phenomenon in large language models (LLMs) where a teacher passes a hidden preference to a student through training data unrelated to that preference. We study whether subliminal learning also occurs in vision-language models (VLMs). We finetune a teacher VLM to prefer a specific animal or facial attribute and use a control teacher from the same base model. Both teachers generate numbers for an unrelated visual task involving geometric shapes. Two students initialized from the same base VLM are finetuned on the same images, using numbers generated by either the biased or control teacher. Across VLMs ranging from 2B to 7B parameters, we find that both animal and facial preferences can transfer through this unrelated task. Students trained on biased-teacher outputs select the target more often than control students, with a difference of up to $\sim$10 percentage points in the animal preference task. Transfer can become stronger with more training data and varies with the target preference, model, and how the numbers are generated. Beyond preferences, we show that the biased student's explanations use more of the same words and phrases as the biased teacher's explanations than those of the control student, even when all three models select the same image. These results matter for training VLMs and show that training on unrelated data may change both a VLM's image preferences and how it explains its choices, and that transfer can become stronger with more training samples.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that subliminal learning, in which a hidden preference transfers through unrelated training data, also occurs in vision-language models. Students trained on a biased teacher's outputs select the target preference more often than control students, by up to about 10 percentage points on the animal preference task.
AI.motivation: Subliminal learning had been shown in LLMs, but it was not known whether hidden preferences transfer through unrelated data in vision-language models, which matters for how VLMs are trained.
AI.method: A teacher VLM is finetuned to prefer a specific animal or facial attribute, with a control teacher from the same base model. Both teachers generate numbers for an unrelated geometric shape task. Two students from the same base VLM are finetuned on the same images with numbers from either the biased or the control teacher.
AI.result: Across VLMs from 2B to 7B parameters, both animal and facial preferences transfer through the unrelated task. Biased-teacher students select the target more often than control students, by up to about 10 percentage points in the animal task. Transfer strengthens with more training data and varies with the preference, model and number-generation method. The biased students' explanations also reuse more of the same words and phrases as the biased teacher's explanations.
AI.conclusion: Training on unrelated data may shift a VLM's image preferences and how it explains its choices, and this transfer can become stronger with more training samples.

title: How Small Can We Go? Calibrating Activation-Cache Compression for SAE Training
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Interpretability as a Science (InterpScience), non-archival. 27 pages, 5 figures, 30 tables
summary: To train a sparse autoencoder (SAE), you need a massive cache of model activations. We look into the effects that compression has on an SAE in two ways: we keep the original fp32-trained SAE and pass the compressed cache into the same SAE to see how many feature activations stay the same (the frozen-SAE test), and we retrain an SAE on the compressed cache and see how many of the original features still exist (the retraining test). We found that in the retraining test, there is no clear scale for retained features. On a GPT-2 cache, rounding everything to fp16 keeps 60.6% of features, but changing one value in a million by the smallest step fp32 allows (a change eight orders of magnitude smaller) keeps only 70.5%. Meanwhile, changing the random seed keeps 23.0%. For the frozen-SAE test, the frozen SAE's correlation with the original increases in order of how precise the codecs are, but plain $L_2$ distance gives nearly the same ordering. We also see the same frozen reading correspond to different percentages retained at different sites. This leaves the question of the right measurement. We build one by calibrating: retraining on identical bytes sets the ceiling, and a reseed sets the floor. We then measure the effect of each compressed codec against its own site's floor. With TopK SAEs on GPT-2 small and Pythia-1.4B at research-scale budgets, naïve per-token int4 loses more features than a reseed everywhere we tested, as do PCA and random projection on GPT-2. Standardizing each channel before quantizing brings int4 back above the floor in terms of retained features, at the same raw file size. At our smallest budget, a bf16 forward pass, which some pipelines use to save memory, loses slightly more features than rotated 8-bit storage. Calibrating a site costs four training runs and two evaluation passes.

AI.tldr: The paper measures how activation-cache compression affects sparse autoencoder training by calibrating against a ceiling set by retraining on identical bytes and a floor set by reseeding. Naive per-token int4 loses more features than a reseed in every setting tested, while standardizing each channel before quantizing brings int4 back above the floor at the same raw file size.
AI.motivation: Training a sparse autoencoder needs a very large cache of model activations, and the effect of compressing that cache on the SAE is not measured on a consistent scale, since the retained-feature count depends on the chosen test.
AI.method: Two tests are compared: a frozen-SAE test that passes compressed activations into the original fp32-trained SAE, and a retraining test that retrains an SAE on the compressed cache. Each compressed codec is measured against its own site's floor, using retraining on identical bytes as the ceiling and a reseed as the floor. Codecs include per-token int4, PCA, random projection, a bf16 forward pass and rotated 8-bit storage, applied to TopK SAEs on GPT-2 small and Pythia-1.4B.
AI.result: On a GPT-2 cache, rounding to fp16 keeps 60.6% of features, changing one value in a million by the smallest fp32 step keeps 70.5%, and changing the random seed keeps 23.0%. Naive per-token int4 loses more features than a reseed everywhere tested, as do PCA and random projection on GPT-2. Standardizing each channel before int4 quantization brings it back above the floor at the same raw file size. At the smallest budget, a bf16 forward pass loses slightly more features than rotated 8-bit storage.
AI.conclusion: The retraining test shows no clear scale for retained features, so the measurement must be calibrated per site against a reseed floor. Calibrating a site costs four training runs and two evaluation passes.

title: Turkish Multimodal Video Fact-Checking: A New Dataset and a Comparison of Zero-Shot Agentic and Fine-Tuned Systems
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. MSc dissertation, Queen Mary University of London, 2026
summary: Video-based misinformation spreads rapidly on social media, but almost all existing fact-checking systems focus exclusively on English text. Tools for low-resource languages such as Turkish are severely limited. In this work, we present TeViD (Turkish Video Fact-checking Dataset), to the best of our knowledge the first multimodal video fact-checking dataset for Turkish. We compiled the dataset from articles published by this http URL, an IFCN-certified organisation, and enriched it with translated Snopes articles and synthetic examples to reduce class imbalance. Building on TeViD, we develop two verification pipelines that share the same open-source base model. First, in 3MFact-TR (Pipeline 1), we adapt the multi-role 3MFact framework to Turkish with the Qwen2.5-7B large language model and the Qwen2-VL-7B vision-language model, and add three modules of our own: a semantic inconsistency checker, a 5W1H question manager, and a bilingual evidence retriever that excludes fact-checking sites to prevent leakage. Second, as our Fine-Tuned Model (Pipeline 2), we fine-tune a single Qwen2.5-7B with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to produce closed-book verdicts from the claim and the video's textual description. We report accuracy, macro F1, True class F1, and True class recall for both systems, together with ablation studies.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TeViD, a multimodal video fact-checking dataset for Turkish, and compares a zero-shot agentic pipeline (3MFact-TR) with a LoRA-fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B, both built on the same open-source base model. The abstract does not report the comparative scores.
AI.motivation: Video-based misinformation spreads rapidly on social media, but most fact-checking systems cover only English text, leaving low-resource languages such as Turkish with very limited tools.
AI.method: TeViD is compiled from articles of an IFCN-certified fact-checking organisation, enriched with translated Snopes articles and synthetic examples to reduce class imbalance. Pipeline 1 adapts the multi-role 3MFact framework to Turkish with Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2-VL-7B and adds a semantic inconsistency checker, a 5W1H question manager and a bilingual evidence retriever that excludes fact-checking sites. Pipeline 2 fine-tunes Qwen2.5-7B with LoRA to produce closed-book verdicts from the claim and the video's textual description.
