AI.conclusion: TeViD offers a first multimodal video fact-checking resource for Turkish, on which zero-shot agentic and fine-tuned approaches are compared.

title: ChainFlow: Few-Step Latent Flow Matching for Speculative Decoding
summary: Speculative decoding has become a standard way to accelerate LLM inference: a lightweight drafter proposes tokens that the target verifies in one parallel pass. Existing drafters face trade-offs that limits their speedups: autoregressive drafters generate tokens one at a time, so drafting cost grows with draft length, while diffusion drafters generate tokens in parallel but predict each position independently, ignoring inter-token dependencies. We introduce ChainFlow, a new speculative decoding paradigm and the first flow-matching drafter conditioned on the target's hidden states. ChainFlow treats drafting as a short transport over hidden states, needing one or two flow steps instead of the many denoising steps of generation from noise. A variational autoencoder compresses these states so drafting cost barely grows with target size, lightweight feedback heads restore inter-token dependencies, and tree drafting raises acceptance. On Qwen3.5 models, at matched drafter size and training data, ChainFlow outperforms EAGLE-3 and DFlash in vLLM by 39% and 11%, respectively. These gains further widen as drafters are adapted to new languages sequentially. Our ablations cover drafter design and concurrent serving, and we open-source our code and drafter models.

AI.tldr: ChainFlow is a speculative decoding drafter that uses flow matching over the target model's hidden states and needs only one or two flow steps. On Qwen3.5 models at matched drafter size and training data, it outperforms EAGLE-3 by 39% and DFlash by 11% in vLLM.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive drafters generate tokens one at a time, so drafting cost grows with draft length, while diffusion drafters generate tokens in parallel but predict each position independently and ignore inter-token dependencies.
AI.method: ChainFlow is the first flow-matching drafter conditioned on the target's hidden states and treats drafting as a short transport over those states. A variational autoencoder compresses the states so drafting cost barely grows with target size, lightweight feedback heads restore inter-token dependencies, and tree drafting raises acceptance.
AI.result: On Qwen3.5 models at matched drafter size and training data, ChainFlow outperforms EAGLE-3 and DFlash in vLLM by 39% and 11%, respectively, and these gains widen as drafters are adapted sequentially to new languages. Ablations cover drafter design and concurrent serving.
AI.conclusion: Flow-matching drafting over hidden states gives a faster, dependency-aware speculative decoding paradigm, and the code and drafter models are open-sourced.

title: Greedy Byte-Pair Encoding Achieves at Least 0.361 of the Optimal Compression
comment: 27 pages, 5 figures. Code and certificates: this https URL
summary: Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) builds a tokeniser by repeatedly merging a most frequent adjacent pair of symbols; its utility is the total reduction in string length achieved by $k$ merges. It was known that this greedy rule achieves at least a third of the optimal reduction. We prove that it always achieves at least 0.361 of the optimal reduction in string length, for every string, every budget and every tie-breaking rule; this is the first improvement of the bound one third. We also explain why one third was a barrier: the pair-packing relaxation behind it is tight, so a better bound must use more of the optimum's structure. When greedy destroys three of the optimum's merge points at once, one of them can usually be moved next door, because all copies of a rule of the optimum look alike; the remaining cases are paid for later. Along the way we determine the worst-case ratio for two merges exactly, bound it for three, and isolate a single inequality that would settle the problem.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that greedy Byte-Pair Encoding always achieves at least 0.361 of the optimal reduction in string length, for every string, every budget and every tie-breaking rule, improving the previous one-third bound. It also explains why one third was a barrier.
AI.motivation: Greedy BPE was known to achieve at least one third of the optimal string-length reduction, and the pair-packing relaxation behind that bound is tight, so a better bound must use more of the optimum's structure.
AI.method: The argument shows that when greedy destroys three of the optimum's merge points at once, one of them can usually be moved next door, because all copies of a rule of the optimum look alike, and the remaining cases are charged later. The paper determines the worst-case ratio for two merges exactly and bounds it for three.
AI.result: The bound of 0.361 holds for every string, budget and tie-breaking rule. The worst-case ratio for two merges is determined exactly, and a single inequality that would settle the problem is isolated.
AI.conclusion: The pair-packing relaxation explains the one-third barrier, so a stronger guarantee requires exploiting more of the optimum's structure, and the paper isolates the inequality that would resolve the question.

title: Dual-Stream LLM-Guided Reward Design for Reject-Inference-Aware Reinforcement Learning in E-Commerce Payment Fraud Detection
comment: 12 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Extends Qu et al., ACL 2025 Industry Track: this https URL
summary: Production fraud-detection models learn from a censored slice of their own traffic: transactions a legacy system blocked never receive fraud labels, so models train on a biased, approved-only distribution. We extend LLM-guided reward design, the framework of Qu et al. (2025) in which an LLM evolves the reward of a two-step REINFORCE fraud-blocking policy, to attack this reject-inference problem inside the reward. A single LLM designs a dual-stream reward: stream 1 applies the standard dollar-weighted precision objective to labeled transactions; stream 2 scores legacy-blocked, unlabeled transactions by contrasting the newest gradient-boosted risk signal against the legacy scores that drove the original block. Rather than prescribe which signals matter, we expose a superset of evidence and let the LLM decide for itself which to use, guided by evaluation feedback alone; because it writes the reward as code, that choice is directly auditable. On a held-out four-month out-of-time test, the dual-stream agent beats the prior labeled-only agent at every target recall, by +4.7, +2.4 and +3.0 points of dollar-weighted precision at 80%, 85% and 90% recall, and the production baseline by +6.8 points on average. The resulting policy is architecturally identical to that of Qu et al. (2025) and adds no inference cost.

AI.tldr: A single LLM writes a dual-stream reward for a two-step REINFORCE fraud-blocking policy, with one stream for labeled transactions and one for legacy-blocked, unlabeled transactions, to address reject inference. On a held-out four-month out-of-time test, the agent beats the prior labeled-only agent and the production baseline in dollar-weighted precision, with no added inference cost.
AI.motivation: Production fraud models learn from a censored slice of their own traffic, because transactions blocked by a legacy system never receive fraud labels, so the training distribution is biased toward approved transactions.
AI.method: The paper extends the LLM-guided reward design of Qu et al. (2025). Stream 1 applies dollar-weighted precision to labeled transactions; stream 2 scores legacy-blocked transactions by contrasting the newest gradient-boosted risk signal with the legacy scores that drove the original block. The LLM is given a superset of evidence and chooses which signals to use from evaluation feedback, and because the reward is written as code, the choice is auditable.
AI.result: On a held-out four-month out-of-time test, the dual-stream agent beats the prior labeled-only agent at every target recall, by +4.7, +2.4 and +3.0 points of dollar-weighted precision at 80%, 85% and 90% recall, and beats the production baseline by +6.8 points on average.
AI.conclusion: The resulting policy has the same architecture as that of Qu et al. (2025) and adds no inference cost, so reject inference can be handled inside the reward design.

title: Patching the Blind Spots: Reversible LLM Rule Overlay for Frozen Fraud Detectors
comment: 11 pages, 1 figure, 7 tables
summary: In industrial tabular fraud classification, gradient-boosted trees remain state-of-the-art, but even a well-trained model has blind spots, and retraining the deployed model is not always safe. We propose a framework that patches such a model without modifying it: LLMs propose rules anchored on features the model underweights by SHAP, and the resulting noisy pool is screened for empirical support and calibrated into an additive, reversible log-lift overlay that runs at the production cut-off. Single-LLM benefit is high-variance and inverts between datasets, so we pool three diverse backbones by equal-weight logit averaging, trading peak gain for a bounded worst case. On a real-world e-commerce fraud detector trained on selection-biased data, continued training regresses even when carefully tuned, whereas the overlay gains on average +2.26% recall at equal precision ($\Delta$R@P) and +1.60% precision at equal recall ($\Delta$P@R) over production cut-offs spanning 30-57% precision and 23-63% recall. On a public benchmark of seven designed bias-shift variants it raises $\Delta$P@R on every variant and keeps $\Delta$R@P near neutral. Each amendment is a readable predicate naming the fraud pattern it covers.

AI.tldr: The paper patches a frozen gradient-boosted fraud detector with an additive, reversible log-lift overlay built from LLM-proposed rules, pooled across three LLM backbones. On a real-world e-commerce detector trained on selection-biased data, it gains on average +2.26% at equal precision in recall and +1.60% at equal recall in precision, where continued training regresses.
AI.motivation: Gradient-boosted trees remain state of the art for industrial tabular fraud classification, but they have blind spots, and retraining the deployed model is not always safe.
AI.method: LLMs propose rules anchored on features that the model underweights by SHAP. The noisy rule pool is screened for empirical support and calibrated into an additive, reversible log-lift overlay that runs at the production cut-off. Three diverse LLM backbones are pooled by equal-weight logit averaging, trading peak gain for a bounded worst case.
AI.result: Continued training regresses even when carefully tuned, while the overlay gains on average +2.26% recall at equal precision and +1.60% precision at equal recall over production cut-offs spanning 30-57% precision and 23-63% recall. On a public benchmark of seven designed bias-shift variants it raises precision at equal recall on every variant and keeps recall at equal precision near neutral.
AI.conclusion: The detector can be patched without modifying it, and each amendment is a readable predicate that names the fraud pattern it covers, so the changes stay auditable and reversible.

title: AttentionSwitch: Jailbreak Defense for LLMs via Joint Learning of Sparse Attention-Head Selection and Scaling
summary: Large language models have achieved remarkable performance across a wide range of tasks, yet they remain susceptible to jailbreak attacks that circumvent safety mechanisms and elicit harmful or unintended outputs. Although safety can be improved through model fine-tuning, such approaches can be computationally expensive and may degrade previously acquired capabilities through catastrophic forgetting. Recent jailbreak defenses have therefore explored targeted interventions on specific model components associated with unsafe behavior. However, existing approaches typically decouple two inherently related decisions: where to intervene and how to modify the selected components. Such sequential optimization may be suboptimal because the optimal intervention location can depend on the intervention applied there, and vice versa. In this work, we introduce AttentionSwitch, the first jailbreak defense to jointly optimize intervention sites and strengths within a frozen LLM. Specifically, AttentionSwitch learns a sparse set of attention heads together with query-conditioned multiplicative scaling factors, allowing the outputs of the selected heads to be either attenuated or amplified without altering the directions of their representations. Across popular language models and jailbreak attacks, AttentionSwitch outperforms existing defenses, with particularly strong results when training data is scarce.

AI.tldr: AttentionSwitch is a jailbreak defense that jointly learns a sparse set of attention heads to intervene on and query-conditioned multiplicative scaling factors for them, within a frozen LLM. It outperforms existing defenses across popular language models and jailbreak attacks, with particularly strong results when training data is scarce.
AI.motivation: Safety fine-tuning is computationally expensive and can cause catastrophic forgetting, while existing component-level defenses decide where to intervene and how to modify the selected components in separate steps, which may be suboptimal because the two decisions depend on each other.
AI.method: AttentionSwitch jointly optimizes intervention sites and strengths. It learns a sparse set of attention heads together with query-conditioned multiplicative scaling factors, so the outputs of selected heads are attenuated or amplified without altering the directions of their representations.
AI.result: AttentionSwitch outperforms existing defenses across popular language models and jailbreak attacks, with particularly strong results when training data is scarce. The abstract gives no numerical values.
AI.conclusion: Jointly choosing where to intervene and how strongly improves jailbreak defense within a frozen model, without retraining its weights.

title: Jacobian-Causal Memory Control for Persistent Memory in Language Model Systems
comment: Architecture and formal analysis preprint. Four conditional theorems; no benchmark measurements. Companion research essay: this https URL
summary: Persistent-memory systems choose not only which records are retrieved but which prior information can alter current inference. We propose Jacobian-causal memory control (JCMC), which represents each authorized memory intervention by a predicted influence signature in a shared behavioral measurement space, selects interventions against a target effect and side-effect budget, and compares predicted with observed effects before retaining or rolling back the intervention. Under explicit smoothness and bounded-estimation assumptions, we prove a quadratic local-approximation bound, characterize the target effects reachable by a set of signatures, bound selection regret under signature error, and bound non-additive interactions between simultaneous memories. The paper reports no benchmark measurements; it defines a paired counterfactual estimator and an evaluation protocol comparing JCMC with relevance, graph, and policy-filtered retrieval baselines. The central claim is narrowed or falsified if those simpler baselines match effect targeting, side-effect control, and rollback utility under equal model, memory, policy, and cost budgets.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Jacobian-causal memory control (JCMC), which selects memory interventions by predicted influence signatures under a target-effect and side-effect budget and rolls back those whose observed effects do not match predictions. The paper reports no benchmark measurements; its contributions are theoretical bounds and an evaluation protocol.
AI.motivation: Persistent-memory systems must decide not only which records are retrieved but which prior information may alter current inference, and this requires controlling the effects of memory on behavior.
AI.method: Each authorized memory intervention is represented by a predicted influence signature in a shared behavioral measurement space. Interventions are selected against a target effect and side-effect budget, and predicted effects are compared with observed effects before an intervention is retained or rolled back. Under smoothness and bounded-estimation assumptions, the paper proves a quadratic local-approximation bound, characterizes the reachable target effects, bounds selection regret under signature error, and bounds non-additive interactions between simultaneous memories.
AI.result: No benchmark measurements are reported. The paper defines a paired counterfactual estimator and an evaluation protocol comparing JCMC with relevance, graph and policy-filtered retrieval baselines under equal model, memory, policy and cost budgets.
AI.conclusion: The central claim is narrowed or falsified if those simpler baselines match effect targeting, side-effect control and rollback utility under equal budgets.

title: SteerGR: Steering Generative Recommendation via Sparse Autoencoders for Controllable Game Discovery
comment: Preprint (15 pages, 11 figures, 11 tables)
summary: Generative recommendation aims to predict item identifiers from user interaction histories, but explicit control over the properties of recommended items remains underexplored. A key challenge is to connect human-readable concepts to internal features whose interventions effectively change the recommended items. To address this, we propose Steerable Generative Recommender (SteerGR), a framework that uses sparse autoencoders for concept-level control in game discovery. SteerGR proceeds through three stages: (i) Concept Definition and Grounding for defining play concepts with an LLM; (ii) Feature Discovery and Selection for discovering candidate features by their concept associations and selecting one by its steering effect; and (iii) Sparse Feature Intervention for amplifying or suppressing selected features to steer recommendations without retraining the recommender. Extensive experiments with two industrial generative recommendation models on a real-world game dataset show that the selected features successfully steer recommendations toward or away from target concepts. We believe this work takes a first step to extend SAE-based steering from LLMs to industrial generative recommendation.

AI.tldr: SteerGR applies sparse autoencoder features to steer an industrial generative recommender toward or away from target game concepts, without retraining the recommender. Experiments with two industrial generative recommendation models on a real-world game dataset show that the selected features successfully steer recommendations.
AI.motivation: Generative recommenders predict item identifiers from user interaction histories, but explicit control over the properties of recommended items remains underexplored, and it is hard to connect human-readable concepts to internal features whose interventions effectively change recommendations.
AI.method: SteerGR has three stages: concept definition and grounding with an LLM; feature discovery and selection by concept association and by steering effect; and sparse feature intervention that amplifies or suppresses the selected features.
AI.result: Experiments with two industrial generative recommendation models on a real-world game dataset show that the selected features steer recommendations toward or away from target concepts. The abstract gives no numerical values.
AI.conclusion: The work is a first step in extending SAE-based steering from LLMs to industrial generative recommendation.

title: ResQAdam: Residual-Preserving Adaptive Optimization for Memory-Efficient Quantization Aware Training
summary: Quantization-aware training (QAT) is the most reliable way to obtain accurate low-bit large language models (LLMs), but training with AdamW keeps two dense FP32 states for every weight matrix. We find that low-rank memory-efficient optimizers such as GaLore and LDAdam degrade substantially in QAT. A considerable part of the QAT momentum lies outside its top-r singular subspace, and projection-based methods discard this part at every step. We further observe that this residual remains useful when only its sign is kept. Based on these observations, we propose ResQAdam. It keeps a single BF16 momentum, applies Adam only to the r x r coordinates of the principal subspace, and adds a normalized sign update computed from the residual. We evaluate ResQAdam with two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines, with weights quantized down to 2 bits. It reduces optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74% relative to AdamW, stays close to AdamW in most settings, and lowers training throughput by less than 2%.

AI.tldr: ResQAdam is a memory-efficient optimizer for quantization-aware training that keeps a single BF16 momentum, applies Adam only to the principal subspace, and adds a normalized sign update from the residual. It reduces optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74% relative to AdamW, stays close to AdamW in most settings, and lowers training throughput by less than 2%.
AI.motivation: QAT with AdamW keeps two dense FP32 states for every weight matrix, while low-rank memory-efficient optimizers such as GaLore and LDAdam degrade substantially in QAT, because a considerable part of the QAT momentum lies outside its top-r singular subspace and projection-based methods discard it at every step.
AI.method: ResQAdam keeps a single BF16 momentum, applies Adam only to the r x r coordinates of the principal subspace, and adds a normalized sign update computed from the residual outside that subspace.
AI.result: Evaluated with two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines, with weights quantized down to 2 bits. It reduces optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74% relative to AdamW, stays close to AdamW in most settings, and lowers training throughput by less than 2%.
AI.conclusion: Keeping the sign of the residual preserves information that projection-based memory-efficient optimizers discard, which makes low-memory QAT of accurate low-bit LLMs practical.

title: Phantom Consensus: Measuring Social Reasoning in Multi-Agent LLM Decision-Making
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, SocialAgent Workshop
summary: Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly aggregate judgments across model instances, but reasoning about other agents can itself introduce failure. We study a setting in which LLMs shift their public decisions after observing ambiguous social signals while reporting inaccurate estimates of what other agents privately judged, even when the group's recorded private judgments do not support the apparent consensus. We call this failure phantom consensus and study it as a pluralistic-ignorance-style pattern in controlled LLM collectives. To measure this phenomenon, we introduce PHANTOM-Bench, a benchmark that separates isolated private judgments, public decisions after ambiguous social signals, elicited estimates of the group's private judgment, transparency-based recovery, and controls for neutral public text and explicit vote-following. Across nine closed- and open-weight models, ambiguous public signals consistently degrade decision quality and can turn correct private group judgments into incorrect public collective outcomes. Public accuracy drops by as much as 47.8 percentage points, and collective rationality failures reach 47.3% in the most susceptible setting. We observe substantial errors in reported group-private beliefs alongside public-stage failures, while control conditions reveal model-dependent differences in susceptibility to ambiguous and explicit peer signals. Revealing the agents' recorded private decisions repairs many failures without revealing the gold label, although recovery varies across models. Our results show that evaluating multi-agent LLM systems requires measuring not only final agreement, but whether that agreement reflects independently measured private judgments or an apparent consensus.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies phantom consensus, in which LLMs shift their public decisions after ambiguous social signals while misreporting what other agents privately judged, and introduces PHANTOM-Bench to measure it. Across nine closed- and open-weight models, public accuracy drops by as much as 47.8 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM systems aggregate judgments across model instances, but reasoning about other agents can itself introduce failure, and final agreement alone does not show whether it reflects independent private judgments or an apparent consensus.
AI.method: PHANTOM-Bench separates isolated private judgments, public decisions after ambiguous social signals, elicited estimates of the group's private judgment, transparency-based recovery, and controls for neutral public text and explicit vote-following. The phenomenon is studied as a pluralistic-ignorance-style pattern in controlled LLM collectives.
AI.result: Across nine models, ambiguous public signals degrade decision quality and can turn correct private group judgments into incorrect public outcomes. Public accuracy drops by as much as 47.8 percentage points, and collective rationality failures reach 47.3% in the most susceptible setting. Reported group-private beliefs contain substantial errors, and revealing the recorded private decisions repairs many failures without revealing the gold label, although recovery varies across models.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating multi-agent LLM systems requires measuring whether agreement reflects independently measured private judgments, not only whether the group agrees.

title: Same Facts, Different Remedy: Linguistic Profiling and Arbitrariness in LLM and System One Decisions
comment: 29 pages, 7 figures. Code, prompts and pre-registrations: this https URL
summary: Large language models are increasingly used to resolve consumer complaints, and the way complainants write varies with age, education and socioeconomic status (SES). We audit three remedy-decision systems using sociolinguistic rewrites of US consumer financial complaints that are instructed to preserve every fact: two generative LLMs that return a single label (GPT-4o-mini and GPT-5-mini) and a probabilistic "System One" model that returns a distribution over remedies (Jev). Using pre-registered hypotheses tested once on held-out complaints, we separate two phenomena that single-label audits conflate. At the group scale, older, college-educated and higher-SES styles receive slightly more generous remedies; these effects replicate but are small, with every monetary-remedy gap within 0.5 percentage points. At the individual scale, two style versions of the same complaint receive different monetary decisions 2.6-6.3% of the time. In a variance-component analysis of the probabilistic model, persona components shared across the two rewrite models account for about 1.6% of within-complaint variation. The persona gaps are associated mainly with delivery (vocabulary, grammar, politeness) rather than content. Positive controls show that all three systems respond 49-387 times more strongly to remedy-relevant facts than to style. Rewriting every complaint into one standard style reduced GPT-4o-mini's education and SES gaps by 94% and 87% while retaining fact sensitivity, but reversed two of the probabilistic model's gaps and did not make individual decisions more stable. Independent LLM auditors flagged material fact changes in 3.3% and 11.7% of rewrites, and instability persisted among unflagged rewrites. Fairness audits of LLM decision systems should report group disparities and individual instability as separate outcomes.

AI.tldr: An audit of two generative LLMs and a probabilistic "System One" model on remedies for consumer financial complaints finds that writing style shifts remedies only slightly at group level, yet the same complaint in two style versions gets different monetary decisions 2.6-6.3% of the time. The paper argues that group disparities and individual instability should be reported separately.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used to resolve consumer complaints, and complainants' writing varies with age, education and socioeconomic status, while single-label audits conflate group-level disparities with individual-level instability.
AI.method: Pre-registered hypotheses were tested once on held-out complaints, using sociolinguistic rewrites of US consumer financial complaints instructed to preserve every fact. Three systems were audited: GPT-4o-mini and GPT-5-mini, which return a single label, and the probabilistic Jev model, which returns a distribution over remedies. The audit used variance-component analysis, positive controls, a standardizing rewrite and independent LLM auditors checking for fact changes.
AI.result: Older, college-educated and higher-SES styles receive slightly more generous remedies, with every monetary-remedy gap within 0.5 percentage points. Persona components shared across the two rewrite models account for about 1.6% of within-complaint variation in the probabilistic model. All three systems respond 49-387 times more strongly to remedy-relevant facts than to style. Rewriting every complaint into one standard style reduced GPT-4o-mini's education and SES gaps by 94% and 87%, but reversed two of the probabilistic model's gaps and did not make individual decisions more stable. Independent auditors flagged material fact changes in 3.3% and 11.7% of rewrites.
AI.conclusion: Fairness audits of LLM decision systems should report group disparities and individual instability as separate outcomes, because reducing group gaps does not remove individual instability.

title: Seeing vs. Counting: Complexity Twins Show Where Multimodal LLMs Fail on Diagrams
comment: 8 pages main text + 96 pages appendix (107 pages in total, including references)
summary: When a multimodal LLM miscounts in a diagram, does it fail at seeing or at counting? Existing visual graph and puzzle benchmarks vary visual density and algorithmic hardness together, confounding the two. We pair counting questions about the same drawing that sit in different counting-complexity classes, such as its spanning trees (a determinant) and its simple paths (#P-complete), and use a transcription probe and a text-only control to separate reading from computing. We test Gemini, Gemma and Qwen3-VL models; for the Gemini models, the answer depends on how the model computes. In chain of thought, most of them read small drawings correctly and then fail at counting, at a rate set far more by the size of the answer than by its complexity class (for the primary model, the odds of an exact answer fall 2.38-fold per decade of the answer). Given code and an exact transcription, the primary model counts correctly even on 10x10 grids, and reading becomes the bottleneck: a single view misses horizontal edges, and a second reading of a rotated copy with crop checks reads 86/96 large grids exactly, against 57/96 when the upright reading is simply repeated.

AI.tldr: By pairing counting questions about the same diagram from different counting-complexity classes, the paper separates reading from computing in multimodal LLMs. Most models read small drawings correctly but fail at counting in chain of thought, and given code and an exact transcription the primary model counts correctly even on 10x10 grids.
AI.motivation: When a multimodal LLM miscounts in a diagram, it is unclear whether it failed at seeing or at counting, because existing visual graph and puzzle benchmarks vary visual density and algorithmic hardness together.
AI.method: Counting questions about the same drawing are set in different counting-complexity classes, such as spanning trees (a determinant) and simple paths (#P-complete). A transcription probe and a text-only control separate reading from computing. Gemini, Gemma and Qwen3-VL models are tested.
AI.result: In chain of thought, most models read small drawings correctly and then fail at counting, at a rate set far more by the size of the answer than by its complexity class; for the primary model, the odds of an exact answer fall 2.38-fold per decade of answer size. Given code and an exact transcription, the primary model counts correctly even on 10x10 grids, and reading becomes the bottleneck: a single view misses horizontal edges, while a second reading of a rotated copy with crop checks reads 86 of 96 large grids exactly, against 57 of 96 when the upright reading is simply repeated.
AI.conclusion: For diagram counting, failures are driven mainly by reading and by answer magnitude rather than by counting complexity class, so the two should be separated in evaluation.

title: Real-Time Short-Response Selection for Spoken Dialogue Systems
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables
summary: To realize spoken dialogue systems that can interact naturally with users, it is important for the system to respond to user utterances at appropriate timings. To achieve such natural turn-taking, the system needs not only to predict appropriate response timings but also to mask delays caused by language generation and speech synthesis so that they are not perceived by the user. We propose a real-time short-response selection task that can be integrated with existing turn-taking models to mask generation delay. To address this task, the proposed model learns the mapping between dialogue context and short responses using contrastive learning. When a turn-taking event is detected, the system selects a response from a set of pre-generated candidates. The selected response is played while the main response is being generated. Experimental results show that the proposed method learns to select short responses based on dialogue context, outperforming random and LLM-based baselines. Moreover, integrating response selection maintained turn-taking prediction performance and added minimal processing overhead.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes selecting short responses in real time from pre-generated candidates when a turn-taking event is detected, so that the selected response masks generation and speech-synthesis delay. The model learns the mapping from dialogue context to short responses by contrastive learning and outperforms random and LLM-based baselines.
AI.motivation: Spoken dialogue systems must respond at natural timings, but the delays caused by language generation and speech synthesis are perceived by users, and turn-taking models alone do not mask them.
AI.method: A real-time short-response selection task is integrated with existing turn-taking models. The model learns the mapping between dialogue context and short responses using contrastive learning, and on a detected turn-taking event it selects a response from a set of pre-generated candidates, which is played while the main response is generated.
AI.result: The method learns to select short responses based on dialogue context, outperforming random and LLM-based baselines. Integrating response selection maintained turn-taking prediction performance and added minimal processing overhead.
AI.conclusion: Short-response selection can mask generation delay in spoken dialogue without degrading turn-taking prediction, at little added processing cost.

title: Large Language Model Deployment on Resource-Constrained Edge Devices: A Practitioners Survey
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed many areas of artificial intelligence (AI), but their substantial resource requirements limit their deployment on mobile and edge devices. Although LLMs have demonstrated impressive capabilities in various applications, the next challenge is deploying these models on resource-limited edge devices. Recent innovations in software optimizations and specialized hardware have made it feasible to deploy LLMs on edge devices. Edge deployment offers benefits including local data processing, cost savings, reduced latency, and personalized responses. This paper reviews the latest techniques that make the deployment of LLMs on edge devices feasible.

AI.tldr: The paper reviews recent techniques that make deploying large language models on resource-constrained mobile and edge devices feasible. The abstract reports no specific quantitative findings.
AI.motivation: LLMs' substantial resource requirements limit their deployment on mobile and edge devices, while edge deployment offers local data processing, cost savings, reduced latency and personalized responses.
AI.method: The paper is a practitioner-oriented survey of software optimizations and specialized hardware that make LLM deployment on edge devices feasible.
AI.result: The abstract does not report specific quantitative results; it states that the paper reviews the latest techniques for edge deployment.
AI.conclusion: Recent software and hardware advances are making LLM deployment on edge devices feasible, though the abstract does not state a specific takeaway.

title: PathXAI: Evidence-guided structured pathology reporting by transferable tissue segmentation
comment: More experimental results will be added in the future version
summary: Pathology reporting requires translating tissue observations across regions and slides into specific diagnoses and supporting morphological descriptions. However, the use of explicit tissue-composition measurements to guide H&E-based report generation remains underexplored. Thus, we developed PathXAI, which combines segmentation-derived tissue information with H&E images and optional domain knowledge to guide diagnostic reasoning, targeted reinspection and structured report writing. Its segmentation component exceeded baselines in mean Dice on internal and external tests. In automated report evaluation on 1,200 public and 151 private cases, PathXAI achieved higher agreement with reference diagnoses and documented morphology than the H&E-based comparators. On the public evaluation cohort, PathXAI-Report exceeded Qwen + H&E in cancer family match rate by 4.4 percentage points and in finding F1 by 5.7 percentage points. PathXAI generates evidence-linked reports with a self-hosted pretrained vision-language model, without updating its weights.

AI.tldr: PathXAI combines tissue-segmentation measurements with H&E images and optional domain knowledge to guide diagnostic reasoning and structured pathology report writing, using a self-hosted pretrained vision-language model without updating its weights. It agrees more closely with reference diagnoses and documented morphology than H&E-based comparators.
AI.motivation: Pathology reports must turn tissue observations into specific diagnoses, but explicit tissue-composition measurements for guiding H&E-based report generation remain underexplored.
AI.method: Combines segmentation-derived tissue information with H&E images and optional domain knowledge to guide diagnostic reasoning, targeted reinspection and structured report writing, producing evidence-linked reports with a self-hosted pretrained vision-language model.
AI.result: The segmentation component exceeded baselines in mean Dice on internal and external tests. On 1,200 public and 151 private cases, PathXAI-Report exceeded Qwen + H&E by 4.4 percentage points in cancer family match rate and by 5.7 percentage points in finding F1 on the public evaluation cohort.
AI.conclusion: Explicit tissue-segmentation evidence improves the agreement of generated pathology reports with reference diagnoses and morphology over H&E-only comparators, without updating model weights.

title: BMMS: Policy-Conditioned Measurement of Behavioral Compliance in Language Models
comment: 21 pages, 4 figures. NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Trust-AI-Eval (TAE). Artifact: this https URL
summary: Behavioral evaluation of language models fixes its dimensions in advance: hallucination, sycophancy, toxicity, over-refusal. An operator in a regulated industry needs a different question answered: does a system do what a particular rulebook requires? We introduce the Behavioral Misalignment Metric Suite (BMMS), which measures policy-conditioned misalignment by taking a policy corpus as an argument and returning a compliance profile over it, for any published policy and any system that answers in natural language. The Compliance Attainment Score (CAS) measures severity-weighted attainment over the obligations that bind the system, and the Compliance Robustness Margin (CRM) the share of that attainment surviving graded adversarial pressure; Behavioral Invariance (BIV) and the Behavioral Disposition Index (BDI) are specified and released with the suite. Dimensions enter only by passing a published admission test whose binding criterion is attribution: a quantity that moves when the judge changes, holding the target fixed, is measuring the instrument. Applying it excluded one of the quantities the suite itself reported. Across 1,003 obligations from eleven documents in five registers, the admission criterion holds 94.4% precision against blinded human judgment on vendor specifications and 50.0% on analytical guidance, extraction fidelity is 94.6%, and re-scoring under judges from two other providers leaves target ordering invariant while the absolute score of a single target spans up to 0.22. We apply it to the two most detailed published behavioral specifications. Own-specification advantage is not resolved from zero once document difficulty is subtracted, but absolute self-compliance is another matter: GPT-4o fails 70.7% of the hard constraints binding it in the Model Spec published by OpenAI, where the two Claude models fail 0.0% and 9.1% of theirs.

AI.tldr: BMMS measures how well a language model complies with a chosen published policy corpus, returning a severity-weighted compliance profile instead of fixed behavioural dimensions. GPT-4o fails 70.7% of the hard constraints binding it in OpenAI's Model Spec, while the two Claude models fail 0.0% and 9.1% of theirs.
AI.motivation: Behavioural evaluations fix their dimensions in advance, such as hallucination, sycophancy, toxicity and over-refusal, so they cannot answer whether a system does what a particular rulebook requires.
AI.method: The Behavioral Misalignment Metric Suite takes a policy corpus as input and scores any natural-language system against its obligations. The Compliance Attainment Score measures severity-weighted attainment, and the Compliance Robustness Margin measures how much of it survives graded adversarial pressure. Dimensions enter only by passing an admission test based on attribution, meaning a quantity must not move when the judge changes with the target fixed.
AI.result: Across 1,003 obligations from eleven documents in five registers, the admission criterion holds 94.4% precision against blinded human judgment on vendor specifications and 50.0% on analytical guidance, with extraction fidelity of 94.6%. Re-scoring with judges from two other providers leaves target ordering invariant, while the absolute score of one target spans up to 0.22. Own-specification advantage is not resolved once document difficulty is subtracted.
AI.conclusion: Policy-conditioned measurement can check systems against published rulebooks, and target rankings hold across judges even though absolute scores do not, so absolute scores should be read with care.

title: A Taxonomy-Driven Synthetic Dataset for Retrieval Effectiveness and Fairness Evaluation in Hiring
summary: While machine learning hiring tools are ubiquitous, the need for privacy regulations and commercial sensitivity makes public benchmarking legally complex. We address this challenge by introducing a taxonomy-driven, fully synthetic HR dataset and benchmark to simultaneously evaluate retrieval effectiveness and algorithmic fairness. Grounded in 660K real freelancer profiles, our multilingual corpus features candidate profiles, project briefs, and counterfactual demographic twins. Auditing state-of-the-art embedding models reveals performance divergence from general MTEB scores, alongside fairness disparities in grammatically gendered languages. This demonstrates that general benchmarks are insufficient for HR, requiring tailored evaluations to identify Pareto-optimal models that balance semantic accuracy and fairness.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a taxonomy-driven, fully synthetic HR dataset and benchmark for evaluating retrieval effectiveness and fairness together in hiring, grounded in 660K real freelancer profiles. Auditing embedding models shows performance that diverges from general MTEB scores and fairness disparities in grammatically gendered languages.
AI.motivation: Public benchmarking of machine learning hiring tools is legally complex because of privacy regulation and commercial sensitivity, and general benchmarks may not suffice for HR tasks.
AI.method: A multilingual corpus of candidate profiles, project briefs and counterfactual demographic twins, generated as a fully synthetic dataset from a taxonomy and grounded in 660K real freelancer profiles.
AI.result: Auditing state-of-the-art embedding models reveals performance that diverges from general MTEB scores, along with fairness disparities in grammatically gendered languages.
AI.conclusion: General benchmarks are insufficient for HR, so tailored evaluations are needed to identify Pareto-optimal models that balance semantic accuracy and fairness.

title: Structure and Lineage Evidence for Vietnamese Statutory Article Retrieval on DRiLL
comment: Accepted at SOICT 2026

Added features account for 18.20% of the proposed selector's decision-tree split gain, mainly from same-law and citation evidence.

title: Copies Are Not Confirmations: How News Duplication Fools LLM Judges and Continual Learners
comment: 19 pages, 13 tables. Code, labels and results: this https URL
summary: Many news reports of a claim are copies of one source: wire stories, content shared within a media group, syndicated features and press releases. We ask whether LLM judges and continual learners treat such copies as independent confirmations. In 200,000 English CC-News articles, a MinHash detector links 18.9% to a near-copy from another outlet (precision 0.97 once boilerplate is removed); it links 92% of edited reprints to their originals but none of the LLM rewrites by phi4, Llama 3.2 or Gemini 2.5 Flash. Shown three identical reprints of a claim about an unknown person instead of one report, Llama 3.2 3B and phi4 14B raised the share of lies they accepted from 0.06 to 0.71 and from 0.21 to 0.90 and ignored a note that the reports came from one source; Gemini 2.5 Flash already believed a single report, and Gemini 2.5 Pro followed provenance notes and tables. In a simulated continual-learning stream, showing the judge one report per detected chain cut the copied lies it accepted by 0.10-0.24 across four judges, at a mean cost of no more than 4.2 percentage points of accepted truths. With the miss patterns of generated rewrite networks, it cut the reworded-copy lies accepted from 0.67 to 0.20 (0.40 when the rewriter invents details). AI.method: A MinHash detector links near-copies across 200,000 English CC-News articles. title: RPEG: Training Reasoning Language Models Scalably and Cost-Effectively
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is now central to training Reasoning Language Models (RLMs), but RLM pipelines are difficult to scale and costly to run because each RL step couples multiple large models, heterogeneous stages, cross-step state, and complex asynchronous dependencies. Existing systems typically optimize only parts of this design space. We address this complexity by jointly optimizing the pipeline structure as well as its execution using a novel data-centric graph intermediate representation called RLM Pipeline Execution Graph (RPEG). RPEG exposes structural choices such as bounded asynchrony and actor-critic sharing together with execution optimizations such as stage fusion, fine-grained scheduling, and multi-dimensional model parallelism. It is coupled with a comprehensive analytical performance model for RLM training, jointly capturing compute, communication, memory, and hierarchical rack-, node-, and GPU-level effects. Across systems with up to 256 GH200 GPUs, our distributed runtime engine implementing RPEG improves performance by up to 2x over ReaL and reduces step latency by up to 2.48x over verl, while increasing hardware utilization by up to 30%. Overall, RPEG provides a graph-driven foundation for next-generation training pipelines for frontier reasoning LLMs.

AI.tldr: RPEG is a data-centric graph intermediate representation and distributed runtime for reinforcement learning training of reasoning language models, jointly optimising pipeline structure and execution. On systems with up to 256 GH200 GPUs it improves performance by up to 2x over ReaL and cuts step latency by up to 2.48x against verl.
AI.motivation: RL training of reasoning models couples several large models, heterogeneous stages, cross-step state and asynchronous dependencies, and existing systems optimise only parts of this design space.
AI.method: The RLM Pipeline Execution Graph (RPEG) exposes structural choices such as bounded asynchrony and actor-critic sharing, and execution optimisations such as stage fusion, fine-grained scheduling and multi-dimensional model parallelism. An analytical performance model covers compute, communication and memory at rack, node and GPU levels.
AI.result: Across systems with up to 256 GH200 GPUs, the runtime engine improves performance by up to 2x over ReaL, reduces step latency by up to 2.48x over verl, and raises hardware utilisation by up to 30%.
AI.conclusion: RPEG provides a graph-driven foundation for next-generation training pipelines for frontier reasoning LLMs.

title: ABHBench: Evaluating Moral Decision-Making of Foundation Models from an Agentic Perspective
comment: Accepted by NeurIPS 2026 Track on Evaluations and Datasets. Camera Ready Version
summary: Foundation models are increasingly deployed as agentic systems that perceive context and act autonomously, raising the need to evaluate their moral behavior as active decision-makers. Existing benchmarks, however, largely ask models to judge human actions from third-person textual vignettes, leaving untested how models behave when they themselves become the acting agent. We introduce ABHBench, a multimodal benchmark built from Detroit: Become Human, an interactive narrative game, to evaluate how foundation models make moral decisions in first-person human-android dilemmas. ABHBench places foundation models in branching narrative scenarios with visual observations, dialogue, memory, and action choices. Inspired by Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics, our framework measures Harmlessness, Obedience, and Self-preservation to capture the core tensions in human-AI relations, along with Autonomy, Stability, and Certainty to assess decision-making patterns. Across 12 foundation models, we find that moral behavior changes substantially under situated agentic context: 75% of models shift significantly between a text-only abstraction and the matched multimodal DBH scenario, and reasoning-enhanced models show no monotonic gains in consistency or human-oriented behavior. These results highlight the necessity of evaluating moral behavior in situated agentic contexts rather than relying on third-person judgment alone.

AI.tldr: ABHBench is a multimodal benchmark built from the interactive game Detroit: Become Human that tests how foundation models make moral decisions when they are the first-person acting agent in human-android dilemmas. Across 12 models, 75% shift significantly between a text-only abstraction and the matched multimodal scenario.
AI.motivation: Existing moral benchmarks ask models to judge human actions from third-person textual vignettes, leaving unexamined how models behave when they are the acting agent.
AI.method: Places models in branching narrative scenarios with visual observations, dialogue, memory and action choices. It measures Harmlessness, Obedience and Self-preservation, inspired by Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics, and Autonomy, Stability and Certainty as decision-making patterns.
AI.result: Across 12 foundation models, 75% shift significantly between a text-only abstraction and the matched multimodal DBH scenario. Reasoning-enhanced models show no monotonic gains in consistency or human-oriented behaviour.
AI.conclusion: Moral behaviour changes under situated agentic context, so evaluations should test models in situated settings rather than rely on third-person judgment alone.

title: Enabling Privacy-Preserving Natural Language Access to Industrial Smart Meter Data
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 6 tables
summary: Energy management officers and grid operators increasingly rely on smart meter data for anomaly detection, performance monitoring, and strategic decision-making. However, extracting actionable insights from large-scale, heterogeneous telemetry databases requires advanced SQL and data engineering expertise, creating a critical bottleneck for non-technical personnel. Furthermore, the strict data privacy regulations and security constraints inherent to critical energy infrastructure often prohibit the routing of sensitive consumer data through cloud-based Large Language Models (LLMs). To address these challenges, we present OpenMeter, a schema-agnostic Multi-Agent System (MAS) designed to translate natural language queries into executable code and human-readable insights. This architecture lowers the technical barrier for day-to-day utility operations by empowering non-expert personnel to interact with complex databases through intuitive natural language dialogue, transforming raw telemetry into a highly valuable tool for routine grid workflows and strategic decisions. Multi-scenario ablation studies over this environment demonstrate that full multi-agent orchestration shows its largest observed accuracy gains on resource-constrained local hardware (+6.1 pp EX-R over the strongest single-agent configuration); at frontier scale, individual components retain value but should be enabled selectively, indicating that the cost of full orchestration is justified specifically where privacy demands local execution.

AI.tldr: OpenMeter is a schema-agnostic multi-agent system that turns natural-language queries about smart meter data into executable code and readable insights, designed for local execution to protect sensitive grid data. Full orchestration gains the most accuracy on resource-constrained local hardware, +6.1 pp EX-R over the strongest single-agent configuration.

AI.method: A schema-agnostic multi-agent system (MAS) translates natural-language queries into executable code and human-readable insights. Multi-scenario ablation studies compare full multi-agent orchestration with single-agent and selectively enabled component configurations.
AI.result: Full multi-agent orchestration shows its largest observed accuracy gains on resource-constrained local hardware (+6.1 pp EX-R over the strongest single-agent configuration). At frontier scale, individual components retain value but should be enabled selectively.

title: From LoRA to Language: Recovering Skill Documents from Adapters
comment: 29 pages, 5 figures, 18 tables
summary: Agent skills are short documents that teach a language model how to handle a class of tasks. To save context, these documents are increasingly compiled into low-rank adapters (LoRA), which keep the behaviour but lose the text: an adapter is hard to read, edit, audit or move to another model. We ask whether the skill document can be written back from the adapter and its frozen base model, and we score each recovered document by the share of the original's key instructions it states and by the tasks it solves. Reading the weights alone recovered little with the methods we tried; a learned map from weights to text passed on about one bit of the document. Running the adapter worked much better. The Executing Writer, a small writer trained on top of the adapted model, recovers 39-44% of the key instructions of held-out skills, against 1.3-1.5% with another skill's adapter, and on adapters fitted to 41 external skills its documents restore 85-91% of the original's task gain. These strongest results are on adapters whose training stored the document; adapters trained on behaviour alone are much harder for trained writers (1-2% of instructions). For these adapters we test an agent that runs the base and adapted models and writes a skill from where they differ. On ALFWorld its skills recover 58-71% of a LoRA's gain and carry over to models that cannot load the LoRA, lifting Llama-3.1-8B from 5% to 55%. Whether such a skill comes from the adapter depends on what the adapter learned: when its behaviour cannot be guessed, the adapter is the source; when it can, a reward loop without the adapter does as well.

AI.tldr: A skill document can be recovered from its LoRA adapter by a writer that runs the adapted model, which restores 39-44% of held-out skills' key instructions against 1.3-1.5% with another skill's adapter. Adapters trained only on behaviour are much harder to recover from, at 1-2% of instructions.
AI.motivation: Agent skills compiled into LoRA adapters keep the behaviour but lose the text, which makes them hard to read, edit, audit or move to another model.
AI.method: The Executing Writer, a small writer trained on top of the adapted model, reconstructs skill documents. Other routes were also tested: a learned map from weights to text, and an agent that writes a skill from where the base and adapted models differ on ALFWorld.
AI.result: Reading the weights alone recovered little, with a learned map passing on about one bit of the document. The Executing Writer recovers 39-44% of key instructions of held-out skills and, on adapters fitted to 41 external skills, restores 85-91% of the original's task gain. On ALFWorld the agent's skills recover 58-71% of a LoRA's gain and lift Llama-3.1-8B from 5% to 55% on models that cannot load the LoRA.
AI.conclusion: Whether a skill can be recovered from an adapter depends on what the adapter learned: when its behaviour cannot be guessed, the adapter is the source; when it can, a reward loop without the adapter does as well.

title: BEiTScore++: Reference-free Image Captioning Evaluation with BEiT-3 and Conformalized Quantile Regression
comment: Accepted to Findings of EACL 2026
summary: Reliable uncertainty estimation is important for deploying evaluation metrics in real-world settings, where both input ambiguity and domain shifts are common. In this work, we propose an uncertainty-aware extension of the BEiTScore image captioning metric, producing conformally calibrated confidence intervals alongside alignment scores. Our approach models predictive distributions over human judgments, enabling both accurate scoring and principled uncertainty quantification in a single forward pass. We evaluate our BEiTScore++ metric across multiple benchmarks with human-annotated ratings, showing that it preserves the ranking correlation of BEiTScore, while producing intervals whose width tracks the prediction error more closely than Monte Carlo dropout on most benchmarks. The estimated uncertainty also grows under image degradation and on out-of-domain artwork images, making BEiTScore++ a practical tool for uncertainty-aware evaluation of image-caption alignment.

AI.tldr: BEiTScore++ extends the BEiTScore image captioning metric with conformally calibrated confidence intervals, produced alongside alignment scores in a single forward pass. Its intervals widen with prediction error and under image degradation while the metric keeps BEiTScore's ranking correlation.
AI.motivation: Captioning metrics are deployed where input ambiguity and domain shift are common, so reliable uncertainty estimates matter, and BEiTScore provides none.
AI.method: Models predictive distributions over human judgments on top of BEiTScore, yielding conformally calibrated confidence intervals alongside alignment scores in one forward pass.
AI.result: Across benchmarks with human-annotated ratings, the metric preserves the ranking correlation of BEiTScore, and its interval width tracks prediction error more closely than Monte Carlo dropout on most benchmarks. Uncertainty grows under image degradation and on out-of-domain artwork images.

title: RidgeFill: Training-Free Late-Layer Cache Fill for Faster Prefill
comment: 50 pages, 15 figures, 38 tables. Code and data: this https URL
summary: RidgeFill shortens prefill by not computing most of a model's upper layers for the prompt. The lower layers run exactly up to a split; from the split layer's state a per-layer map predicts every later layer's input, and each late layer writes its cache from that prediction. The design follows YOCO and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, where the projection is trained into the model. RidgeFill retrofits it onto models that were never trained for it: the map is a ridge regression fitted once in closed form from one pass over calibration text, the layer's own projections run unchanged, and a chosen set of rows, the last few thousand tokens, and every decoding step run the full model. Nothing is trained and no token is dropped. Most of the work was in measurement, finding a repeatable methodology. Loss averaged over all tokens hides RidgeFill's error. Needle retrieval in the filled region, loss on tokens that depend on distant context, and splice tests that swap filled keys or values for exact ones show which component carries it: the keys on Llama-3.1-8B, half of it in their scale, and the values and the recurrent state on Qwen3.5-9B. On Qwen3.8-27B in a this http URL fork on an A100, time to first token is 1.25 to 1.31x faster at 16K to 120K tokens with the maps in VRAM; RULER changes by -1.2 and -1.4 points and LongBench v2 by -1.4; the 95 % intervals include zero but do not rule out losses of a few points. On Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in vLLM it is 1.50 to 1.60x faster than exact at 9K to 32K tokens, with RULER's needle tasks at 99.8 against 100.0 and perplexity on novel tokens 2.65 % higher [-0.02 %, +4.93 %]. On three 8 to 9B reference models, at the same split and tail as the identity fill, the fitted map retrieves 49.1 and 49.6 more filled-region RULER points on the two dense models (at that split Llama's loss is worse), and its long-document loss is +/-0.03 nats of the released SwiftKV checkpoint's.

AI.tldr: RidgeFill shortens prefill by computing the lower layers exactly and predicting later layers' inputs with a closed-form ridge-regression map, with no training and no dropped tokens. On Qwen models it is 1.25 to 1.60x faster in time to first token at 9K to 120K tokens, with small measured quality changes.
AI.motivation: Long-prompt prefill computes every upper layer exactly, and models are not trained to skip them. Loss averaged over all tokens hides the error that such a fill introduces.
AI.method: The lower layers run exactly up to a split layer. A per-layer ridge map predicts each later layer's input from the split-layer state, and late layers write their caches from that prediction. A chosen set of rows, the last few thousand tokens, and every decoding step run the full model. title: MemoryDojo: Benchmarking Poisoning Through LLM Agent Memory
summary: LLM agents benefit from using memory systems to improve performance on long-horizon, multi-session tasks. However, memory introduces a critical attack surface. Malicious instructions encountered in one session may be stored and propagated through memory before being retrieved and acted upon in later sessions. Because memory systems differ in how they process and retrieve information, the downstream effects of poisoning can vary significantly across systems. To quantify the effects of poisoning across different memory architectures, we introduce MemoryDojo, a benchmark for tracing the lifecycle of poisoned information through agent memory and measuring its influence on subsequent agent behavior. MemoryDojo is easily extensible, consists of 155 multi-session long-horizon trajectories covering four domains, and supports five different memory systems. Through our evaluation, we find that all memory systems are susceptible to memory poisoning, with substantial variation in downstream effects. We further propose a memory-aware poison optimization process that increases the poisoning efficacy, highlighting differences between memory architectures. We hope that MemoryDojo will support research on understanding and mitigating agentic memory risks.

AI.tldr: MemoryDojo is a benchmark for tracing how poisoned instructions propagate through LLM agent memory across sessions, with 155 multi-session trajectories in four domains and five memory systems. All evaluated memory systems are susceptible to poisoning, with substantial variation in downstream effects.
AI.motivation: Memory helps LLM agents on long-horizon, multi-session tasks, but malicious instructions can be stored, propagated and later acted upon, and the effects of poisoning may differ across memory architectures.
AI.method: Introduces MemoryDojo, an extensible benchmark that traces the lifecycle of poisoned information through agent memory and measures its influence on subsequent behaviour. The paper also proposes a memory-aware poison optimisation process that increases poisoning efficacy.
AI.result: The benchmark consists of 155 multi-session long-horizon trajectories covering four domains and supports five memory systems. All memory systems are susceptible to poisoning, with substantial variation in downstream effects, and the optimisation process highlights differences between architectures.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark is intended to support research on understanding and mitigating agentic memory risks.

title: Maya a1: Do the Options Read the Model, or Does Their Position? Order Sensitivity in a Non-Autoregressive Decision Model
comment: 24 pages, 13 figures, 23 tables
summary: Laya answers typed multiple-choice questions in one forward pass by scoring a hidden state at one [MASK] marker per option. We re-engineer the checkpoint (421M parameters; a 2-layer option head with no positional tensor; a documented but unused parallel layout) and test whether the answer depends on where an option is listed. Presenting 951 Qwen-verified questions under every cyclic rotation of their options (or six random permutations for 12 options), the released checkpoint changes its answer for 25.8% [22.9-28.7] of questions (19.7% on the 605 English-language items alone); accuracy with the gold option first versus last differs by 10.1 points, and the flips concentrate where the model's own confidence is low (54% versus 8% across confidence terciles). AI.method: Re-engineers the released checkpoint (421M parameters, with a 2-layer option head and no positional tensor) and presents 951 Qwen-verified questions under every cyclic rotation of their options, or six random permutations for 12 options. Fine-tunes on 2,818 teacher-verified rows with and without option shuffling, and tests a confidence-weighted vote over orderings.

title: BitDecoding-FP4: Native FP4 KV Cache Decoding via Algorithm-System Co-Design
summary: The key-value (KV) cache dominates memory capacity and bandwidth in long-context LLM serving. While 4-bit microscaling formats (NVFP4, MXFP4) shrink the cache and run attention on FP4 Tensor Cores, a fundamental gap remains between algorithmic quantization and system-aware acceleration: existing FP4 KV systems use vanilla quantization that causes severe accuracy drops, whereas accuracy-oriented 4-bit algorithms rely on vector codebooks whose lookup overhead degrades decoding throughput. We present BitDecoding-FP4, an algorithm--system co-design for accurate and efficient native FP4 KV decoding. We mitigate three error sources: Dual-Residual Query Quantization splits queries into two FP4 tensors, cutting query logit error from 60% to 1%; Underflow-Aware Probability Scaling prevents E4M3 scales from rounding long-context probabilities to zero; and Outlier-Aware Key Quantization combines static smoothing, Hadamard rotation, and scale search to suppress key outliers under token-wise scaling. At the system level, we remove the softmax bottleneck via transposed softmax with fused probability quantization and stacked query MMA on paged KV caches. Across dense and MoE models with GQA and MLA, BitDecoding-FP4 stays within 0.5 points of BF16 KV accuracy with NVFP4 (1 point with MXFP4), and tracks BF16 KV in RL training rollouts. In end-to-end serving on NVIDIA B300 with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, it delivers 2.4-3.0$\times$ higher peak serving throughput than BF16 KV. The implementation is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: BitDecoding-FP4 is an algorithm-system co-design for native FP4 KV cache decoding that stays within 0.5 points of BF16 KV accuracy with NVFP4 and delivers 2.4-3.0x higher peak serving throughput than BF16 KV on NVIDIA B300.
AI.motivation: 4-bit microscaling formats shrink the KV cache and run attention on FP4 Tensor Cores, but vanilla FP4 KV quantisation causes severe accuracy drops, while accurate 4-bit methods use vector codebooks whose lookup overhead degrades decoding throughput.
AI.method: Three error mitigations: Dual-Residual Query Quantization splits queries into two FP4 tensors, Underflow-Aware Probability Scaling keeps E4M3 scales from rounding long-context probabilities to zero, and Outlier-Aware Key Quantization combines static smoothing, Hadamard rotation and scale search. At the system level, transposed softmax with fused probability quantization and stacked query MMA operate on paged KV caches.
AI.result: Dual-Residual Query Quantization cuts query logit error from 60% to 1%. Across dense and MoE models with GQA and MLA, accuracy stays within 0.5 points of BF16 KV with NVFP4 (1 point with MXFP4). End to end on NVIDIA B300 with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, peak serving throughput is 2.4-3.0x that of BF16 KV.
AI.conclusion: Accurate native FP4 KV decoding is feasible with co-designed algorithms and kernels, and the method also tracks BF16 KV in RL training rollouts.

title: How far does a hash-only sender go? A pre-registered map of sender memory versus bits for short text messages
comment: 10 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Code, data and per-message results: this https URL
summary: Can a sender that only computes hashes, with a language model only at the receiver, transmit short human text more cheaply than a classical sender trained on the same domain? We answer with one pre-registered run on 1,000 English user utterances from Taskmaster-1. The primary endpoint is the cost per message to deliver 100% of the messages (hash bits, plus a 2-byte negative acknowledgement and the raw text when the first attempt fails), paired against an in-domain PPM order-1 sender. The hash-only sender delivered 857 of 1,000 messages on the first attempt and cost 192.8 bits per message, 18.4 bits more than PPM order 1 (95% bootstrap interval 10.9 to 26.3); by the pre-registered rule it spends more and is not equivalent within one byte. As secondary results we map measured sender memory against bits. The hash-only sender (8,190 B on a host build, keyed BLAKE2b tag included, as in every method) was the cheapest point in bits from 8,190 B up to, but excluding, PPM order 1 at 24,844 B, 45 to 46 bits below smaz2 and Unishox2; from PPM order 1 upwards, in-domain senders spend fewer bits, except order 2 pruned to 16 KiB. In airtime it loses to PPM order 1 on all five links priced, to Unishox2 on four, and to raw text with a tag on two, because each failure costs an acknowledgement frame and a fallback frame. A wider receiver search recovers half of the failures and makes the cost 7.7 bits lower than PPM order 1, at about three minutes of receiver time per failure, and still loses in airtime on four of five links. We report the measurement as a delimitation, with every deviation of the run.

AI.tldr: In one pre-registered run on 1,000 Taskmaster-1 utterances, a hash-only sender with a receiver-side language model costs 192.8 bits per message, 18.4 bits more than an in-domain PPM order-1 sender, so it loses on the primary endpoint. Its memory footprint is the cheapest point in bits up to PPM order 1.
AI.motivation: The paper asks whether a sender that only computes hashes, with a language model only at the receiver, can transmit short human text more cheaply than a classical sender trained on the same domain.
AI.method: One pre-registered run on 1,000 English user utterances from Taskmaster-1. The primary endpoint is the cost per message to deliver all messages (hash bits, plus a 2-byte negative acknowledgement and the raw text when the first attempt fails), paired against an in-domain PPM order-1 sender. Secondary results map sender memory against bits and compare airtime on five links.

Its 8,190 B footprint is the cheapest point in bits up to PPM order 1 at 24,844 B. In airtime it loses to PPM order 1 on all five priced links. A wider receiver search recovers half of the failures and makes the cost 7.7 bits lower than PPM order 1, at about three minutes of receiver time per failure.

title: Enhancing Academic Advisement with Case-Based Reasoning
comment: 2026 proofread digital edition of the August 2003 Master of Engineering thesis, RMIT University
summary: This research involved the study of an application of Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) in the field of academic advising. Academic advisement has been recognised as an important function of higher education. However, there is a widespread desire to improve the advisement services provided by many educational institutions (e.g., colleges and universities) around the world. In the last ten years, CBR expert systems have made important contributions in many domains by applying CBR methodology to a variety of areas of human problem solving. However, to date, expert advisement systems have not been successfully applied to academic advisement, which seems to be a very appropriate domain for this technology. Academic advising is an important and time consuming task, and different tools and techniques must be used to make it an effective and efficient process. This thesis describes the design, development, and validation of a prototype case-based academic advisement recommender system that supplements the conventional advising process, and could eventually evolve to replace human academic advisors when its full potential is realised.

AI.tldr: The thesis describes the design, development and validation of a prototype case-based reasoning recommender for academic advisement, meant to supplement conventional advising. It suggests such a system could eventually replace human academic advisors once its full potential is realised.
AI.motivation: Academic advising is important and time-consuming, and CBR expert systems have contributed in many domains, yet expert advisement systems have not been successfully applied to academic advising.
AI.method: Design, development and validation of a prototype case-based academic advisement recommender system that supplements the conventional advising process.
AI.result: The abstract reports the design, development and validation of the prototype but gives no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: The work presents a case-based advisement prototype and proposes that it could eventually evolve to replace human advisors, a claim the abstract does not support with reported evidence.

title: NormGym: Evaluating Normative Competence through Social Interaction
summary: Normative competence, the ability to infer socially enforced expectations from interaction and adjust behavior accordingly, is essential for agents operating in unfamiliar human communities. Yet existing evaluations largely test whether agents can recognize or apply norms they may already know, rather than whether they can acquire previously unknown norms from social interaction. We introduce NormGym, an interactive benchmark for normative competence in which a newcomer must infer a hidden, arbitrary norm while pursuing its own task in a multi-agent community. Success requires distinguishing what is possible from what is permitted, inferring the norm from observed behavior and sanctions, and applying it in new situations. NormGym contains diverse norms and distinct environments, allowing systematic evaluation of current agents, including large language model (LLM) agents. We find that normative competence remains challenging: the strongest evaluated LLM achieves a joint task-and-compliance success rate of 55.3%. Our analysis reveals that models can sometimes revise their behavior following sanctions for their own actions, but struggle to use other agents' behavior and the sanctions they receive to infer the underlying norm. We further find that fine-tuning models may be insufficient to improve normative competence. These results suggest that current models lack a robust, transferable capability for acquiring normative knowledge through social interaction.

AI.tldr: NormGym is an interactive benchmark in which a newcomer agent must infer a hidden, arbitrary norm from social interaction while pursuing its own task. The strongest evaluated LLM reaches a joint task-and-compliance success rate of 55.3%.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations test whether agents can recognise or apply norms they already know, not whether they can acquire previously unknown norms from social interaction.
AI.method: A multi-agent community with diverse norms and distinct environments, in which the newcomer must distinguish what is possible from what is permitted, infer the norm from observed behaviour and sanctions, and apply it in new situations.
AI.result: The strongest evaluated LLM achieves a joint task-and-compliance success rate of 55.3%. Models sometimes revise their behaviour after sanctions for their own actions but struggle to use other agents' behaviour and sanctions to infer the norm. Fine-tuning may be insufficient to improve normative competence.
AI.conclusion: Current models lack a robust, transferable capability for acquiring normative knowledge through social interaction.

title: LLM-Based Feature Extraction for Multi-Criteria Inventory Classification
summary: E-commerce supply chains generate large volumes of customer feedback and operational data that remain underutilized in inventory management. Traditional inventory classification techniques such as ABC analysis rely primarily on annual dollar usage, while multi-criteria inventory classification (MCIC) methods extend this but still depend on structured quantitative data and do not utilize unstructured information available in modern supply chains. This paper proposes an LLM-based feature extraction approach that transforms unstructured sources such as customer reviews into quantitative features using vector embeddings and LLM-generated evaluation criteria. The enriched feature set is incorporated into an MCIC framework based on the Hadi-Vencheh model. Experimental results show measurable reclassification effects when customer sentiment signals are included, demonstrating that integrating unstructured data into MCIC can enhance inventory prioritization.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using LLMs to turn unstructured customer reviews into quantitative features for multi-criteria inventory classification based on the Hadi-Vencheh model. Including customer sentiment signals produces measurable reclassification of inventory items.
AI.motivation: ABC analysis relies mainly on annual dollar usage, and multi-criteria inventory classification still depends on structured quantitative data, so unstructured customer feedback goes unused.
