AI.motivation: Forcing every input through long reasoning causes overthinking and unnecessary cost, and single-reference offline objectives misweight one mode when fast answers and slow traces come from distinct behavior policies.
AI.method: DR-BOLT separates the desired fast/slow mixture reference from the sampling distribution and corrects their mismatch in reward-weighted training; a fast/slow partition competition explains routing in the optimal target, and an efficient source-wise correction approximates the exact objective when response formats are well separated; comparisons use Qwen3-VL with identical candidate banks.
AI.result: DR-BOLT improves score-length trade-offs over evaluated offline and online baselines on ScienceQA and three held-out transfer benchmarks, with a 24.1% cross-benchmark slow ratio and a 2.90-fold end-to-end training speedup over reproduced GRPO.
AI.conclusion: Dual-reference correction supports adaptive fast/slow reasoning in the studied two-reference setting, although broader robustness remains open.

title: Evaluation of a Multi-Link Machine Learning Approach for Rainfall Detection Using Satellite Microwave Links
summary: The impacts of climate change have increased the need for reliable real-time rainfall monitoring systems. This study investigates rainfall detection using a network of opportunistic sensors based on satellite microwave links (SMLs) combined with machine learning (ML) classifiers. Two models, a random forest (RF) and a convolutional neural network (CNN), were trained on aggregated SML data, including information from neighboring links. The results demonstrate that leveraging information from multiple links substantially enhances the detection of both wet and dry periods compared to single-link approaches. Moreover, the RF model consistently provides a more stable and reliable trade-off than CNN, improving rainfall detection and reducing misclassifications overall, with particularly strong performance during harsh weather conditions. The study spanned up to 32 rainy days between 2021 and 2024.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that combining information from multiple satellite microwave links with a random forest or CNN improves rainfall detection over single-link approaches, with the random forest giving the more stable and reliable trade-off.
AI.motivation: Reliable real-time rainfall monitoring is increasingly needed under climate change, and satellite microwave links offer opportunistic sensing whose use for rainfall detection with machine learning had to be evaluated.
AI.method: A random forest (RF) and a convolutional neural network (CNN) were trained on aggregated satellite microwave link (SML) data, including information from neighboring links, and compared against single-link approaches.
AI.result: Multi-link information substantially enhances detection of both wet and dry periods; RF gives a more stable and reliable trade-off than CNN, reducing misclassifications overall with particularly strong performance in harsh weather; the study spanned up to 32 rainy days between 2021 and 2024.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting neighboring links with a simple random forest is an effective and robust approach for rainfall detection from satellite microwave link networks.

title: TailDART: Compute-Efficient Foundation Models for Financial Time-Series Forecasting
summary: Although time-series foundation models (TSFMs) achieve strong zero-shot transferability across high-information-density physical systems, applying overparameterized TSFMs to quantitative finance is fundamentally constrained by low signal-to-noise ratios, non-stationarity, and prohibitive autoregressive decoding latency. To reconcile representation learning with institutional operational constraints, this study presents TailDART, a dense 2.68 million-parameter foundation model engineered for financial time-series forecasting. By integrating grouped-query attention into a lightweight backbone, the architecture drastically reduces Key-Value cache memory bandwidth overhead, achieving major inference acceleration (up to 48.1%) over prevailing state-of-the-art TSFMs to enable low-latency, high-throughput streaming execution. Furthermore, multi-asset benchmarks across varying temporal resolutions show that a compact model can remain competitive for market forecasting: TailDART matches the predictive fidelity of substantially larger baselines while demonstrating superior error resilience in high-volatility regimes.

AI.tldr: TailDART is a compact 2.68-million-parameter time-series foundation model for financial forecasting that uses grouped-query attention to cut inference latency while staying competitive with much larger baselines.
AI.motivation: Overparameterized time-series foundation models are costly for quantitative finance, where signal-to-noise ratios are low, series are non-stationary, and autoregressive decoding latency is prohibitive.
AI.method: The model integrates grouped-query attention into a lightweight dense backbone to reduce Key-Value cache memory bandwidth overhead for streaming inference.
AI.result: TailDART achieves inference acceleration of up to 48.1% over prevailing state-of-the-art time-series foundation models across multi-asset benchmarks at varying temporal resolutions, matches the predictive fidelity of substantially larger baselines, and shows superior error resilience in high-volatility regimes.
AI.conclusion: A compact foundation model with grouped-query attention can be low-latency and high-throughput for market forecasting while remaining competitive with larger models.

title: Analyzing Code Provenance in LLMs for Programming Education
summary: Large language models (LLMs) play an increasing role in programming education, challenging traditional assessment methods as they can generate fully functional code instantly. This disrupts the reliability of student submissions as indicators of learning and effort. To address this issue, code provenance is essential for tracing the origins of code and distinguishing student-authored, AI-generated, and externally sourced components. We extend the Min-K% probability approach by incorporating synthetic non-member code generation and apply it to Python code for membership inference and provenance tracking. Evaluations cover free LLMs such as GPT-2, DistilGPT-2, and DialoGPT, as well as state-of-the-art commercial models including GPT-5, Gemini 2.5, Mistral, DeepSeek, and LLaMA 3.3. Before evaluating our approach on higher-education student assignments, we validate its feasibility using Stack Overflow data. The results show that free models enable more sensitive code memorization detection than commercial models. By systematically comparing these LLMs, we assess trade-offs between detection accuracy and privacy protection, taking an initial step toward effective assessment of AI-assisted programming education through combined provenance detection and process visibility.

AI.tldr: The paper extends the Min-K% probability membership inference approach with synthetic non-member code to trace whether Python code was memorized from LLMs, aiming to separate student-authored, AI-generated and externally sourced code in programming education.
AI.motivation: LLMs can generate functional code instantly, which undermines student submissions as evidence of learning and effort, so tracing the provenance of code is needed.
AI.method: The Min-K% probability approach is extended with synthetic non-member code generation and applied to Python code for membership inference and provenance tracking; free models (GPT-2, DistilGPT-2, DialoGPT) and commercial models (GPT-5, Gemini 2.5, Mistral, DeepSeek, LLaMA 3.3) are evaluated, with feasibility first validated on Stack Overflow data.
AI.result: Free models enable more sensitive code memorization detection than commercial models, and the comparison clarifies trade-offs between detection accuracy and privacy protection.
AI.conclusion: Combining provenance detection with process visibility is an initial step toward assessing AI-assisted programming education, with model choice trading detection sensitivity against privacy.

title: Large Language Model Consensus and Corpus-Adaptive Topic Modeling for Classifying and Mapping Patent Innovation
summary: Patent analytics increasingly relies on transformer representations and large language models (LLMs), yet linking conceptual classification, topic formation and interpretation requires explicit decisions about model roles and the evidence retained at each stage. In this design-oriented study, we propose and demonstrate a patent analytics pipeline that links these tasks and keeps each decision open to audit. Three LLMs separately classify each patent by novelty (radical or incremental) and innovation type (product, process, service). Radical and innovation-type labels each require two supporting votes, with Incremental used as the fallback novelty label. Topics are discovered by clustering PatentSBERTa embeddings, with parameter ranges scaled to corpus size. A patent-specific stopword list is applied only when topics are represented with class-based term frequency--inverse document frequency (c-TF-IDF), and a second embedding model supports inter-topic similarity, hierarchical refinement and visualization. An LLM then labels each topic from its ranked keywords and representative patents. We demonstrate the pipeline on 30,964 public-sector-related patents retrieved from this http URL. Across five category corpora ranging from 591 to 29,215 patents, the pipeline produced 74 category-specific topic instances with a macro-average document coverage of 98.1% and topic diversity of 0.900--1.000, and fewer than 1% of classification outputs returned UNKNOWN. Because every model vote and the evidence behind each topic label are retained, analysts can audit and revise the outputs. The demonstration establishes the feasibility and traceability of the pipeline; testing its labels against expert coding and benchmarking it against alternative pipelines are identified as the next steps. The pipeline offers a reusable basis for LLM-assisted patent analysis in technology intelligence.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an auditable LLM-assisted patent analytics pipeline that classifies patents by novelty and innovation type with majority votes, clusters PatentSBERTa embeddings into topics and labels them with an LLM, and retains all evidence for analyst review.
AI.motivation: Patent analytics using LLMs and transformer representations lacks explicit decisions about model roles and retained evidence at each stage, making classification and topic interpretation hard to audit.
AI.method: Three LLMs independently classify each patent by novelty (radical or incremental) and innovation type (product, process or service), requiring two supporting votes for radical and innovation-type labels with Incremental as fallback; topics come from clustering PatentSBERTa embeddings with corpus-scaled parameters, c-TF-IDF with a patent-specific stopword list, a second embedding model for inter-topic similarity and hierarchical refinement, and an LLM labels each topic from keywords and representative patents.
AI.result: On 30,964 public-sector-related patents across five category corpora of 591 to 29,215 patents, the pipeline yields 74 category-specific topic instances with macro-average document coverage of 98.1%, topic diversity of 0.900-1.000, and fewer than 1% of classification outputs returning UNKNOWN.
AI.conclusion: The pipeline demonstrates feasibility and traceability of LLM-assisted patent analysis; testing labels against expert coding and benchmarking against alternative pipelines remain as next steps.

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning via Probabilistic Option Shielding
comment: Accepted at the NEmo workshop @ NeurIPS 2026
summary: Shielding is a safe reinforcement learning technique that provides safety guarantees while learning, by blocking unsafe actions. Traditional shielding relies on a complete model of the environment to provide long-term guarantees. Probabilistic logic shielding (PLS) lifts the requirement of having such model, but only considers safety in the short term, typically looking only one or few steps ahead. We propose Probabilistic Option Shielding (POS), which extends PLS to the option level, recovering long-horizon safety without reintroducing the need for a complete environment model. POS learns a model-free critic directly from one-step PLS signals, to estimate the probability that an entire option will complete safely under uncertainty. We evaluate POS on safe navigation tasks in the LogiCity environment, and show that it achieves considerably safer training while matching the task performance of standard step-level PLS and other safety related reinforcement learning baselines.

AI.tldr: Probabilistic Option Shielding (POS) extends probabilistic logic shielding from single steps to whole options, using a model-free critic to estimate the probability that an option completes safely, and yields safer training with matched task performance.
AI.motivation: Probabilistic logic shielding (PLS) avoids needing a full environment model but only guarantees safety one or a few steps ahead, leaving long-horizon safety unaddressed.
AI.method: POS learns a model-free critic from one-step PLS signals to estimate the probability that an entire option will complete safely under uncertainty, providing option-level shielding without a complete environment model.
AI.result: On safe navigation tasks in the LogiCity environment, POS achieves considerably safer training while matching the task performance of step-level PLS and other safety-related reinforcement learning baselines.
AI.conclusion: Option-level shielding recovers long-horizon safety without requiring a complete environment model.

title: Fused-Softmax for efficient quantized attention
summary: Low-precision matrix throughput on modern GPUs is growing far faster than vector-arithmetic throughput. Attention therefore cannot realize the available GEMM performance because softmax has become the pipeline bottleneck. We introduce Fused-Softmax Attention, a training-free algorithm that reformulates and approximates softmax to fold its dominant operations into the attention GEMMs, moving work from vector units to matrix cores. Implemented for the AMD CDNA 4 architecture, our MXFP8, MXFP6 and MXFP4 kernels reach approximately 3.0, 4.0 and 4.6 PFLOP/s on an AMD Instinct MI355X GPU, yielding speedups of $2.1\times$, $2.8\times$ and $3.2\times$ over the BF16 attention. Importantly, the additional error introduced by Fused-Softmax remains below the error floor set by quantizing the GEMM operands. On Wan2.2-T2V-A14B, a hybrid MXFP6/4 schedule delivers up to $2.05\times$ end-to-end speedup while preserving the visual quality of the outputs. The kernels ship in AMD's open-source AITER library, and they powered AMD's MLPerf Inference v6.1 Wan2.2 submission, which ran $1.7\times$ faster than AMD's previous-round result on the same hardware. Our results show that redesigning softmax to utilize the matrix pipeline enables attention to capitalize on continued growth in low-precision matrix throughput.

AI.tldr: Fused-Softmax Attention is a training-free reformulation of softmax that folds its dominant operations into attention GEMMs, reaching about 3.0 to 4.6 PFLOP/s with MXFP8 to MXFP4 kernels on an AMD MI355X and speedups of 2.1x to 3.2x over BF16 attention.
AI.motivation: Low-precision matrix throughput on modern GPUs grows much faster than vector throughput, so softmax has become the bottleneck that prevents attention from realizing available GEMM performance.
AI.method: The algorithm reformulates and approximates softmax to move its work from vector units to matrix cores, implemented for the AMD CDNA 4 architecture with MXFP8, MXFP6 and MXFP4 kernels shipped in AMD's open-source AITER library.
AI.result: The kernels reach approximately 3.0, 4.0 and 4.6 PFLOP/s on an AMD Instinct MI355X, giving speedups of 2.1x, 2.8x and 3.2x over BF16 attention; the added error stays below the error floor set by quantizing GEMM operands; on Wan2.2-T2V-A14B a hybrid MXFP6/4 schedule gives up to 2.05x end-to-end speedup while preserving visual quality; the kernels powered AMD's MLPerf Inference v6.1 Wan2.2 submission, 1.7x faster than its previous round.
AI.conclusion: Redesigning softmax to use the matrix pipeline lets attention exploit continued growth in low-precision matrix throughput.

title: RAG-Enhanced LLMs for Interactive Explainability in Clinical Decision Support Systems
comment: Published in HC_AIxIA_HYDRA 2025, Communications in Computer and Information Science, vol. 2830, pp. 50-63, Springer, 2026. Please cite the published version: doi:https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-16708-8_4
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in high-risks decision-making systems across domains such as healthcare, finance, and the judicial system. As reliance on predictive models grows, so does the demand for Explainable AI (XAI) to ensure transparency, trust, and interpretability. However, existing XAI approaches often fail to present explanations in a format accessible to domain experts, limiting their practical utility. Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a bridge between complex models and end-users, offering natural language explanations. Yet, their use introduces new risks, including hallucinated outputs and lack of source traceability. To address these challenges, we propose a Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) that not only combines standard predictive models with XAI techniques but also incorporates a Retrieval-Augmented Generation module as an interactive enhancer. This module grounds explanations in verified medical knowledge, reformulates technical outputs into a human-like format, and enables users-such as clinicians-to actively query the system. By fostering an interactive, human-in-the-loop environment, our approach empowers domain experts to explore model decisions, contextualize explanations, and build trust in AI-assisted diagnostics. The study concludes with preliminary experiments validating the proposed methodology.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a clinical decision support system that pairs predictive models and explainable AI with a retrieval-augmented LLM module that grounds explanations in verified medical knowledge and lets clinicians query them interactively.
AI.motivation: XAI outputs often are not presented in a form accessible to domain experts, and LLM-generated explanations risk hallucination and lack of source traceability in high-stakes clinical settings.
AI.method: A clinical decision support system combines standard predictive models with XAI techniques and a retrieval-augmented generation module that reformulates technical outputs into human-like explanations and supports interactive user queries.
AI.result: The abstract reports only preliminary experiments validating the proposed methodology, with no quantitative figures stated.
AI.conclusion: Grounded, interactive LLM explanations are presented as a way for clinicians to explore model decisions and build trust in AI-assisted diagnostics, pending further study.

title: MM-DyGraph: A Dataset, Benchmark, and Model for Multimodal Dynamic Graphs
summary: Multimodal dynamic graphs are pervasive in real-world applications, where nodes and edges are accompanied by multimodal signals, including text and images. Despite their practical importance, benchmarks and methods that explicitly study multimodal learning in dynamic graphs remain scarce, hindering the full understanding and effective utilization of multimodal information for downstream tasks. To address this gap, we introduce MM-DyGraph, to the best of our knowledge, the first benchmark for multimodal dynamic graph learning, consisting of diverse real-world datasets with fine-grained temporal graph evolution and rich multimodal attributes. MM-DyGraph provides three evaluation tasks to comprehensively assess model performance in dynamic settings. We benchmark representative state-of-the-art dynamic graph methods and reveal that naive feature concatenation yields target-level inconsistencies: multimodal inputs benefit certain prediction targets while harming others. This observation indicates that the modality informativeness depends on the specific prediction target over time. Building on these observations, we propose a Target-aware Spatial-Temporal Multimodal Fusion (TST-MF) framework, which jointly conditions multimodal fusion on the prediction target and spatial-temporal relations, enabling context-adaptive cross-modal interplay for target-specific representations. Extensive experiments over diverse datasets and tasks show that TST-MF delivers robust and competitive performance, achieving clear gains in multimodal settings.

AI.tldr: MM-DyGraph is the first benchmark for multimodal dynamic graph learning, and TST-MF, a target-aware spatio-temporal fusion framework, conditions cross-modal fusion on the prediction target to achieve clear gains in multimodal settings.
AI.motivation: Benchmarks and methods for multimodal learning on dynamic graphs with text and image attributes are scarce, and naive feature concatenation causes target-level inconsistencies where multimodal inputs help some targets and hurt others.
AI.method: The authors introduce MM-DyGraph with diverse real-world datasets, three evaluation tasks and fine-grained temporal evolution, benchmark representative dynamic graph methods, and propose Target-aware Spatial-Temporal Multimodal Fusion (TST-MF), which jointly conditions multimodal fusion on the prediction target and spatio-temporal relations.
AI.result: Naive feature concatenation shows target-level inconsistencies across prediction targets; TST-MF delivers robust and competitive performance across diverse datasets and tasks, with clear gains in multimodal settings.
AI.conclusion: Modality informativeness depends on the prediction target over time, so target-conditioned multimodal fusion is needed for dynamic graphs.

title: Zero-Query Transferable Pretend Benign Attacks with Amortized Online Generation for Cooperative Perception
summary: Cooperative perception enables an ego agent to acquire information from collaborators beyond its own sensors' reach. Yet, the most beneficial messages are often the hardest to verify from local observations. Pretend Benign (PB) exploits this asymmetry by targeting regions with weak local verifiability and applying multi-objective perturbations, making harmful feature changes appear to be benign assistance. However, PB is victim-dependent: selecting regions and optimizing perturbations require the victim model's architecture, parameters, and gradients, limiting transfer to unseen victims. A transferable attack must capture properties shared across cooperative detection models rather than those specific to one network. We address this by building a victim-agnostic attack from a heterogeneous ensemble of surrogate models and encoding its capabilities in a reusable dictionary to reduce per-message generation cost. Specifically, Transferable Pretend Benign (TrPB) transfers PB's region selection criterion and multi-objective perturbation strategy across heterogeneous surrogates to construct an offline attack. We further propose RT-TrPB, which encodes transferable regions and perturbation patterns into a region predictor and reusable perturbation dictionary, amortizing per-message attack generation. Experiments on widely used cooperative perception benchmarks show that RT-TrPB bypasses the consensus-based defenses ROBOSAC and FLD with success rates approaching 100% and generates each perturbation in under 56 ms. To counter PB-style attacks masquerading as benign collaboration, we also propose STTrust, which verifies received messages using spatial and temporal consistency and incorporates identity-level trust. STTrust detects over 90% of PB-style attacks and restores perception performance to near the attack-free level.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces transferable and amortized pretend-benign attacks (TrPB and RT-TrPB) on cooperative perception that transfer to unseen victims and bypass consensus defenses, along with STTrust, a defense that detects over 90% of such attacks.
AI.motivation: Pretend Benign attacks depend on the victim model's architecture, parameters and gradients, which limits their transfer to unseen victims, and existing defenses such as ROBOSAC and FLD can be bypassed.
AI.method: TrPB builds a victim-agnostic offline attack from a heterogeneous ensemble of surrogate models by transferring region selection and multi-objective perturbation strategy; RT-TrPB encodes transferable regions and perturbation patterns into a region predictor and reusable perturbation dictionary to amortize generation; STTrust verifies received messages using spatial and temporal consistency with identity-level trust.
AI.result: On widely used cooperative perception benchmarks, RT-TrPB bypasses ROBOSAC and FLD with success rates approaching 100% and generates each perturbation in under 56 ms; STTrust detects over 90% of PB-style attacks and restores perception performance to near the attack-free level.
AI.conclusion: Victim-agnostic, amortized attacks threaten consensus-based cooperative perception, and spatio-temporal consistency with identity trust offers an effective countermeasure.

title: Forecasting cumulative intraoperative hypotension burden: patient-disjoint evaluation of quantile boosting and alert policies
summary: Background: Binary hypotension forecasts do not describe the depth and duration of future low pressure. Burden forecasts may support graded early warning, but better forecast scores need not yield more useful alerts. Objective: To evaluate conditional quantiles of the next 15-minute mean arterial pressure (MAP) deficit below 65 mmHg and distinguish forecasting performance from episode-warning performance. Methods: Public VitalDB numeric arterial MAP was reduced to 10-second medians without forward filling. Subject-disjoint training, validation and test splits included 70,402, 14,270 and 15,575 labeled windows. We compared climatology, calibrated persistence, last-MAP-only boosting, and direct and residual quantile boosting, with and without additional MAP-history features. Patient-weighted pinball loss and subject-bootstrap intervals evaluated forecasting. Validation selected alert thresholds before a hash-recorded test evaluation. Results: In the test split, the prespecified residual-versus-persistence comparison at the 90th percentile yielded losses of 2.256 and 2.900 mmHg-min, respectively (difference -0.644; 95% interval -0.814 to -0.487). Direct prediction achieved 2.196, and direct prediction with additional MAP features achieved 2.193. Episode-warning results were sensitive to the alert rule and operating threshold. Conclusions: This retrospective benchmark separates burden-forecast skill from warning-policy performance. Findings support further study of direct burden estimation; they do not establish patient benefit, prospective reliability or transportability beyond the source hospital.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates quantile boosting for forecasting the cumulative 15-minute burden of intraoperative hypotension and shows that better forecast scores do not guarantee more useful episode alerts, using a retrospective VitalDB benchmark with patient-disjoint splits.
AI.motivation: Binary hypotension forecasts miss the depth and duration of low pressure, and burden forecasts may support graded early warning, yet forecast skill and alert usefulness need separate evaluation.
AI.method: Public VitalDB arterial MAP was reduced to 10-second medians without forward filling; climatology, calibrated persistence, last-MAP-only boosting, and direct and residual quantile boosting, with and without MAP-history features, were compared using patient-weighted pinball loss, subject-bootstrap intervals and validation-selected alert thresholds, with a hash-recorded test evaluation.
AI.result: At the 90th percentile in the test split, residual quantile boosting yields 2.900 mmHg-min versus 2.256 for persistence (difference -0.644; 95% interval -0.814 to -0.487) as prespecified; direct prediction achieves 2.196 and direct prediction with additional MAP features achieves 2.193; episode-warning results are sensitive to the alert rule and operating threshold.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark separates burden-forecast skill from warning-policy performance and supports further study of direct burden estimation, but does not establish patient benefit, prospective reliability or transportability beyond the source hospital.

title: Model-based learning for DoA estimation and array calibration via continuous sparse recovery
summary: Direction of arrival (DoA) estimation, a classical signal processing problem, has experienced renewed interest with the advent of integrated sensing and communication (ISAC). While decades of research have yielded highly accurate DoA estimators, hardware impairments have frequently been neglected, despite degrading both DoA estimation accuracy and downstream communication performance in ISAC systems. This work introduces a joint array calibration and DoA estimation method based on the simultaneous orthogonal matching pursuit (SOMP) algorithm, following the model-based machine learning paradigm. The proposed method enables the calibration of antenna arrays subject to severe gain-phase and antenna location impairments through projected gradient descent (PGD), with either supervised or unsupervised objectives. Additionally, DoA estimation is enhanced by extending SOMP to continuous dictionaries via PGD refinement steps. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method enables efficient hardware impairment compensation, even without labeled samples, while outperforming conventional sparse recovery and subspace-based DoA estimation baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a model-based machine learning method that jointly calibrates antenna arrays and estimates directions of arrival using continuous sparse recovery, working with or without labelled data.
AI.motivation: Hardware impairments such as gain-phase errors and antenna location errors degrade DoA estimation and communication performance in integrated sensing and communication systems, and are often neglected.
AI.method: The method extends simultaneous orthogonal matching pursuit (SOMP) and calibrates arrays with severe gain-phase and antenna location impairments through projected gradient descent (PGD), using supervised or unsupervised objectives, and refines DoA estimates on continuous dictionaries with PGD steps.
AI.result: Simulations show efficient hardware impairment compensation even without labelled samples, with the method outperforming conventional sparse recovery and subspace-based DoA estimation baselines.
AI.conclusion: Model-based learning with continuous sparse recovery offers a practical way to compensate array hardware impairments for DoA estimation in ISAC systems.

title: Nudging Decision Models: Do Digital Nudges Steer Fast, Generation-Free AI Agents?
comment: Under Review
summary: LLM-based agents increasingly automate business and consumer tasks but are slow and expensive. Decision models, a new class that chooses among options without generating text, are far faster and less costly. Developers call them "System One models," referencing dual process theory. We ask whether such models can be steered by digital nudges online and whether, as the theory predicts, automatic nudges affect them more than reflective ones. We adapted an online shopping experiment, previously run with humans and LLM agents, to three decision models (Jev, Decision-1, d1). Across 600 runs per model, they chose a preselected default in 97.5-99.9% and a product with social influence information in 75-96% of choices, versus 47-49% in the control. All responded more strongly to the automatic nudge, the opposite of what has been reported for reasoning-capable LLM agents. We provide first evidence that non-generative decision models are susceptible to digital nudges in a System 1 pattern, implying agent-type-specific nudge effects.

AI.tldr: Decision models that choose among options without generating text are susceptible to digital nudges, responding more strongly to automatic nudges than to reflective ones, the opposite of the pattern reported for reasoning-capable LLM agents.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents are slow and expensive, and whether fast, non-generative decision models can be steered by digital nudges, and whether dual-process theory predicts their response, was unknown.
AI.method: An online shopping experiment previously run with humans and LLM agents was adapted to three decision models (Jev, Decision-1, d1), with 600 runs per model comparing a preselected default and a socially influenced product against a control.
AI.result: The models chose the preselected default in 97.5-99.9% of runs and the product with social influence information in 75-96% of choices, versus 47-49% in the control, and all responded more strongly to the automatic nudge.
AI.conclusion: Non-generative decision models show a System 1 pattern of nudge susceptibility, implying that nudge effects are agent-type specific.

title: Zero-Shot Weight-Space Programming Across a Difficulty-Graded Ladder of Two-Player Games
summary: Weight-space programming sets every weight of a feed-forward network by hand, from an explicit specification of the desired computation, with no gradient descent and no training data anywhere in the construction. We ask how far a large language model can carry this practice, zero-shot, across games of deliberately increasing difficulty. We design a four-rung ladder (Nim, tic-tac-toe, two sizes of Connect Four, and a chess endgame) spanning four axes of difficulty, and build a second, independent network at each rung, using a structurally unrelated game at matched difficulty, to separate what a rung's finding says about the difficulty level from what it says about the one game used to measure it. Ten networks are built and independently verified. Six admit a complete, non-statistical proof of correctness against an independent oracle. The chess-endgame rung is exact where correctness is cheap, move legality and, in one network, an exact one-ply mate detector, and collapses where it is expensive, composing a multi-move mating plan, from 84.1-100% success at the one-ply tactics it was built to get right down to 0.57-9.13% in full adversarial play; its replicate shows this collapse is an order of magnitude less severe under a shorter required plan and exact rather than heuristic safety checks. The standard-sized rung confirms, by holding hand-set evaluation weights fixed and adding only shallow search, that the remaining gap is an architectural ceiling rather than a matter of engineering effort, and this exact collapse reproduces across two structurally unrelated games. We release all ten networks, their independent oracles, construction-cost measurements, and a cold-prompt protocol for a future cross-model comparison

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether an LLM can zero-shot write the weights of feed-forward networks for two-player games of rising difficulty, and finds that exact construction works for cheap-to-verify tactics but collapses on multi-move chess endgame play.
AI.motivation: Weight-space programming sets network weights by hand from an explicit specification without gradient descent or training data, and how far an LLM can carry this practice across games of increasing difficulty was an open question.
AI.method: A four-rung ladder (Nim, tic-tac-toe, two sizes of Connect Four, and a chess endgame) spanning four difficulty axes was built, with a second structurally unrelated game at each rung to separate difficulty from game-specific effects; ten networks were built and independently verified against independent oracles, six with complete non-statistical proofs of correctness.
AI.result: The chess-endgame rung is exact for move legality and an exact one-ply mate detector in one network, but success falls from 84.1-100% on one-ply tactics to 0.57-9.13% in full adversarial play; a replicate with a shorter plan and exact safety checks shows a collapse an order of magnitude less severe; holding hand-set evaluation weights fixed and adding shallow search on the standard-sized rung shows the gap is an architectural ceiling, reproduced across two unrelated games.
AI.conclusion: The remaining gap in zero-shot weight-space programming reflects an architectural ceiling rather than a matter of engineering effort, and the networks, oracles, cost measurements and a cold-prompt protocol are released for future cross-model comparison.

title: PHISHREV+: An ASP-Based Post-Hoc Defeasible Machine Learning Framework for Phishing Detection
summary: Phishing website detection remains a critical cybersecurity challenge. Although machine learning classifiers achieve high accuracy on benchmark datasets, they suffer from a fundamental limitation: once trained, their decision boundaries are fixed and cannot incorporate new contextual evidence without retraining the model. This work presents \textbf{PHISHREV+}, a hybrid framework that instantiates the notion of \textit{post-hoc defeasible machine learning}. This framework does not replace the classifier. It treats the initial classifier predictions as defeasible beliefs and revises them through an Answer Set Programming based non-monotonic reasoning(NMR) layer. The framework operates in two phases. In the machine learning phase, four classifiers (SVM, KNN, DT and RF) are trained on the 87 feature benchmark dataset. In the post-hoc NMR phase, four defeasible rules derived from exploratory data analysis of the training set, and validated through Chi-square and Mann-Whitney U tests, formally revise initial predictions. The proposed framework achieves consistent false positive reduction across all our classifiers SVM (41$\rightarrow$39), KNN (47$\rightarrow$46), DT (62$\rightarrow$61), and RF (52$\rightarrow$51) while maintaining complete false negative parity with zero increase overhead. A comprehensive ablation studies across seven rule configurations confirms that the hierarchical combination of all four defeasible rules is necessary to achieve this optimal balance. Instance level explainability is provided through eXplainable ASP (XASP), which generates formal derivation graphs showing which defeasible rules fired and why the initial belief was retracted, a capability absent from all existing phishing detection approaches.

AI.tldr: PHISHREV+ is a hybrid framework that treats classifier predictions as defeasible beliefs and revises them with answer set programming rules, reducing false positives across four classifiers on phishing detection without increasing false negatives.
AI.motivation: Trained phishing classifiers have fixed decision boundaries and cannot incorporate new contextual evidence without retraining.
AI.method: Four classifiers (SVM, KNN, DT and RF) are trained on an 87-feature benchmark dataset, then four defeasible rules derived from exploratory data analysis and validated with Chi-square and Mann-Whitney U tests revise their predictions through an answer set programming non-monotonic reasoning layer, with eXplainable ASP providing derivation graphs.
AI.result: False positives drop across all classifiers, SVM from 41 to 39, KNN from 47 to 46, DT from 62 to 61 and RF from 52 to 51, with false negative parity maintained; an ablation over seven rule configurations shows the combination of all four rules is needed for the best balance.
AI.conclusion: Post-hoc defeasible reasoning can add explainable false-positive reduction on top of existing classifiers without retraining them.

title: Atik: A Shared-Mesh Transformer Accelerator for RISC-V
summary: Transformer inference repeatedly invokes dense matrix multiplication and attention, including its data-dependent softmax normalization. We present Atik, an open-source RoCC accelerator for RocketChip that executes matrix multiplication and dense attention through one shared fixed-point MAC mesh. Atik accepts and returns BF16 tensors, uses a streaming online-softmax schedule that never materializes the full score matrix, and is invoked through a small descriptor-based ABI. We evaluate three meshes cycle-by-cycle on FireSim and report standalone Sky130 physical-design area. Across 137 logged FireSim test records, all tests pass their benchmark tolerance with zero reported output mismatches. Relative to the same scalar Rocket BF16 reference, the 8x8 configuration reaches 31.5x peak matmul speedup and 225.8x peak attention speedup. Hybrid projections for the single-layer workload-derived C models, using directly measured accelerator-kernel cycles, give aggregate speedups of 44.2x, 77.1x, and 32.3x for ViT, TinyBERT, and GPT-2 prefill, respectively; these are not full-model hardware replays.

AI.tldr: Atik is an open-source RoCC accelerator for RocketChip that runs matrix multiplication and dense attention on one shared fixed-point MAC mesh, with BF16 tensor I/O. On FireSim, the 8x8 configuration reaches 31.5x peak matmul and 225.8x peak attention speedup over a scalar Rocket BF16 reference.
AI.motivation: Transformer inference relies on dense matrix multiplication and data-dependent softmax attention, and a general-purpose RISC-V core runs these slowly. The abstract frames the need as a hardware path that handles both operations without materializing the full attention score matrix.
AI.method: Atik uses one shared fixed-point MAC mesh for matmul and dense attention, a streaming online-softmax schedule that never materializes the full score matrix, and a small descriptor-based ABI. Three mesh sizes are evaluated cycle by cycle on FireSim, and standalone Sky130 physical-design area is reported.
AI.result: Across 137 logged FireSim test records, all tests pass their benchmark tolerance with zero reported output mismatches. Relative to the scalar Rocket BF16 reference, the 8x8 configuration reaches 31.5x peak matmul and 225.8x peak attention speedup. Hybrid projections from single-layer workload-derived C models give aggregate speedups of 44.2x for ViT, 77.1x for TinyBERT and 32.3x for GPT-2 prefill, and these are not full-model hardware replays.
AI.conclusion: The shared mesh gives large speedups on both matmul and attention for transformer kernels on an open RISC-V platform. The workload-level numbers are projections from measured kernel cycles, so full-model hardware performance is not established.

title: StockASkill: A Local-First AgentSkill for Intelligent Stock Selection
summary: Quantitative equity selection and portfolio construction in emerging and cross-border markets frequently suffer from computational bottlenecks, remote API fragility, survivorship bias, and rigid execution constraints such as discrete board lots and investor-mandated drawdown limits. In this paper, we present StockASkill, a local-first, full-data-driven AgentSkill engineered as a specialized Quant Co-Processor for autonomous AI agents and quantitative researchers. Tailored for agile portfolios (10^5 ~ 10^7 RMB) where discrete lot execution and capital protection are mandatory, StockASkill embeds a columnar DuckDB OLAP engine over 42.44 million historical price records and 186,432 financial disclosures spanning 26 years across China A-shares, Hong Kong, US equities, and ETFs. By eliminating ad-hoc network dependencies during analysis, StockASkill reduces cross-sectional screening latency across 5,400+ equities from over 25 seconds to sub-0.5 seconds (a 95%+ reduction). We formalize an end-to-end mathematical pipeline integrating a 7+1 factor alpha model, an SLSQP convex optimizer under smooth CVaR drawdown surrogates with exact path projection, dynamic 100-share board lot integer quantization, and an autonomous thesis lifecycle finite-state machine. Furthermore, we provide a zero-disk, strongly-typed JSON streaming interface designed for high-throughput LLM tool-calling. Open-sourced at this https URL, comprehensive empirical benchmarks from 2018 to 2024 demonstrate that the architecture achieves annualized Sharpe ratios exceeding 1.48 and Calmar ratios up to 2.17, while reducing max drawdown by up to 85% relative to benchmark indices.

AI.tldr: StockASkill is a local-first AgentSkill for quantitative stock selection in emerging and cross-border markets, built on a columnar DuckDB engine over 42.44 million price records and 186,432 financial disclosures. It cuts cross-sectional screening latency across 5,400+ equities from over 25 seconds to under 0.5 seconds.
AI.motivation: Quantitative equity selection in emerging and cross-border markets suffers from computational bottlenecks, fragile remote APIs, survivorship bias, and execution constraints such as discrete board lots and drawdown limits. The abstract notes that these problems are especially acute for small portfolios of 10^5 to 10^7 RMB.
AI.method: The system embeds a DuckDB OLAP engine over 26 years of data covering China A-shares, Hong Kong, US equities and ETFs, and avoids network calls during analysis. The pipeline combines a 7+1 factor alpha model, an SLSQP convex optimizer under smooth CVaR drawdown surrogates with exact path projection, 100-share board lot integer quantization, and a thesis lifecycle finite-state machine. It also exposes a zero-disk, strongly typed JSON streaming interface for LLM tool calling.
AI.result: Screening latency falls from over 25 seconds to sub-0.5 seconds across 5,400+ equities, a reduction of more than 95 percent. Benchmarks from 2018 to 2024 report annualized Sharpe ratios above 1.48 and Calmar ratios up to 2.17, with maximum drawdown reduced by up to 85 percent relative to benchmark indices.
AI.conclusion: The paper argues that a local, full-data system can serve as a fast quant co-processor for autonomous agents and researchers working under real lot and drawdown constraints. The performance claims are reported from the authors' own benchmarks.

title: PreForceVision: Physics-Guided Optical Estimation of Bolt Preload from Bolt-Head Deformation
comment: 9 pages, Proceedings of the ASME 2026 International Mechanical Engineering Congress and Exposition (IMECE 2026), November 8-12, 2026, Vancouver, Canada. Accepted and under publication
summary: Bolt preload is a decisive functional quantity in bolted joints because it determines whether external loads are transmitted primarily through frictional clamping or directly through the bolt. Existing preload measurement techniques, including strain-gauge bolts, force washers, ultrasonic methods, and bolt-length measurements, are effective in certain applications but require additional hardware, coupling, calibration, or joint modifications. This limits their scalability for large numbers of standard fasteners and motivates a non-contact optical approach. This paper proposes PreForceVision, a physics-guided optical framework for estimating bolt preload from preload-induced surface deformation of the bolt-head front face. The method treats preload estimation as an inverse deformation-to-force problem, where deformation of the optically accessible bolt-head surface is extracted from reference-loaded image pairs and related to the internal preload state. Preliminary results for an M16 strength class 8.8 bolt show an approximately \SI{12}{\micro\meter} simulated head-face depression at \SI{90}{\kilo\newton}, strain-gauge measurements of comparable magnitude, and an optical 3D measured central depression of approximately \SIrange{10}{20}{\micro\meter}. The contribution is a physics-guided optical methodology combining controlled image-pair acquisition, DIC- or optical-flow-based deformation extraction, multimodal validation, and uncertainty-aware regression for rough preload estimation under controlled conditions.

AI.tldr: PreForceVision estimates bolt preload without contact by measuring the surface deformation of the bolt-head face in reference-loaded image pairs, then regressing to preload. Preliminary results on an M16 class 8.8 bolt are reported under controlled conditions.
AI.motivation: Bolt preload determines how external loads are carried in a bolted joint, but existing measurement methods need extra hardware, coupling, calibration, or joint modification. These requirements limit scalability to large numbers of standard fasteners.
AI.method: The framework treats preload estimation as an inverse deformation-to-force problem. It extracts head-face deformation with DIC or optical flow from image pairs, validates against multimodal references, and uses uncertainty-aware regression to estimate preload.
AI.result: For an M16 class 8.8 bolt, the simulated head-face depression is about 12 micrometers at 90 kN, and strain-gauge measurements are of comparable magnitude. The optical 3D measured central depression is about 10 to 20 micrometers.
AI.conclusion: The work offers a non-contact, physics-guided optical method for rough preload estimation under controlled conditions. The abstract presents it as preliminary, and it still needs broader validation before general use.

title: CID: Measuring Cognitive Work Through Semantic State Change
comment: 12 pages, 1 figure, 12 equations
summary: Traditional information theory provides powerful tools for analyzing statistical properties of information but offers limited insight into meaning and semantic transformation. It has never been possible to quantify the meaning of an arbitrary piece of information. Large language models represent information as vectors embedded within high-dimensional semantic spaces, enabling meaning to be analyzed geometrically. This paper defines semantic state as the vector representation of information within a model's semantic space and defines cognitive work as the transformation between semantic states, movement through semantic space. To quantify this transformation, we introduce the Contextual Information Differential (CID), a covariance-aware metric based on Mahalanobis distance measuring semantic displacement relative to the structure of the embedding manifold. By treating meaning as a geometric property of semantic space, CID provides a practical method for measuring semantic change, cognitive transformation, and information processing. This framework establishes a foundation for analyzing cognitive processing, learning, reasoning, knowledge generation, synthetic expertise, and human/AI collaboration through implementation-independent measurement of semantic state change in both human and artificial systems.

AI.tldr: The paper defines semantic state as a model's embedding of information and cognitive work as the transformation between such states. It introduces the Contextual Information Differential (CID), a Mahalanobis-distance metric that measures semantic displacement relative to the embedding manifold.
AI.motivation: Classical information theory measures statistical properties of information but says little about meaning or semantic transformation. The abstract argues that no existing method quantifies the meaning of an arbitrary piece of information.
AI.method: The framework represents information as vectors in an LLM's high-dimensional semantic space. CID is a covariance-aware Mahalanobis-based displacement measure, so that movement is scored relative to the structure of the embedding manifold.
AI.result: The abstract reports no experiments or numerical results. It claims CID gives a practical way to measure semantic change and cognitive transformation.
AI.conclusion: The paper proposes a foundation for analyzing cognitive processing, learning, reasoning and human-AI collaboration through implementation-independent measurement of semantic state change. These applications are stated as a research agenda and are not empirically demonstrated in the abstract.

title: CoMoFlow: Controllable Protein Conformational Ensemble Generation via Explicit Collective-Mode Modeling
summary: Protein conformational ensemble generation aims to efficiently characterize the structural variations accessible to a protein beyond a single static structure. Recent flow-based methods efficiently generate conformational ensembles, but they model coordinated structural variation implicitly, which can limit ensemble fidelity and hinder direct control. To address this limitation, we propose CoMoFlow, a controllable framework for generating protein backbone conformational ensembles by explicitly modeling collective variation. CoMoFlow constructs protein-specific collective modes from the equilibrium structure, learns the distribution of their coefficients across the molecular dynamics (MD) ensemble, and uses sampled collective variations to guide SE(3) flow matching through feature conditioning and prior recentering. Experiments on ATLAS and de novo proteins show that CoMoFlow improves reconstruction of MD conformational distributions and coordinated structural variation relative to strong flow-based baselines, while enabling direct control over targeted conformational changes.

AI.tldr: CoMoFlow generates protein backbone conformational ensembles by explicitly modeling collective variation modes and using them to guide SE(3) flow matching. The method allows direct control over targeted conformational changes.
AI.motivation: Recent flow-based generators produce protein conformational ensembles, but they model coordinated structural variation only implicitly. The abstract argues that this limits ensemble fidelity and makes direct control hard.
AI.method: CoMoFlow builds protein-specific collective modes from the equilibrium structure and learns the distribution of their coefficients over the molecular dynamics ensemble. Sampled collective variations guide SE(3) flow matching through feature conditioning and prior recentering.
AI.result: On ATLAS and de novo proteins, CoMoFlow improves reconstruction of MD conformational distributions and coordinated structural variation relative to strong flow-based baselines. It also enables direct control over targeted conformational changes.
AI.conclusion: Explicit collective-mode modeling makes flow-based ensemble generation both more faithful to MD distributions and controllable. The abstract does not report quantitative margins.

title: Alignment by Confident Debate: Preference Learning from Multi-Agent Debate
comment: 53 pages, 9 Figures, 31 Tables
summary: Post-training language models for reasoning typically rely on gold answers, task-specific verifiers, or learned reward models, limiting scalability when such signals are scarce. Multi-agent debate offers a self-supervised alternative, but converting debate into reliable training supervision remains challenging: majority voting weights agreeing responses equally, lacks a principled tie-breaking rule, and is ill-defined for open-ended tasks without a canonical answer; likelihood-based scoring can conflate fluency with correctness; and homogeneous committees may reinforce correlated errors. We introduce Alignment by Confident Debate (AbCD), which converts debate traces into preference data without gold answer labels. A sampling-diverse committee debates each problem, after which final answers are clustered by task-level semantic equivalence. We use verifiable tasks (mathematical reasoning, multiple-choice quantitative QA, and executable code-generation) as a controlled test bed: their answer keys or executable checkers let us evaluate the quality of debate-derived supervision against ground truth, even though the oracle itself never uses gold labels. Post-training on the resulting preferences outperforms inference-only ensembling and debate, as well as SFT on the same traces, across five model families spanning 1B to 8B parameters and four datasets, improving consensus accuracy, with a maximum gain of $21.5_{pp}$. Ablations show that the approach transfers to a larger model and to code generation, while also revealing limitations of heterogeneous committees and agreement-based weighting. Overall, the results suggest that debate traces can yield useful preference supervision when answer equivalence is combined with confidence-weighted disagreement.

AI.tldr: Alignment by Confident Debate (AbCD) turns multi-agent debate traces into preference data without gold labels, using clustering of final answers by semantic equivalence and confidence-weighted disagreement. Post-training on these preferences improves consensus accuracy across five model families of 1B to 8B parameters.
AI.motivation: Post-training for reasoning usually needs gold answers, task verifiers, or reward models, which are scarce. Converting debate into supervision is hard because majority voting has no principled tie-break and is ill-defined for open-ended tasks, likelihood scoring conflates fluency with correctness, and homogeneous committees share correlated errors.
AI.method: A sampling-diverse committee debates each problem, and the final answers are clustered by task-level semantic equivalence. The resulting debate traces are converted into preference pairs. Verifiable tasks (math reasoning, multiple-choice quantitative QA and executable code generation) serve as a test bed, where answer keys or checkers measure the quality of the debate-derived supervision.
AI.result: Post-training on the preferences outperforms inference-only ensembling and debate, and SFT on the same traces, across five model families from 1B to 8B and four datasets. The maximum gain in consensus accuracy is 21.5 percentage points. Ablations show transfer to a larger model and to code generation, and show limitations of heterogeneous committees and agreement-based weighting.
AI.conclusion: Debate traces can yield useful preference supervision when answer equivalence is combined with confidence-weighted disagreement. The abstract presents this as a usable signal for scaling post-training when gold labels are scarce.

title: Not Your Diary, Just Your Topic: Grading the Wrong-User Control
comment: 21 pages. NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Personalized, Aligned, Long-Term Memory for AI Systems (PALM)
summary: A common test of personalization replaces a user's history with someone else's and measures the drop in accuracy. But this swap also changes the topics in the history, so the drop may reflect topic mismatch. We examine this problem with a frozen language model on LaMP-2 news categorization, using histories from similar users and synthetic histories assembled from other users' articles. The user's own history improves accuracy by 2.3 percentage points over a model trained without history. Removing history only at evaluation makes this gain appear larger, at 4.8 points. Category labels alone reproduce 86% of the accuracy gap between the user's own history and a random user's history. With synthetic histories matched on labels and text similarity, the gap falls to 0.9 points. Across two user splits and three training seeds, the advantage over a similar user's history is 3.2 points for users seen during training and 0.65 points for unseen users, where the evidence for an advantage remains inconclusive. A small movie-tagging experiment with one training seed also finds no advantage over other users' histories. These findings show why personalization should be evaluated on unseen users, with histories of similar content and a model trained without history as comparisons. We also find that adding gated cross-attention improves on a prefix-only model under our training setup; whether this holds more broadly remains open.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the usual wrong-user control for personalization confounds user identity with topic, because swapping histories also changes content. Using matched synthetic histories, most of the apparent advantage of a user's own history disappears, and the authors argue that personalization should be evaluated on unseen users.
AI.motivation: A common test of personalization replaces a user's history with another user's and measures the accuracy drop. The abstract notes that this swap also changes the topics in the history, so the drop may reflect topic mismatch rather than personal signal.
AI.method: The study uses a frozen language model on LaMP-2 news categorization, comparing the user's own history, histories of similar users, and synthetic histories built from other users' articles. Synthetic histories are matched on labels and text similarity. Two user splits and three training seeds are used, along with a small movie-tagging experiment with one seed.
AI.result: The user's own history improves accuracy by 2.3 points over a model trained without history, and removing history only at evaluation makes the gain appear as 4.8 points. Category labels alone reproduce 86 percent of the gap between the user's own history and a random user's history. With matched synthetic histories the gap falls to 0.9 points. The advantage over a similar user's history is 3.2 points for seen users and 0.65 points for unseen users, where the evidence is inconclusive. The movie-tagging experiment finds no advantage over other users' histories.
AI.conclusion: Personalization gains are largely explained by topic and label overlap in this setting, so evaluation should use unseen users, similar-content histories, and a model trained without history as comparisons. The abstract also reports that gated cross-attention beats a prefix-only model under its setup, and notes that this may not hold more broadly.

title: Attend at the Right Resolution: Head-Adaptive Sparse Attention via Query-Key Interaction Structure
summary: Attention is a major scalability bottleneck in large language models (LLMs), with its computational cost and key-value (KV) memory traffic becoming increasingly prohibitive as context length grows. Sparse attention addresses this bottleneck by restricting each query to a subset of the context, but its effectiveness hinges on identifying relevant regions both cheaply and reliably. Existing training-free methods primarily rely on runtime relevance estimates, with selection dimensionality and granularity typically governed by fixed heuristics rather than the intrinsic interaction structure of pretrained attention heads. We take a different perspective: the query-key operator of each pretrained head defines a characteristic response structure that determines the resolution needed for sparse selection, both across feature directions and across context tokens. Building on this insight, we propose Head-Adaptive Sparse Attention (HASA), a training-free sparse attention framework that jointly adapts selection resolution along these two dimensions. Along the feature dimension, the singular spectrum of each head's query-key operator determines an effective rank, yielding a compact, head-specific response space. Along the sequence dimension, neighboring regions are progressively merged according to the directional coherence of their token responses in this same space, while heterogeneous regions remain separate. Exact attention is then computed using the original full-dimensional KV states of the selected regions. HASA captures 88.1% of dense-attention mass and, compared with UNIQUE, a strong recent sparse-attention baseline, improves accuracy by up to 3.47 and 2.57 points on RULER and LongBench-Pro, respectively, and accelerates self-attention by up to 1.32x, while achieving up to 14.07x speedup over dense attention.

AI.tldr: HASA is a training-free sparse attention method that sets selection resolution per head, using the singular spectrum of each query-key operator along the feature dimension and directional coherence of token responses along the sequence dimension. It captures 88.1 percent of dense-attention mass and speeds up attention by up to 14.07x over dense attention.
AI.motivation: Attention cost and KV memory traffic grow with context length in LLMs. Existing training-free sparse methods rely on runtime relevance estimates, and their selection granularity and dimensionality follow fixed heuristics rather than the structure of pretrained attention heads.
AI.method: For each head, the effective rank of the singular spectrum of the query-key operator defines a compact response space. Neighboring context regions are merged progressively according to directional coherence of their token responses in that space, while heterogeneous regions stay separate. Exact attention is then computed on the selected regions using the original full-dimensional KV states.
AI.result: HASA captures 88.1 percent of dense-attention mass. Compared with UNIQUE, a recent sparse baseline, it improves accuracy by up to 3.47 points on RULER and 2.57 points on LongBench-Pro. It accelerates self-attention by up to 1.32x and reaches up to 14.07x speedup over dense attention.
AI.conclusion: Adapting selection resolution to each head's query-key structure yields both accuracy and speed gains over a strong sparse baseline without training. The abstract does not separate the two speedup figures by setting.

title: Intent-Aware Caching for Efficient LLM Serving
comment: NeurIPS 2026 | Code: this https URL
summary: Modern LLM serving systems use prefix caching to accelerate multi-turn conversational workloads. They cache the key-value states of previous conversation prefixes and reuse them when subsequent requests share the same prefix, to avoid redundant prefill computation and reduce serving latency. However, achieving a high cache hit rate remains challenging because cache reuse depends on whether a conversation continues and how soon the next turn arrives. Our analysis of real workloads shows that user intent is a useful signal for this behavior, as different intents exhibit different continuation probabilities and inter-turn delays. Based on this key insight, we propose Intent-Aware Caching (IAC), an online eviction policy that classifies requests by intent, learns lightweight reuse statistics from recent serving logs and leverages these statistics to guide an oracle-inspired eviction strategy. Extensive evaluation on real workloads (WildChat and ShareChat) shows that IAC reaches a 34.6% cache hit rate. This substantially outperforms both the previous learning-based approach (18.8%) and traditional methods such as least recently used (LRU, 12.2%), while reducing average serving latency by up to 46.1%.

AI.tldr: Intent-Aware Caching (IAC) is an online KV-cache eviction policy for prefix caching in multi-turn LLM serving. It classifies requests by intent and uses learned reuse statistics to guide oracle-inspired eviction, reaching a 34.6 percent cache hit rate on WildChat and ShareChat.
AI.motivation: Prefix caching reuses KV states of earlier conversation turns, but hit rates depend on whether a conversation continues and how soon the next turn arrives. The authors observe in real workloads that user intent is a useful signal, since different intents show different continuation probabilities and inter-turn delays.
AI.method: IAC classifies each request by intent and learns lightweight reuse statistics from recent serving logs. It uses these statistics to guide an oracle-inspired eviction strategy, applied online.
AI.result: On WildChat and ShareChat, IAC reaches a 34.6 percent cache hit rate. This compares with 18.8 percent for the previous learning-based approach and 12.2 percent for least recently used. Average serving latency drops by up to 46.1 percent.
AI.conclusion: Intent is a practical signal for predicting cache reuse, and using it improves hit rate and latency over both learned and classic eviction baselines. The abstract does not state the exact latency reduction for each baseline.

title: FOSCAR: Accelerating Decode Attention over 2- and 4-Bit KV Caches through Affine Folding
summary: Large-language-model decode attention streams the key-value (KV) cache for every generated token. Packing that cache into 2-bit or 4-bit quantized integers reduces memory traffic but does not automatically translate into latency saving. Existing 2-bit fused kernels reach under 31%/15% of peak HBM throughput on H100/B200. Converting each value and applying its scale and offset before feeding Tensor Cores is a major bottleneck because instruction-issue throughput is scarce on modern GPUs. Instead of applying scale and offset to each KV value, FOSCAR uses affine folding to apply them to the other operand or the output of decode-attention matrix products, depending on the quantization scheme (token-wise or channel-wise). This reduces scale-and-offset operations by up to two orders of magnitude while preserving the dequantized attention output in exact arithmetic. FOSCAR also uses bit manipulation to feed KV operands to Tensor Cores efficiently, requiring only 1 and 0.19 ALU instructions per INT2 element on H100 and B200, respectively. Finally, FOSCAR builds warp-specialized GPU pipelines for Hopper (H100) and Blackwell (B200) using wgmma and tcgen05. On H100, FOSCAR INT2 and INT4 kernels achieve geo-mean speedups of $3.36\times$ and $2.83\times$ over FlashInfer BF16, and $2.03\times$ and $1.71\times$ over TensorRT-LLM FP8. On B200, the corresponding INT2 and INT4 speedups are $2.67\times$ and $2.30\times$ over FlashInfer BF16, $1.48\times$ and $1.28\times$ over TensorRT-LLM FP8, and $1.16\times$ and $1.00\times$ over TensorRT-LLM NVFP4. We integrate FOSCAR into SGLang to benchmark serving efficiency. On long-context serving workloads, FOSCAR increases peak aggregate throughput by up to 170% and 341% over 2-bit and 16-bit baselines, respectively. We open-source FOSCAR as a kernel library at this https URL.

AI.tldr: FOSCAR is a decode-attention kernel library for 2-bit and 4-bit quantized KV caches that uses affine folding to move scale and offset operations onto the matrix product operands or output. It reports geo-mean speedups over FlashInfer BF16 and TensorRT-LLM FP8 on H100 and B200 GPUs.
AI.motivation: Packing the KV cache into 2-bit or 4-bit integers reduces memory traffic but does not automatically cut latency. Existing 2-bit fused kernels reach under 31 percent and 15 percent of peak HBM throughput on H100 and B200, and per-element dequantization limits throughput because instruction issue is scarce on modern GPUs.
AI.method: Instead of applying scale and offset to each KV value, affine folding applies them to the other operand or to the output of the decode-attention matrix products, depending on whether quantization is token-wise or channel-wise. Bit manipulation feeds INT2 operands to Tensor Cores, and warp-specialized pipelines are built with wgmma for Hopper and tcgen05 for Blackwell. FOSCAR is also integrated into SGLang for serving tests.
AI.result: On H100, the INT2 and INT4 kernels reach geo-mean speedups of 3.36x and 2.83x over FlashInfer BF16, and 2.03x and 1.71x over TensorRT-LLM FP8. On B200, INT2 and INT4 reach 2.67x and 2.30x over FlashInfer BF16, 1.48x and 1.28x over TensorRT-LLM FP8, and 1.16x and 1.00x over TensorRT-LLM NVFP4. In SGLang, peak aggregate throughput rises by up to 170 percent over 2-bit baselines and up to 341 percent over 16-bit baselines on long-context workloads.
AI.conclusion: Restructuring scale and offset application removes most per-element dequantization work and makes low-bit KV caches faster than the baselines on both GPU generations. The gains are kernel-level and serving-level results reported by the authors.

title: What to Delegate, What to Preserve: Human Preferences for Agentic AI Across Everyday Life and Work
summary: AI agents can execute multi-step tasks on users' behalf, yet the boundaries of acceptable delegation remain unclear. We report a scenario-based survey of 289 U.S. adults with prior AI experience covering 45 use cases across nine life domains. Each respondent evaluated one scenario per domain, producing repeated measures of automation preference, trust, collaboration, AI leadership, privacy concern, and willingness to pay. Automation preferences varied substantially across domains. Generalized estimating equation models showed that greater trust in the AI agent, desired AI leadership, prior task-specific AI use, and anticipated financial savings were associated with greater automation preference. In contrast, concerns that automation would reduce personal fulfillment predicted lower automation preference. Open-ended responses further revealed a preference for bounded autonomy, with participants often favoring substantial AI execution while retaining human involvement, oversight, or final authority. We argue that delegation is best understood as a configuration of execution, collaboration, leadership, and authority.

AI.tldr: A scenario-based survey of 289 U.S. adults with prior AI experience finds that preferences for delegating tasks to AI agents vary widely by life domain. Automation preference rises with trust, desired AI leadership, prior use and expected savings, and falls with concern about loss of personal fulfillment.
AI.motivation: The boundaries of acceptable delegation to multi-step AI agents remain unclear. The abstract argues that this needs measurement across everyday life and work contexts, not a single answer.
AI.method: Respondents evaluated one of 45 use cases across nine life domains, one scenario per domain, which gives repeated measures of automation preference, trust, collaboration, AI leadership, privacy concern and willingness to pay. Generalized estimating equation models analyze the associations, and open-ended responses are coded alongside them.
AI.result: Automation preferences differ substantially across domains. Greater trust, desired AI leadership, prior task-specific AI use and anticipated financial savings are associated with higher automation preference. Concern that automation reduces personal fulfillment is associated with lower preference. Open-ended answers show a preference for bounded autonomy, with substantial AI execution alongside human involvement, oversight or final authority.
AI.conclusion: The authors argue that delegation is best understood as a configuration of execution, collaboration, leadership and authority, rather than a binary choice. The sample is U.S. adults with prior AI experience, so the findings may not transfer to other populations.

title: Continuous wavelet-based feature extraction for laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy classification of human plasma samples
summary: Extracting discriminative features from laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) spectra is important for the classification of complex biological samples. This study evaluates continuous wavelet transform (CWT)-based spectral peak extraction for distinguishing human plasma samples labeled as SARS-CoV-2-positive or negative. Plasma specimens from 181 individuals, comprising 53 positive samples and 128 negative controls, were deposited as 5 {\mu}L droplets on silicon substrates and dried before analysis. Spectra were acquired using a nanosecond Nd:YAG laser operating at 1064 nm, with 100 single-shot measurements collected per specimen and averaged after intensity-based outlier rejection. CWT-based peak detection was coupled with a support vector machine (SVM) classifier. The reported leave-one-out evaluation yielded an accuracy of 93.00%, sensitivity of 94.67%, and specificity of 91.61%; these estimates remain provisional pending reconciliation with specimen-level predictions. Features identified by the CWT pipeline included emission lines assigned to Ca II, K I, and N I. The workflow provides a basis for examining spectral features associated with the studied plasma groups. Independent validation and assessment of specimen, substrate, and acquisition-related variability are required to establish generalizability and diagnostic relevance.

AI.tldr: The paper applies continuous wavelet transform peak extraction to LIBS spectra of human plasma and classifies SARS-CoV-2-positive versus negative samples with an SVM. Leave-one-out accuracy is reported as 93.00 percent, but the authors call these estimates provisional.
AI.motivation: Discriminative features from LIBS spectra are important for classifying complex biological samples. The study asks whether wavelet-based peak extraction can separate plasma from SARS-CoV-2-positive and negative individuals.
AI.method: Plasma from 181 individuals (53 positive and 128 negative) is deposited as droplets on silicon substrates and dried. Spectra are taken with a nanosecond Nd:YAG laser at 1064 nm, using 100 single-shot measurements per specimen averaged after intensity-based outlier rejection. CWT-based peak detection feeds a support vector machine classifier, evaluated by leave-one-out.
AI.result: Leave-one-out evaluation gives 93.00 percent accuracy, 94.67 percent sensitivity and 91.61 percent specificity. The CWT pipeline selects emission lines assigned to Ca II, K I and N I. The abstract states that these estimates remain provisional pending reconciliation with specimen-level predictions.
AI.conclusion: The workflow offers a basis for examining spectral features linked to the plasma groups. Independent validation and assessment of specimen, substrate and acquisition variability are needed before claims of generalizability or diagnostic relevance.

title: Assessing the Impact of Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Algorithmic Problem-Solving
summary: Competitive programming problems pose distinctive challenges for Large Language Models, as they demand not only proficient code generation but also advanced algorithmic reasoning. This study presents a Retrieval-Augmented Generation approach specifically designed to enhance the capacity of Large Language Models to address such problems. Our approach integrates an embedding-based retrieval mechanism and a similarity search algorithm to identify analogous problems within a knowledge database, employing a dynamically adjusted threshold to mitigate retrieval noise. We conducted an evaluation using the CodeContests dataset, focusing on the test split problems that exhibit similarity to instances from the training split. The experimental framework considered three conditions: (i) problems provided solely with their original descriptions, (ii) problems supplemented with randomly selected examples from the training split, and (iii) problems augmented with similar examples retrieved through the proposed method. In addition, we incorporated a Min-K membership inference analysis to examine whether the generated code solutions were influenced by potential memorization of training data within the evaluated Large Language Models. This complementary perspective enables a deeper understanding of model behavior by distinguishing genuine generalization through retrieval from implicit recall of pretraining samples. Performance was assessed using both pass rates and the CodeForces Elo rating of the problems. The results provide empirical evidence that similarity-based retrieval substantially enhances Large Language Models performance in competitive programming scenarios, offering an scalable framework for improving code generation in algorithmic problem-solving contexts.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a retrieval-augmented generation method that retrieves similar problems from a knowledge base to help LLMs solve competitive programming tasks. It is evaluated on CodeContests with a dynamic similarity threshold and a Min-K membership inference analysis for memorization.
AI.motivation: Competitive programming demands both code generation and algorithmic reasoning, which LLMs find hard. The abstract also raises the concern that generated solutions may reflect memorized training data rather than generalization.
